The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire collapsed when [[Mehmed the Conqueror]] [[Fall of Constantinople|conquered Constantinople]] on 29 May 1453.<ref>{{cite web |author=Korkut Ozgen |date= 2002 |title=Mehmet II |website=Theottomans.org |access-date=3 April 2007 |url=http://www.theottomans.org/english/family/mehmet2.asp }}</ref>

== Society ==
[[File:Foro romano dal campidoglio 04.JPG|thumb|upright=0.8|The [[Roman Forum]], the political, economic, cultural, and religious centre of the city during the Republic and later Empire]]
The imperial city of Rome was the largest urban centre in the empire, with a population variously estimated from 450,000 to close to one million.{{sfnp|Duiker|Spielvogel|2001|p=[https://archive.org/details/worldhistoryto1500duik/page/149/mode/1up 149]}}<ref>{{cite journal |last=Storey |first=Glenn R. |date=December 1997 |title=The population of ancient Rome |journal=[[Antiquity (journal)|Antiquity]] |volume=71 |issue=274 |pages=966–978 |doi=10.1017/S0003598X00085859 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/BACD7DF32B0B77609CD6713B8AF88882/S0003598X00085859a.pdf/the-population-of-ancient-rome.pdf }}{{pb}}^ {{cite journal |last=Oates |first=Whitney J. |author-link=Whitney J. Oates |date=April 1934 |title=The Population of Rome |journal=Classical Philology |volume=29 |issue=2 |pages=101–116 |doi=10.1086/361701 }}</ref> Around 20% of the population under jurisdiction of ancient Rome (25–40%, depending on the standards used, in Roman Italy)<ref>{{cite book |last=Morley |first=Neville |date=1996 |title=Metropolis and Hinterland. The City of Rome and the Italian Economy 200 B.C.–A.D. 200 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |pages=174–83 |isbn=9780521560061 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-roman-studies/article/abs/n-morley-metropolis-and-hinterland-the-city-of-rome-and-the-italian-economy-200-bcad-200-cambridge-cambridge-university-press-1996-pp-xi-210-4-figs-3-maps-isbn-0521560063-3000/A4C5B8FF1683BA44367273A695B94484 }}</ref> lived in innumerable urban centres, with population of 10,000 and more and several [[military settlement]]s, a very high rate of urbanisation by pre-industrial standards. Most of those centres had a [[Forum (Roman)|forum]], temples, and other buildings similar to Rome's. The average life expectancy in the Middle Empire was about 26–28 years.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gawande |first=Atul |author-link=Atul Gawande |date=2014 |title=[[Being Mortal|Being Mortal. Illness, Medicine and what Matters in the End]] |publisher=[[Profile Books]] |page=[https://dn720006.ca.archive.org/0/items/being-mortal_202212/Being%20Mortal.pdf 32] |isbn=9781846685828 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Rossi |first=Lino |date=1981 |title=Rotocalchi di pietra. Segni e disegni dei tempi sui monumenti trionfali dell'Impero romano |language=it |publisher=Jaca Book |page=59 |isbn=9788816400719 }}</ref>

=== Law ===
{{Main|Roman law}}
The roots of the legal principles and practices of the [[Outline of ancient Rome|ancient Romans]] may be traced to the [[Law of the Twelve Tables]] promulgated in 449&nbsp;BC and to the codification of law issued by order of Emperor [[Justinian I]] around 530&nbsp;AD (see {{lang|la|[[Corpus Juris Civilis]]}}). Roman law, as preserved in Justinian's codes, continued into the [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine Roman Empire]] and formed the basis of similar codifications in continental Western Europe. Roman law continued, in a broader sense, to be applied throughout most of Europe until the end of the 17th century.

The major divisions of the law of ancient Rome, as contained within the Justinian and Theodosian law codes, consisted of {{lang|la|Jus civile}}, {{lang|la|[[Jus gentium]]}}, and {{lang|la|Jus naturale}}. The {{lang|la|Jus civile}} ('citizen law') was the body of common laws that applied to Roman citizens.{{Sfnp|Adkins|Adkins|1998|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=9JJdqJ8YGH8C&pg=PA46 46]}} The {{lang|la|[[praetores urbani]]}} ({{sg.}} {{lang|la|Praetor Urbanus}}) were the people who had jurisdiction over cases involving citizens. The {{lang|la|Jus gentium}} ('law of nations') was the body of common laws that applied to foreigners and their dealings with Roman citizens.{{r|n=DuikerSpiel2001_146|r={{harvp|Duiker|Spielvogel|2001|p=[https://archive.org/details/worldhistoryto1500duik/page/146/mode/1up 146]}}.}} The {{lang|la|[[praetores peregrini]]}} ({{sg.}} {{lang|la|Praetor Peregrinus}}) were the people who had jurisdiction over cases involving citizens and foreigners. {{lang|la|Jus naturale}} encompassed natural law, the body of laws that were considered common to all beings.

=== Class structure ===
{{Main|Social class in ancient Rome|Status in Roman legal system}}
[[File:Arringatore 04.JPG|thumb|upright=0.8|''[[The Orator]]'', c.&nbsp;100 BC, from the [[National Archaeological Museum of Florence]], Italy, an Etrusco-Roman bronze statue depicting Aule Metele (Latin: Aulus Metellus), an Etruscan man wearing a Roman [[toga]] while engaged in [[rhetoric]]; the statue features an inscription in the [[Etruscan language]]]]
Roman society is largely viewed as [[social hierarchy|hierarchical]], with [[slavery in antiquity|slaves]] ({{lang|la|servi}}) at the bottom, [[freedmen]] ({{lang|la|liberti}}) above them, and free-born citizens ({{lang|la|cives}}) at the top. Free citizens were subdivided by class. The broadest, and earliest, division was between the [[patricians]], who could trace their ancestry to one of the 100 [[patriarch]]s at the founding of the city, and the [[plebeians]], who could not. This became less important in the later Republic, as some plebeian families became wealthy and entered politics, and some patrician families fell economically. Anyone, patrician or plebeian, who could count a consul as his ancestor was a [[nobility|noble]] ({{lang|la|nobilis}}); a man who was the first of his family to hold the consulship, such as [[Gaius Marius|Marius]] or [[Cicero]], was known as a {{lang|la|[[novus homo]]}} ('new man') and ennobled his descendants. Patrician ancestry, however, still conferred considerable prestige, and many religious offices remained restricted to patricians.

A [[class division]] originally based on military service became more important. Membership of these classes was determined periodically by the [[Roman censor|censors]], according to property. The wealthiest were the Senatorial class, who dominated politics and command of the army. Next came the [[Equestrian order|equestrians]] ({{lang|la|[[equites]]}}, sometimes translated "knights"), originally those who could afford a warhorse, and who formed a powerful mercantile class. Several further classes, originally based on the military equipment their members could afford, followed, with the ''[[proletarii]]'', citizens who had no property other than their children, at the bottom. Before the reforms of Marius they were ineligible for military service and are often described as being just above freed slaves in wealth and prestige.

Voting power in the Republic depended on class. Citizens were enrolled in voting "tribes", but the tribes of the richer classes had fewer members than the poorer ones, all the {{lang|la|proletarii}} being enrolled in a single tribe. Voting was done in class order, from top down, and stopped as soon as most of the tribes had been reached, so the poorer classes were often unable to cast their votes.

[[Women in ancient Rome]] shared some basic rights with their male counterparts, but were not fully regarded as citizens and were thus not allowed to vote or take part in politics. At the same time the limited rights of women were gradually expanded (due to [[emancipation]]) and women reached freedom from {{lang|la|[[pater familias]]}}, gained property rights and even had more juridical rights than their husbands, but still no voting rights, and were absent from politics.<ref>{{cite book |last=Frost Abbott |first=Frank |author-link=Frank Frost Abbott |date=2009 |orig-date=1909 |title=Society and Politics in Ancient Rome |publisher=[[BiblioBazaar]] |page=41 }}</ref>

Allied foreign cities were often given the [[Latin Rights]], an intermediary level between full citizens and foreigners ({{lang|la|peregrini}}), which gave their citizens rights under [[Roman law]] and allowed their leading magistrates to become full Roman citizens. While there were varying degrees of Latin rights, the main division was between those {{lang|la|cum suffragio}} ('with vote'; enrolled in a [[Roman tribe#The Servian tribes|Roman tribe]] and able to take part in the {{lang|la|comitia tributa}}) and {{lang|la|sine suffragio}} ('without vote'; could not take part in Roman politics). Most of Rome's Italian allies were given full citizenship after the [[Social War (91–88&nbsp;BC)|Social War]] of 91–88&nbsp;BC, and full [[Roman citizenship]] was extended to all free-born men in the Empire by [[Caracalla]] in 212, with the exception of the {{lang|la|dediticii}}, people who had become subject to Rome through surrender in war, and freed slaves.{{efn|name=Constitutio_Antoniniana}}

=== Education ===
{{Main|Education in ancient Rome}}
[[File:Busto maschile.JPG|thumb|[[Roman portraiture]] fresco of a young man with a [[papyrus]] scroll, from [[Herculaneum]], 1st century&nbsp;AD]]

In the early Republic, there were no public schools, so boys were taught to read and write by their parents, or by educated [[List of slaves|slaves]], called {{lang|la|[[paedagogi]]}}, usually of Greek origin.{{r|n=Lecture_13|r={{cite web |author=Steven Kreis |date=11 October 2006 |title=Lecture 13: A Brief Social History of the Roman Empire |website=historyguide.org |url=http://www.historyguide.org/ancient/lecture13b.html |access-date=2 April 2007 }}}}{{Sfnp|Adkins|Adkins|1998|p=211}}{{Sfnp|Werner|1978|p=31}} The primary aim of education during this period was to train young men in agriculture, warfare, [[Culture of ancient Rome|Roman traditions]], and public affairs.{{r|Lecture_13}} Young boys learned much about civic life by accompanying their fathers to religious and political functions, including the Senate for the sons of nobles.{{Sfnp|Adkins|Adkins|1998|p=211}} The sons of nobles were apprenticed to a prominent [[political figure]] at the age of 16, and campaigned with the army from the age of 17.{{Sfnp|Adkins|Adkins|1998|p=211}} Educational practices were modified after the conquest of the Hellenistic kingdoms in the 3rd century BC and the resulting Greek influence, although Roman educational practices were still much different from Greek ones.{{Sfnp|Adkins|Adkins|1998|p=211}}{{Sfnp|Duiker|Spielvogel|2001|p=[https://archive.org/details/worldhistoryto1500duik/page/143/mode/1up 143]}} If their parents could afford it, boys and some girls at the age of 7 were sent to a private school outside the home called a {{lang|la|ludus}}, where a teacher (called a {{lang|la|litterator}} or a {{lang|la|magister ludi}}, and often of Greek origin) taught them basic reading, writing, arithmetic, and sometimes Greek, until the age of 11.{{Sfnp|Adkins|Adkins|1998|p=211}}{{Sfnp|Werner|1978|p=31}}{{r|n=LatinExcet_1998|r={{cite web |author=Ginny Lindzey |date=September 1998 |title=Roman Education |website=Latin Excet Preparation - Texas Classical Association |url=http://www.txclassics.org/exceteducation.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071225125840/http://www.txclassics.org/exceteducation.htm |archive-date=25 December 2007 |access-date=27 March 2007 }}}}

Beginning at age 12, students went to secondary schools, where the teacher (now called a {{lang|la|grammaticus}}) taught them about [[Greek literature|Greek]] and [[Roman literature]].{{Sfnp|Adkins|Adkins|1998|p=211}}{{r|LatinExcet_1998}} At the age of 16, some students went on to [[rhetoric]] school (where the teacher, usually Greek, was called a {{lang|la|rhetor}}).{{Sfnp|Adkins|Adkins|1998|p=211}}{{r|LatinExcet_1998}} Education at this level prepared students for legal careers, and required that the students memorise the laws of Rome.{{Sfnp|Adkins|Adkins|1998|p=211}}

=== Government ===
{{Main|Roman Constitution|History of the Roman Constitution}}
{{Further|History of citizenship#Roman conceptions of citizenship}}
Initially, Rome was ruled by [[Roman Kingdom|kings]], who were elected from each of Rome's major tribes in turn.{{Sfnp|Matyszak|2003|pp=16–42}} The exact nature of the king's power is uncertain. He may have held near-absolute power, or may have merely been the chief executive of the Senate and the people. In military matters, the king's authority ({{lang|la|[[Imperium]]}}) was likely absolute. He was also the head of the [[Religion in ancient Rome|state religion]]. In addition to the authority of the King, there were three administrative assemblies: the [[Roman Senate|Senate]], which acted as an advisory body for the King; the [[Comitia Curiata]], which could endorse and ratify laws suggested by the King; and the [[Roman assemblies|Comitia Calata]], which was an assembly of the priestly college that could assemble the people to bear witness to certain acts, hear proclamations, and declare the [[Festival|feast]] and holiday schedule for the next month.

[[File:Cicero Denounces Catiline in the Roman Senate by Cesare Maccari.png|thumb|upright=1.15|Representation of a sitting of the [[Roman Senate]]: [[Cicero]] attacks [[Catilina]], from a 19th-century fresco by [[Cesare Maccari]], in [[Palazzo Madama, Rome|Palazzo Madama]], home to Italy's Senate]]
The [[class struggle]]s of the Roman Republic resulted in an unusual mixture of democracy and [[oligarchy]]. The word republic comes from the Latin {{lang|la|[[res publica]]}}, which literally translates to 'public business'. [[Roman laws]] traditionally could only be passed by a vote of the Popular assembly ([[Comitia Tributa]]). Likewise, candidates for public positions had to run for election by the people. However, the [[Roman Senate]] represented an oligarchic institution, which acted as an advisory body.

In the Republic, the Senate held actual authority ({{lang|la|[[auctoritas]]}}), but no real legislative power; it was technically only an advisory council. However, as the Senators were individually very influential, it was difficult to accomplish anything against the collective will of the Senate. New senators were chosen from among the most accomplished [[patricians]] by [[Roman censor|censors]] ({{lang|la|Censura}}), who could also remove a senator from his office if he was found "morally corrupt". Later, under the reforms of the dictator [[Sulla]], [[quaestor]]s were made automatic members of the Senate, though most of his reforms did not survive.

The Republic had no fixed [[bureaucracy]], and collected taxes through the practice of [[tax farming]]. Government positions such as quaestor, [[aedile]], or [[Prefect|praefect]] were funded by the office-holder. To prevent any citizen from gaining too much power, new [[magistrate]]s were elected annually and had to share power with a colleague. For example, under normal conditions, the highest authority was held by two consuls. In an emergency, a temporary [[Roman dictator|dictator]] could be appointed. Throughout the Republic, the administrative system was revised several times to comply with new demands. In the end, it proved inefficient for controlling the ever-expanding dominion of Rome, contributing to the establishment of the [[Roman Empire]].

In the early Empire, the pretence of a republican form of government was maintained. The [[Roman emperor]] was portrayed as only a {{lang|la|[[princeps]]}}, or 'first citizen', and the Senate gained legislative power and all legal authority previously held by the popular assemblies. However, the rule of the Emperors became increasingly [[autocratic]], and the Senate was reduced to an advisory body appointed by the Emperor. The Empire did not inherit a set bureaucracy from the Republic, since the Republic did not have any permanent governmental structures apart from the Senate. The Emperor appointed assistants and advisers, but the state lacked many institutions, such as a centrally planned budget. Some historians have cited this as a significant reason for the [[decline of the Roman Empire]].

=== Military ===
{{Main|Military history of ancient Rome|Military of ancient Rome|Structural history of the Roman military|Roman army|Roman navy}}
{{Ancient Rome military sidebar}}
[[File:Altar Domitius Ahenobarbus Louvre n3bis.jpg|thumb|[[Altar of Domitius Ahenobarbus]], c.&nbsp;122&nbsp;BC; the altar shows two Roman infantrymen equipped with long {{lang|la|[[Scutum (shield)|scuta]]}} and a cavalryman with his horse. All are shown wearing [[chain mail]] armour.]]
[[File:Römerturm, Auf dem Gaulskopf.jpg|thumb|upright=0.8|Roman tower ([[Reconstruction (architecture)|reconstruction]]) at [[Upper Germanic-Rhaetian Limes|Limes]] – [[Taunus]] / Germany]]
The early [[Roman army]] ({{Circa|500&nbsp;BC|lk=no}}) was, like those of other contemporary [[city-state]]s influenced by Greek civilisation, a citizen {{lang|la|[[militia]]}} that practised [[hoplite]] tactics. It was small and organised in five classes (in parallel to the {{lang|la|[[Roman assemblies|comitia centuriata]]}}, the body of citizens organised politically), with three providing hoplites and two providing light infantry. The early Roman army was tactically limited and its stance during this period was essentially defensive.{{r|n=Keegan1993_2634|r={{harvp|Keegan|1993|pp=[https://archive.org/details/historyofwarfare00keeg/page/263 263–4]}}.}}{{r|n=Potter2004_6770|r={{harvp|Potter|2004|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=i1rQqJo_flwC&pg=PA67 67–70]}}.}}{{efn|For a discussion of hoplite tactics and their sociocultural setting, see Victor Hanson's 1989 work.<ref>{{Cite book |first=Victor Davis |last=Hanson |author-link=Victor Davis Hanson |date=1989 |title=The Western Way of War: Infantry Battle in Classical Greece |publisher=[[Alfred A. Knopf]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=I3IZwXGqXicC&pg=PA27 27 ff.] |isbn=9780394571881 }}</ref>}}

By the 3rd century&nbsp;BC, the Romans abandoned the hoplite formation in favour of a more flexible system in which smaller groups of 120 (or sometimes 60) men called '{{lang|la|[[Maniple (military unit)|maniples]]}} could manoeuvre more independently on the battlefield. Thirty maniples arranged in three lines with supporting troops constituted a [[Roman legion|legion]], totalling between 4,000 and 5,000 men.{{r|Keegan1993_2634}}{{r|Potter2004_6770}} The early Republican legion consisted of five sections: manipular heavy infantry ({{lang|la|[[hastati]]}}, {{lang|la|[[principes]]}} and {{lang|la|[[triarii]]}}), a force of light infantry ({{lang|la|[[velites]]}}), and the cavalry ({{lang|la|[[equites]]}}). With the new organisation came a new orientation toward the offensive and a much more aggressive posture toward adjoining city-states.{{r|Keegan1993_2634}}

Until the late Republican period, the typical legionary was a property-owning citizen farmer from a rural area (an {{lang|la|adsiduus}}) who served for particular (often annual) campaigns,{{Efn|Between 343 and 241&nbsp;BC, the Roman army fought in every year but five.{{sfnp|Oakley|2004|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=i1rQqJo_flwC&pg=PA27 27]}}}} and who supplied his own equipment. After 200&nbsp;BC, economic conditions in rural areas deteriorated as manpower needs increased, so that the property qualifications for compulsory service were gradually reduced. Beginning in the 3rd century&nbsp;BC, legionaries were paid a [[stipend]]. By the time of Augustus, the ideal of the citizen-soldier had been abandoned and the legions had become fully professional. At the end of the [[Final War of the Roman Republic|Civil War]], Augustus reorganised Roman military forces, discharging soldiers and disbanding legions. He retained 28 legions, distributed through the provinces of the Empire.{{efn|The historian Mackay points out that the number of legions grew to 30 by 125&nbsp;AD and 33 during the [[Severan]] period (200–235&nbsp;AD).{{sfnp|Mackay|2004|pp=[https://archive.org/details/ancientromemilit0000mack/page/249/mode/1up 249–50]}}}}

During the [[Principate]], the tactical organisation of the Army continued to evolve. The {{lang|la|auxilia}} remained independent cohorts, and legionary troops often operated as groups of cohorts rather than as full legions. A new and versatile type of unit, the {{lang|la|cohortes equitatae}}, combined cavalry and legionaries in a single formation. They could be stationed at garrisons or outposts and could fight on their own as balanced small forces or combine with similar units as a larger, legion-sized force. This increase in organizational flexibility helped ensure the long-term success of Roman military forces.{{Sfnp|Goldsworthy|1996|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=55KE-nNtTRUC&pg=PA36 36–7]}} The Emperor [[Gallienus]] (253–268&nbsp;AD) began a reorganisation that created the last military structure of the late Empire. Withdrawing some legionaries from the fixed bases on the border, Gallienus created mobile forces (the {{lang|la|[[comitatenses]]}}, or field armies) and stationed them behind and at some distance from the borders as a strategic reserve. The border troops ({{lang|la|[[limitanei]]}}) stationed at fixed bases continued to be the first line of defence. The basic units of the field army were regimental; {{lang|la|legiones}} or {{lang|la|auxilia}} for infantry and {{lang|la|[[vexillation]]es}} for cavalry. Nominal strengths may have been 1,200 men for infantry regiments and 600 for cavalry, but actual troop levels could have been much lower—800 infantry and 400 cavalry.{{Sfnp|Elton|1996|pp=89–96}} Many infantry and cavalry regiments operated in pairs under the command of a {{lang|la|[[comes]]}}. Field armies included regiments recruited from allied tribes and known as {{lang|la|[[foederati]]}}. By 400&nbsp;AD, {{lang|la|foederati}} regiments had become permanently established units of the Roman army, paid and equipped by the Empire, led by a Roman tribune and used just as Roman units were used. The Empire also used groups of barbarians to fight along with the legions as allies without integration into the field armies, under overall command of a Roman general, but led by their own officers.{{Sfnp|Elton|1996|pp=89–96}}

Military leadership evolved over the course of the history of Rome. Under the monarchy, the hoplite armies were led by the kings. During the early and middle Roman Republic, military forces were under the command of one of the two elected [[Roman consul|consuls]] for the year. During the later Republic, members of the Roman Senatorial elite, as part of the normal sequence of elected public offices known as the {{lang|la|[[cursus honorum]]}}, would have served first as {{lang|la|[[quaestor]]}} (often posted as deputies to field commanders), then as {{lang|la|[[praetor]]}}.{{sfnp|Brennan|2004|loc=pp.[https://books.google.ca/books?id=i1rQqJo_flwC&pg=PA56 56], Appendix (pp. 61-5)}}{{Sfnp|Goldsworthy|1996|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=55KE-nNtTRUC&pg=PA121 121–25]}} Following the end of a term as praetor or consul, a Senator might be appointed by the Senate as a {{lang|la|[[propraetor]]}} or {{lang|la|[[proconsul]]}} (depending on the highest office held before) to govern a foreign province. Under Augustus, whose most important political priority was to place the military under a permanent and unitary command, the Emperor was the legal commander of each legion but exercised that command through a {{lang|la|[[legatus]]}} (legate) he appointed from the Senatorial elite. In a province with a single legion, the legate commanded the legion ({{lang|la|[[legatus legionis]]}}) and served as provincial governor, while in a province with more than one legion, each legion was commanded by a legate and the legates were commanded by the provincial governor (also a legate but of higher rank).{{Sfnp|Mackay|2004|pp=[https://archive.org/details/ancientromemilit0000mack/page/245/mode/1up 245–52]}}

During the later stages of the Imperial period (beginning perhaps with [[Diocletian]]), the Augustan model was abandoned. Provincial governors were stripped of military authority, and command of the armies in a group of provinces was given to generals ({{lang|la|[[duces]]}}) appointed by the Emperor. These were no longer members of the Roman elite but men who came up through the ranks and had seen much practical soldiering. With increasing frequency, these men attempted (sometimes successfully) to usurp the positions of the Emperors. Decreased resources, increasing political chaos and civil war eventually left the Western Empire vulnerable to attack and takeover by neighbouring barbarian peoples.<ref>{{Harvp|Mackay|2004|pp=[https://archive.org/details/ancientromemilit0000mack/page/295/mode/1up 295–6]}}. Also chapters 23–24.</ref>

==== Roman navy ====
[[File:D473-birème romaine-Liv2-ch10.png|thumb|A Roman naval [[bireme]] depicted in a relief from the [[Temple of Fortuna Primigenia]] in [[Praeneste]] ([[Palestrina, Lazio|Palastrina]]),<ref>{{Cite book |last=Saddington |first=Denis B. |date=2011 |orig-date=2007 |chapter=Classes: the Evolution of the Roman Imperial Fleets |editor-last=Erdkamp |editor-first=Paul |title=A Companion to the Roman Army |page=[https://books.google.co.bw/books?id=nqdVEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA201 201–217 (Plate 12.2 on p. 204)] |publisher=[[Wiley-Blackwell]] |isbn=9781405121538 }}</ref> which was built {{Circa|120 BC}};<ref>{{cite book |last=Coarelli |first=Filippo |author-link=Filippo Coarelli |date=1987 |title=I Santuari del Lazio in età repubblicana |language=it |location=Rome |publisher=NIS-La nuova Italia Scientifica |pages=35–84 |isbn=9788843006793 }}</ref> exhibited in the Pius-Clementine Museum ([[Museo Pio-Clementino]]) in the [[Vatican Museums]].]]

Less is known about the [[Roman navy]] than the Roman army. Prior to the middle of the 3rd century&nbsp;BC, officials known as {{lang|la|duumviri navales}} commanded a fleet of twenty ships used mainly to control piracy. This fleet was given up in 278&nbsp;AD and replaced by allied forces. The [[First Punic War]] required that Rome build large fleets, and it did so largely with the assistance of and financing from allies. This reliance on allies continued to the end of the Roman Republic. The [[quinquereme]] was the main warship on both sides of the Punic Wars and remained the mainstay of Roman naval forces until replaced by the time of Caesar Augustus by lighter and more manoeuvrable vessels.{{r|n=Potter2004_7678|r={{harvp|Potter|2004|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=i1rQqJo_flwC&pg=PA76 76–8]}}.}}

As compared with a [[trireme]], the quinquereme permitted the use of a mix of experienced and inexperienced crewmen (an advantage for a primarily land-based power), and its lesser manoeuvrability permitted the Romans to adopt and perfect [[Corvus (weapon)|boarding tactics]] using a troop of about 40 marines in lieu of the [[Naval tactics in the Age of Galleys|ram]]. Ships were commanded by a {{lang|la|[[navarch]]}}, a rank equal to a centurion, who was usually not a citizen. Potter suggests that because the fleet was dominated by non-Romans, the navy was considered non-Roman and allowed to atrophy in times of peace.{{r|Potter2004_7678}}

Information suggests that by the time of the late Empire (350&nbsp;AD), the Roman navy comprised several fleets including warships and merchant vessels for transportation and supply. Warships were oared sailing galleys with three to five banks of oarsmen. Fleet bases included such ports as Ravenna, Arles, Aquilea, Misenum and the mouth of the Somme River in the West and Alexandria and Rhodes in the East. Flotillas of small river craft ({{lang|la|classes}}) were part of the {{lang|la|limitanei}} (border troops) during this period, based at fortified river harbours along the Rhine and the Danube. That prominent generals commanded both armies and fleets suggests that naval forces were treated as auxiliaries to the army and not as an independent service. The details of command structure and fleet strengths during this period are not well known, although fleets were commanded by prefects.{{Sfnp|Elton|1996|pp=99–101}}

=== Economy ===
{{Main|Roman economy|Roman agriculture|Roman commerce|Roman finance|Roman currency|Roman metallurgy}}
[[File:Pompeii - Fullonica of Veranius Hypsaeus 1 - MAN.jpg|thumb|Workers at a cloth-processing shop, in a painting from the {{lang|la|'[[fullonica]]}} of Veranius Hypsaeus in Pompeii]]
Ancient Rome commanded a vast area of land, with tremendous natural and human resources. As such, Rome's economy remained focused on [[Farming in ancient Rome|farming]] and trade. Agricultural [[free trade]] changed the Italian landscape, and by the 1st century&nbsp;BC, vast grape and [[olive]] estates had supplanted the [[yeoman]] farmers, who were unable to match the imported grain price. The annexation of Egypt, Sicily and [[Tunisia]] in North Africa provided a continuous supply of grains. In turn, [[olive oil]] and [[Ancient Rome and wine|wine]] were Italy's main exports. Two-tier [[crop rotation]] was practised, but farm productivity was low.

Industrial and manufacturing activities were small. The largest such activities were the mining and [[quarry]]ing of stones, which provided basic construction materials for the buildings of that period. In manufacturing, production was on a relatively small scale, and generally consisted of workshops and small factories that employed at most dozens of workers. However, some brick factories employed hundreds of workers.

The economy of the early Republic was largely based on [[smallholding]] and paid labour. However, foreign wars and conquests made [[slavery in antiquity|slaves]] increasingly cheap and plentiful, and by the late Republic, the economy was largely dependent on [[slave labour]] for both skilled and unskilled work. Slaves are estimated to have constituted around 20% of the Roman Empire's population at this time and 40% in the city of Rome. Only in the Roman Empire, when the conquests stopped and the prices of slaves increased, did hired labour become more economical than slave ownership.

[[File:Mercati di Traiano, 2013.jpg|thumb|left|View of [[Trajan's Market]], built by [[Apollodorus of Damascus]]]]
Although [[barter]] was used in ancient Rome, and often used in tax collection, Rome had a very developed coinage system, with brass, bronze, and precious metal coins in circulation throughout the Empire and beyond—some have even been discovered in India. Before the 3rd century&nbsp;BC, copper was traded by weight, measured in unmarked lumps, across [[central Italy]]. The original [[British coinage|copper coins]] ({{lang|la|[[As (Roman coin)|as]]}}) had a face value of one [[Pound (weight)#Origins|Roman pound]] of copper, but weighed less. Thus, Roman money's utility as a unit of exchange consistently exceeded its intrinsic value as metal. After [[Nero]] began debasing the silver [[denarius]], its [[legal tender|legal]] value was an estimated one-third greater than its intrinsic value.

Horses were expensive and other [[pack animal]]s were slower. Mass trade on the [[Roman roads]] connected military posts, where Roman markets were centered.<ref>{{Cite book |editor-last1=Sabin |editor-first1=Philip |editor-link1=Philip Sabin |editor-last2=van Wees |editor-first2=Hans |editor-link2=Hans van Wees |editor-last3=Whitby |editor-first3=Michael |author-link3=Michael Whitby |date=2007 |title=The Cambridge History of Greek and Roman Warfare |volume=II - Rome from the Late Republic to the Late Empire |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=4aX-W6AVNv8C&pg=PA231 231] |isbn=9780521782746 }}</ref> These roads were designed for wheels.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Heseltine |first=John |date=2005 |title=Roads to Rome |publisher=J. Paul Getty Museum |page=11 |isbn=9780711225527 |url=https://www.getty.edu/research/collections/component/10V0M9 }} See also [https://www.johnwheseltine.com/work#/roads-to-rome/ Project Roads to Rome] by John Heseltine.</ref> As a result, there was transport of [[Commodity (type of good)|commodities]] between Roman regions, but increased with the rise of [[Roman commerce#Sea routes|Roman maritime trade]] in the 2nd century BC. During that period, a trading vessel took less than a month to complete a trip from [[Cádiz|Gades]] to [[Alexandria]] via [[Ostia Antica|Ostia]], spanning the entire length of the [[Mediterranean]].{{Sfnp|Scarre|1995}}{{page needed|date=May 2026}} Transport by sea was around 60 times cheaper than by land, so the volume for such trips was much larger.

Some economists consider the Roman Empire a [[market economy]], similar in its degree of capitalistic practices to the 17th-century Netherlands and 18th-century England.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Temin |first=Peter |author-link=Peter Temin |date=2013 |title=The Roman Market Economy |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=KIW8fg1pS00C&pg=PA260 260] |isbn=9780691147680 }}</ref>

=== Family ===
{{Main|Family in ancient Rome}}
[[File:Galla Placidia (rechts) und ihre Kinder.jpg|thumb|A [[gold glass]] portrait of a family from [[Roman Egypt]]. The Greek inscription on the medallion may indicate either the name of the artist or the {{lang|la|[[pater familias]]}} who is absent in the portrait.{{efn|The Brescia Medallion, a [[List of gold-glass portraits|gold glass portrait]], was most likely crafted by [[History of Alexandria|Alexandrian Greek]] artisans, due to [[Ancient Greek dialects|the Egyptian dialect of the inscription]], in the 3rd century,<ref>{{cite book |last=Howells |first=Daniel Thomas |date=2015 |title=A Catalogue of the Late Antique Gold Glass in the British Museum |publisher=[[British Museum]] - Arts and Humanities Research Council |page=7 |isbn=9780861591985 |access-date=16 July 2023 |url=https://britishmuseum.iro.bl.uk/concern/books/5ca470ad-23ea-4df2-8454-7dfc8150b147 |format=PDF }}</ref> although others propend for craftmen with Alexandrian influence working in Italy; "since there is no doubt that all kind of Greek might have been written in the [Roman] metropolis, the main sequences suggest a Roman origin".<ref>{{cite book |last=Beckwith |first=John Gordon |author-link=John Beckwith (curator) |date=1979 |orig-date=1970 |title=Early Christian and Byzantine Art |edition=2nd |publisher=[[Yale University Press]] |page=[https://archive.org/details/earlychristianby0000beck/page/24/mode/2up 25] |isbn=0300052960 }}</ref>}}<ref>{{Cite web |title=La Croce di Desiderio |trans-title=Desiderius' Cross |website=Fondazione Brescia Musei |language=it |url=http://www.bresciamusei.com/nsantagiulia.asp?nm=14&t=Masterpieces%2E+Desiderius%27+Cross |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211019100706/https://www.bresciamusei.com/nsantagiulia.asp?nm=14&t=Masterpieces.+Desiderius%27+Cross |archive-date=19 October 2021 |access-date=2 October 2016 }}{{pb}}^ {{cite book |editor-last=Boardman |editor-first=John |editor-link=John Boardman (art historian) |date=2001 |orig-date=1993 |title=The Oxford History of Classical Art |publisher=[[Oxford University Press|OUP]] |pages=338–40 |isbn=0192854437 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-7_pAAAAMAAJ}}{{pb}}^ {{cite book |last=Grig |first=Lucy |author-link=Lucy Grig |date=2004 |title=Portraits, Pontiffs and the Christianization of Fourth-Century Rome |series=Papers of the British School at Rome – vol. 72 |volume=72 |at=p. 207 (203–30) |publisher=[[British School at Rome|BSR]] |jstor=40311081 }}{{pb}}^ {{cite book |last=Elsner |first=Jás |author-link=Jaś Elsner |date=1998 |chapter=The Changing Nature of Roman Art and the Art-Historical Problem of Style |title=Imperial Rome and Christian Triumph: The Art of the Roman Empire A.D. 100–450, 11–18. |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |at=pp. [https://archive.org/details/imperialromechri0000elsn/page/22/mode/1up 22–3] (15–23) |isbn=0192842013 }}</ref>]]
[[File:Rilievo funerario dei vibii, fine del I secolo ac..JPG|thumb|A funerary relief with members of the {{lang|la|[[gens]]}} [[Vibia gens|Vibia]], late 1st century&nbsp;BC, [[Vatican Museums]]]]

The basic units of Roman society were households and families.{{r|DuikerSpiel2001_146}} Groups of households connected through the male line formed a family ({{lang|la|[[gens]]}}), based on blood ties, a common ancestry or [[Adoption in ancient Rome|adoption]]. During the Republic, some powerful families, or {{lang|la|[[Gens|Gentes Maiores]]}}, came to dominate political life. Families were headed by their oldest male citizen, the {{lang|la|[[pater familias]]}} (father of the family), who held lawful authority ({{lang|la|patria potestas}}, 'father's power') over wives, sons, daughters, and slaves of the household, and the family's wealth.{{r|DuikerSpiel2001_146}}

The extreme expressions of this power—the selling or killing of family members for moral or civil offences, including simple disobedience—were very rarely exercised, and were forbidden in the Imperial era. A {{lang|la|pater familias}} had moral and legal duties towards all family members. Even the most despotic {{lang|la|pater familias}} was expected to consult senior members of his household and {{lang|la|gens}} over matters that affected the family's well-being and reputation. Traditionally, such matters were regarded as outside the purview of the state and its magistrates; under the emperors, they were increasingly subject to state interference and legislation.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Parkin |first1=Tim |last2=Pomeroy |first2=Arthur |date=2007 |title=Roman Social History, a Sourcebook |publisher=[[Routledge]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=1dsBzRWtoe0C&pg=PA72 72] |isbn=9780415426756 }}</ref>

Once accepted into their birth family by their fathers, children were potential heirs. They could not be lawfully given away, or sold into slavery. If parents were unable to care for their child, or if its paternity was in doubt, they could resort to [[infant exposure]] (Boswell translates this as being "offered" up to care by the gods or strangers). If a deformed or sickly newborn was patently "unfit to live", killing it was a duty of the {{lang|la|pater familias}}. A citizen father who exposed a healthy freeborn child was not punished, but automatically lost his {{lang|la|potestas}} over that child. Abandoned children were sometimes adopted; some would have been sold into slavery.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Boswell |first=John Eastburn |author-link=John Boswell |date=February 1984 |title=Expositio and Oblatio: The Abandonment of Children and the Ancient and Medieval Family |journal=American Historical Review |volume=89 |issue=1 |at=p. 12 (10-33) |doi=10.2307/1855916 |jstor=1855916 |pmid=11611460 }}</ref> Slavery was near-ubiquitous and almost universally accepted. In the early Republic, citizens in debt were allowed to sell their labour, and perhaps their sons, to their debtor in a limited form of slavery called {{lang|la|[[nexum]]}} but this was abolished in the middle Republic. Freedom was considered a natural and proper state for citizens; slaves could [[Manumission|be lawfully freed]], with consent and support of their owners, and still serve their owners' family and financial interests, as freedmen or freed women. This was the basis of the [[Patronage in ancient Rome|client-patron relationship]], one of the most important features of Rome's economy and society.{{r|n=Casson1998_101_2432|r={{harvp|Casson|1998|loc=pp. [https://books.google.ca/books?id=8UoqKfh2azIC&pg=PA10 10–11], [https://books.google.ca/books?id=8UoqKfh2azIC&pg=PA24 24–32]}}.}}

In law, a {{lang|la|pater familias}} held {{lang|la|potestas}} over his adult sons with their own households. This could give rise to legal anomalies, such as adult sons also having the status of minors. No man could be considered a {{lang|la|pater familias}}, nor could he truly hold property under law, while his own father lived.{{r|Casson1998_101_2432}}<ref>{{cite web |last=Saller |first=Richard |author-link=Richard Saller |date=2001 |title=Family Values in Ancient Rome |website=Fathom Archive |access-date=14 April 2007 |url=http://fathom.lib.uchicago.edu/1/777777121908/ }}</ref> During Rome's early history, married daughters came under the control ({{lang|la|manus}}) of their husbands' {{lang|la|pater familias}}. By the late Republic, most married women retained lawful connection to their birth family, though any children from the marriage belonged to her husband's family.{{Sfnp|Adkins|Adkins|1998|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=9JJdqJ8YGH8C&pg=PA39 39–40]}} The mother or an elderly relative often raised both boys and girls.{{sfnp|Rawson|1987|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=85Gdul_43DEC&pg=PA7 7]}} Roman moralists held that marriage and child-raising fulfilled a basic duty to family, {{lang|la|gens}}, and the state. Multiple remarriages were not uncommon. Fathers usually began seeking husbands for their daughters when these reached an age between twelve and fourteen, but most commoner-class women stayed single until their twenties, and in general seem to have been far more independent than wives of the elite. Divorce required the consent of one party, along with the return of any dowry. Both parents had power over their children during their minority and adulthood, but husbands had much less control over their wives.<ref>Frier, Bruce W., and McGinn, Thomas A. J. ''A Casebook on Roman Family Law'', Oxford University Press: American Philological Association, 2004, p. 20</ref>

Roman citizen women held a restricted form of citizenship; they could not vote but were protected by law. They ran families, could own and run businesses, own and cultivate land, write their own wills, and plead in court on their own behalf, or on behalf of others, all under dispensation of the courts and the nominal supervision of a senior male relative. Throughout the late Republican and Imperial eras, a declining birthrate among the elite, and a corresponding increase among commoners was cause of concern for many {{lang|la|gentes}}; [[Augustus]] tried to address this through state intervention, offering rewards to any woman who gave birth to three or more children, and penalising the childless. The latter was much resented, and the former had seemingly negligible results. Aristocratic women seem to have been increasingly disinclined to childbearing.<ref>{{harvp|Rawson|1987|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=85Gdul_43DEC&pg=PA30 30, 40–1]}}{{pb}}^ {{cite book |last=Galinsky |first=Karl |author-link=Karl Galinsky |date=1998 |title=Augustan Culture: An Interpretive Introduction |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=Ejwhh6cXwoQC&pg=PA130 130–2] |isbn=9780691058900}}</ref>

=== Time and dates ===
{{See also|Roman timekeeping|Roman calendar|Roman consul#Consular dating}}
Roman hours were counted ordinally from dawn to dawn. Thus, if sunrise was at 6&nbsp;am, then 6 to 7&nbsp;am was called the 'first hour'. Midday was called {{lang|la|meridies}}, and it is from this word that the terms ''am'' ({{lang|la|ante meridiem}}) and ''pm'' ({{lang|la|post meridiem}}) stem. The English word "noon" comes from {{lang|la|nona}} ('ninth (hour)'), which referred to 3&nbsp;pm in ancient Rome.{{Efn|Later in Christian liturgy, "noon" came to describe the [[Nones (liturgy)|nones]], a time of prayer originally at 3&nbsp;pm but later at midday, so "noon" became synonymous with midday.}} The Romans had clocks ({{lang|la|horologia}}), which included giant public [[sundial]]s ({{lang|la|solaria}}) and water clocks ({{lang|la|[[Water clock#Greco-Roman world|clepsydrae]]}}).

The ancient Roman week originally had eight days, which were identified by letters A to H, with the eighth day being the {{lang|la|[[nundinum]]}}, or market day, a kind of weekend when farmers sold their produce on the streets. The [[seven-day week]], introduced from the East during the early Empire, was officially adopted during the reign of [[Constantine the Great|Constantine]]. Romans [[names of the days of the week|named week days]] after celestial bodies from at least the 1st century&nbsp;AD.

The Roman year originally had ten months from Martius (March) to December, with the winter period not included in the calendar. The first four months were named after gods (Martius, Aprilis, Maius, Junius) and the others were numbered (Quintilis, Sextilis, September, October, November, and December). [[Numa Pompilius]], the second king of Rome (716–673 BC), is said to have introduced the months of January and February, both also named after gods, beginning the 12-month calendar still in use today. In 44&nbsp;BC, the month Quintilis was renamed to Julius (July) after Julius Caesar and in 8&nbsp;BC, Sextilis was renamed to Augustus (August) after Augustus.

The Romans had several ways of tracking years. One widespread way was the [[Roman consul#Consular dating|consular dating]], which identified years by the two [[Roman consul|consuls]] who ruled each year. Another way, introduced in the late 3rd century&nbsp;AD, was counting years from the {{lang|la|[[indiction|indictio]]}}, a 15-year period based on the announcement of the delivery of food and other goods to the government. Another way, less popular but more similar to present day, was {{lang|la|[[ab urbe condita]]}}, which counted years from the mythical foundation of Rome in 753&nbsp;BC.

== Culture ==
{{Main|Culture of ancient Rome}}
[[File:Seven Hills of Rome.svg|thumb|upright=1.3|The [[seven hills of Rome]]]]
Life in ancient Rome revolved around the city of Rome, located on [[Seven hills of Rome|seven hills]]. The city had a vast number of monumental structures like the [[Colosseum]], the [[Trajan's Forum]] and the [[Pantheon, Rome|Pantheon]]. It had [[Roman theatre (structure)|theatres]], [[gymnasium (ancient Greece)|gymnasiums]], marketplaces, functional sewers, [[thermae|bath complexes]] complete with libraries and shops, and fountains with fresh drinking water supplied by hundreds of miles of [[Roman aqueduct|aqueducts]]. Throughout the territory under the control of ancient Rome, residential architecture ranged from modest houses to [[Roman villa|country villas]].

In Rome, there were [[Roman Empire|imperial]] residences on [[Palatine Hill]]. The low [[plebeian]] and middle [[Equestrian order|equestrian]] classes lived in the city centre, packed into apartments, or [[Insula (building)|insulae]], which were almost like modern [[ghetto]]s. These areas, often built by upper class property owners to rent, were often centred upon [[collegia]] or [[taberna]]. These people, provided with a [[Grain supply to the city of Rome|free supply of grain]], and entertained by [[gladiator]]ial games, were enrolled as [[Patronage in ancient Rome|clients of patrons]] among the upper class [[patricians]], whose assistance they sought and whose interests they upheld.

=== Language ===
[[File:Roman Empire 180 CE.png|thumb|right|350px|The Roman Empire in 180 AD. Latin had a great influence in the western part of the empire, both as a native language and as an administrative language. In the eastern part, the Greek language was predominant.]]

{{Main|Latin}}
The native [[language]] of the Romans was [[Latin]], an [[Italic language]] the [[Latin grammar|grammar of which]] relies little on word order, conveying meaning through a system of [[affix]]es attached to [[word stem]]s.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lehmann |first1=Winfred P. |author-link1=Winfred P. Lehmann |date=2026 |last2=Slocum |first2=Jonathan |title= Latin Online: Series Introduction |website=The [[University of Texas at Austin]] - Linguistics Research Center |access-date=18 July 2026 |url=https://lrc.la.utexas.edu/eieol/latol/0 }}</ref> Its [[Latin alphabet|alphabet]] was based on the [[Old Italic alphabet|Etruscan alphabet]], which was in turn based on the [[Greek alphabet]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Calvert |first=J.B. |date=8 August 1999 |title=The Latin Alphabet |website=[[University of Denver]] |url=http://www.du.edu/~etuttle/classics/latalph.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070403040205/http://www.du.edu/~etuttle/classics/latalph.htm |archive-date=3 April 2007 }}</ref> Although surviving [[Latin literature]] consists almost entirely of [[Classical Latin]], an artificial and highly stylised and polished [[literary language]] from the 1st century&nbsp;BC, the [[spoken language]] of the Roman Empire was [[Vulgar Latin]], which significantly differed from Classical Latin in [[grammar]] and [[vocabulary]], and eventually in pronunciation.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20070810033726/http://classics.lss.wisc.edu/courses/Classical_Latin_Supplement.pdf Classical Latin Supplement]. p. 2. Retrieved 2 April 2007.</ref>{{full citation needed|date=July 2026}} Speakers of Latin could understand both until the 7th century when spoken Latin began to diverge so much that 'Classical' or 'Good Latin' had to be learned as a second language.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Herman |first=József |date=2000 |title=Vulgar Latin |translator=Roger Wright |publisher=[[Penn State University Press]] |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=RJco4ioXigYC&pg=PA109 109–14] |isbn=9780271020013 }}</ref>

While Latin remained the main written language of the Roman Empire, Greek came to be the language spoken by the well-educated elite, as most of the literature studied by Romans was written in Greek. Most of the emperors were bilingual but had a preference for Latin in the public sphere for political reasons, a practice that first started during the [[Punic wars]].{{Sfnmp|Rochette|2023|1pp=263,268|Rochette|2018|2pp=114-115,118}} In the eastern part of the Roman Empire (and later the [[Eastern Roman Empire]]), Latin was never able to replace Greek, a legacy of the [[Hellenistic period]].{{Sfnp|Rochette|2018|p=108}} Justinian would be the last emperor to use Latin in government and marks when Greek officially took over.{{Sfnmp|1a1=Adkins|1a2=Adkins|1y=1998|1p=203|2a1=Kaldellis|2y=2023|2p=289|3a1=Rochette|3y=2011|3p=562|4a1=Rochette|4y=2023|4p=283}} The expansion of the Roman Empire spread Latin throughout Europe, and Vulgar Latin evolved into many distinct [[Romance languages]].

=== Religion ===
{{Main|Religion in ancient Rome|Roman mythology|Roman temple}}
{{Further|Constantine the Great and Christianity|State church of the Roman Empire}}
[[File:Pompeii - Casa dei Vettii - Ixion.jpg|thumb|Punishment of [[Ixion]]: in the centre is [[Mercury (mythology)|Mercury]] holding the [[caduceus]] and on the right [[Juno (mythology)|Juno]] sits on her throne. Behind her [[Iris (mythology)|Iris]] stands and gestures. On the left is [[Vulcan (mythology)|Vulcan]] (blond figure) standing behind the wheel, manning it, with Ixion already tied to it. [[Nephele]] sits at Mercury's feet; a Roman fresco from the eastern wall of the [[triclinium]] in the [[House of the Vettii]], [[Pompeii]], [[Pompeian Styles|Fourth Style]] (60–79 AD).]]
Archaic [[Roman religion]], at least concerning the gods, was made up not of written narratives, but rather of complex interrelations between gods and humans.{{Sfnp|Matyszak|2003|p=24}} Unlike in [[Greek mythology]], the gods were not personified, but were vaguely defined sacred spirits called {{lang|la|[[numina]]}}. Romans also believed that every person, place or thing had its own {{lang|la|[[genius (mythology)|genius]]}}, or divine soul. During the [[Roman Republic]], Roman religion was organised under a strict system of priestly offices, which were held by men of senatorial rank. The College of Pontifices was uppermost body in this hierarchy, and its chief priest, the {{lang|la|[[Pontifex Maximus]]}}, was the head of the state religion. [[Flamen]]s took care of the cults of various gods, while [[augur]]s were trusted with taking the [[auspice]]s. The [[Rex Sacrorum|sacred king]] took on the religious responsibilities of the deposed kings. In the Roman Empire, deceased emperors who had ruled well were deified by their successors and the Senate.{{sfnp|Gibbon|1836|loc=chapter 3.1, [https://archive.org/details/historyofdecline00ingibb/page/28/mode/1up p. 28]}}<ref>{{Cite book |editor-last=Rines |editor-first=George E. |editor-link=George Edwin Rines |date=1919 |title=The Encyclopedia Americana: A Library of Universal Knowledge |publisher=Encyclopedia Americana Corporation |page=644  |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=a75PAAAAMAAJ }}</ref> and the formalised [[Imperial cult (ancient Rome)|imperial cult]] became increasingly prominent.

As contact with the [[Ancient Greece|Greeks]] increased, the old [[Roman mythology|Roman gods]] became increasingly associated with [[Greek gods]].{{Sfnp|Willis|1996|pp=166–8}} Under the Empire, the Romans absorbed the mythologies of their conquered subjects, often leading to situations in which the temples and priests of traditional Italian deities existed side by side with those of foreign gods.{{Sfnp|Willis|1996|p=166}}

Beginning with Emperor [[Nero]] in the 1st century AD, Roman official policy towards Christianity was negative, and at some point, being a Christian could be punishable by death. Under Emperor [[Diocletian]], the [[persecution of Christians]] reached its peak. However, it became an officially supported religion in the Roman state under Diocletian's successor, [[Constantine I]], with the signing of the [[Edict of Milan]] in 313, and quickly became dominant. All religions except Christianity were prohibited in 391&nbsp;AD by an edict of Emperor [[Theodosius I]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Woods |first=David |date=2 February 1999 |title=Theodosius I (379–395 AD) |website=De Imperatoribus Romanis |url=https://www.roman-emperors.sites.luc.edu/theo1.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190802133157/http://www.roman-emperors.org/theo1.htm |archive-date=2 August 2019 }}</ref>

=== Ethics and morality ===
Like many ancient cultures, concepts of ethics and morality, while sharing some commonalities with modern society, differed greatly in several important ways. Because ancient civilisations like Rome were under constant threat of attack from marauding tribes, their culture was necessarily militaristic with martial skills being a prized attribute.{{r|n=Astore_2013|r={{Cite web |last=Astore |first=William |date=2013 |title=Bread and Circuses in Rome and America |website=HuffPost |url=https://www.huffingtonpost.com/william-astore/bread-and-circuses-in-rom_b_3414248.html |access-date=11 August 2017 }}}} Whereas modern societies consider [[compassion]] a virtue, Roman society considered it a vice, a moral defect. One of the primary purposes of the gladiatorial games was to inoculate Roman citizens from this weakness.{{efn|"... where compassion was regarded as a moral defect ...".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Spielvogel |first=Jackson J. |author-link=Jackson J. Spielvogel |date=2003 |title=Western Civilization |volume=1 |edition=12th |publisher=[[McGraw Hill Education|McGraw-Hill]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=87_ImL1ryQ8C&focus=searchwithinvolume&q=defect 68] |isbn=9780536701930 }}</ref>{{pb}}^ "Gladatorial games were popular because the Romans actually believed that compassion was a vice and a weakness."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jackson |first=Michael A. |date=2004 |title=Look Back to Get Ahead: Life Lessons from History's Heroes |publisher=[[Arcade Publishing|Arcade]] |page=174 |isbn=9781559707275 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZkU9IuW1IuAC }}</ref>}}{{r|Astore_2013}} Romans instead prized virtues such as courage and conviction ({{lang|la|virtus}}), a sense of duty to one's people, moderation and avoiding excess ({{lang|la|moderatio}}), forgiveness and understanding ({{lang|la|clementia}}), fairness ({{lang|la|severitas}}), and loyalty ({{lang|la|[[pietas]]}}).<ref>{{Cite book |editor-last=Harvey |editor-first=Brian K. |date=2016 |title=Daily Life in Ancient Rome: A Sourcebook |publisher=[[Hackett Publishing Company|Hackett]] |isbn=9781585107957 |pages=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=agyhCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA21 21–8] }}</ref>

Roman society had well-established and restrictive norms related to sexuality, though as with many societies, the lion's share of the responsibilities fell on women. Women were generally expected to be monogamous having only a single husband during their life ({{lang|la|univira}}), though this was much less regarded by the elite, especially under the empire. Women were expected to be modest in public avoiding any provocative appearance and to demonstrate absolute fidelity to their husbands ({{lang|la|pudicitia}}). Wearing a veil was a common expectation to preserve modesty. Sex outside of marriage was generally frowned upon for men and women and was made illegal during the imperial period.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Langlands |first=Rebecca |author-link=Rebecca Langlands |date=2006 |title=Sexual Morality in Ancient Rome |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=GBLnttutuOMC&pg=PA3 3–20] |isbn=9780521859431 }}</ref> Nevertheless, prostitution was an accepted and regulated practice.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Dillon |first1=Matthew |last2=Garland |first2=Lynda |author2-link=Lynda Garland |date=2005 |title=Ancient Rome: From the Early Republic to the Assassination of Julius Caesar |publisher=[[Taylor & Francis]] |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=qMNL0jqhygoC&pg=PA382 382] |isbn=9780415224598 }}</ref>

Public demonstrations of death, violence, and brutality were used as a source of entertainment in Roman communities; however it was also a way to maintain social order, demonstrate power, and signify communal unity.

=== Art, music and literature ===
{{Main|Roman art|Latin literature|Music of ancient Rome|Roman sculpture|Theatre of ancient Rome|Art collection in ancient Rome}}
{{See also|Ancient Rome (painting)}}
[[File:Villa of the Mysteries (Pompeii) - frescos 02.jpg|thumb|Frescoes from the [[Villa of the Mysteries]] in [[Pompeii]], Italy, [[Roman art]]work dated to the mid-1st century BC]]
[[File:P. Fannius Synistor anagoria links.JPG|right|thumb|Woman playing a ''[[kithara]]'', from the [[Villa Boscoreale]], Italy, circa 40–30&nbsp;BC]]
Roman painting styles show [[Ancient Greece|Greek]] influences, and surviving examples are primarily [[fresco]]es used to adorn the walls and ceilings of [[Villa rustica|country villas]], though Roman literature includes mentions of paintings on wood, [[ivory]], and other materials.{{r|n=AdkinsAdkins1998_3502|r={{harvp|Adkins|Adkins|1998|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=9JJdqJ8YGH8C&pg=PA350 350–2]}}.}}<ref>{{cite web |title=Roman Painting |series=(In Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History) |website=[[Metropolitan Museum of Art|The Metropolitan Museum of Art]] - Department of Greek and Roman Art |date=October 2004 |access-date=22 April 2007 |url=http://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/ropt/hd_ropt.htm }}</ref> Several examples of Roman painting have been found at [[Pompeii]], and from these art historians divide the history of Roman painting into [[Pompeian Styles|four periods]].

The first style of Roman painting was practised from the early 2nd century BC to the early- or mid-1st century BC. It was mainly composed of imitations of [[marble]] and [[masonry]], though sometimes including depictions of mythological characters.
The second style began during the early 1st century BC and attempted to depict realistically three-dimensional architectural features and landscapes. The third style occurred during the reign of [[Augustus]] (27&nbsp;BC&nbsp;– 14&nbsp;AD), and rejected the [[Realism (visual arts)|realism]] of the second style in favour of simple ornamentation. A small architectural scene, landscape, or abstract design was placed in the centre with a [[monochrome]] background. The fourth style, which began in the 1st century AD, depicted scenes from mythology, while retaining architectural details and abstract patterns.

Portrait sculpture used youthful and classical proportions, evolving later into a mixture of realism and [[idealism]]. During the [[Antonine]] and [[Severan]] periods, ornate hair and bearding, with deep cutting and drilling, became popular. Advancements were also made in [[relief]] sculptures, usually depicting Roman victories.

[[Roman music]] was largely based on [[Music of ancient Greece|Greek music]], and played an important part in many aspects of Roman life.{{r|n=GroutPalisca1988_234|r={{Cite book |last1=Grout |first1=Donald Jay|author-link1=Donald Jay Grout |last2=Palisca |first2=Claude V. |author-link2=Claude V. Palisca |date=1988 |orig-date=1960 |title=A history of western music |edition=4th |publisher=[[W. W. Norton & Company|Norton]] |pages=[https://archive.org/details/historyofwestern0004grou/page/23/mode/1up 23-4] |isbn=9780393956276 }}}} In the [[Roman military]], musical instruments such as the {{lang|la|tuba}} (a long trumpet) or the {{lang|la|cornu}} were used to give various commands, while the {{lang|la|[[buccina]]}} (possibly a trumpet or horn) and the {{lang|la|[[lituus]]}} (probably an elongated J-shaped instrument), were used in ceremonial capacities.{{Sfnp|Adkins|Adkins|1998|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=9JJdqJ8YGH8C&pg=PA89 89]}} Music was used in the [[Roman amphitheatre]]s between fights and in the {{lang|la|[[odeon (building)|odea]]}}, and in these settings is known to have featured the {{lang|la|cornu}} and the {{lang|la|[[hydraulis]]}} (a type of water organ).{{Sfnp|Adkins|Adkins|1998|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=9JJdqJ8YGH8C&pg=PA349 349–50]}} Most religious rituals featured musical performances.{{Sfnp|Adkins|Adkins|1998|p=300}} Some music historians believe that music was used at almost all public ceremonies.{{r|GroutPalisca1988_234}}

The [[graffiti]], [[brothel]]s, paintings, and sculptures found in [[Pompeii]] and [[Herculaneum]] suggest that the Romans had a sex-saturated culture.{{Sfnp|Grant|2001|pp=[https://archive.org/details/citiesofvesuvius00gran_0/page/130/mode/1up?q=Primogenes 130–4]}}

==== Literature and libraries ====
[[Latin literature]] was, from its start, influenced heavily by Greek authors. Some of the earliest extant works are of historical [[Epic poetry|epics]] telling the early military history of Rome. As the Republic expanded, authors began to produce poetry, comedy, history, and [[tragedy]].

Ancient Rome's literary contributions are still recognised today and the works by ancient Roman authors were available in bookshops as well as in public and private libraries. Many scholars and statesmen of ancient Rome cultivated private libraries that were used both as demonstrations of knowledge and displays of wealth and power.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dix |first=T. Keith |date=1994 |title="Public Libraries" in Ancient Rome: Ideology and Reality |journal=Libraries & Culture |volume=29 |issue=3 |pages=282–296 |jstor=25542662 |issn=0894-8631 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25542662 }}</ref>

Although Julius Caesar had intended to establish public libraries to further establish Rome as a great cultural centre like Athens and Alexandria, he died before this was accomplished. Caesar's former lieutenant, [[Gaius Asinius Pollio]], took up the project and opened the first public library in Rome in the [[Atrium Libertatis]].{{sfnp|Pliny's Natural History|loc=Book XXXV.2 - The Honour Attached to Portraits p. [https://books.google.ca/books?id=9zwZAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA224 224]}} Emperors Augustus, Tiberius, [[Vespasian]], Domitian, and Trajan also founded or expanded public libraries in Rome during their reigns.<ref>{{cite EBO |short=yes |last=Foskett |first=Douglas John |author-link=Douglas John Foskett |date=15 July 2026 |title=Library - Ancient Rome |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/library/Rome }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Houston |first=George W. |date=2008 |title=Tiberius and the Libraries: Public Book Collections and Library Buildings in the Early Roman Empire |journal=Libraries & the Cultural Record |volume=43 |issue=3 |pages=247–269 |doi=10.1353/LAC.0.0032 |jstor=25549495 |s2cid=161471143 |issn=2166-3033 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25549495 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Staikos |first=Konstantinos |author-link=Konstantinos Staikos |date=25 October 2021 |title=The History of the Library in Western Civilization |volume=II - From Cicero to Hadrian: The Roman World from the Beginnings of Latin Literature to the Monumental and Private Libraries of the Empire |publisher=[[Brill Publishers|Brill]] |isbn=9789004473508 |access-date=29 November 2023 |url=https://brill.com/display/title/26053 }}</ref> These included the [[Ulpian Library]] in Trajan's Forum and libraries in the [[Temple of Apollo Palatinus]], the [[Temple of Peace, Rome|Temple of Peace]] in the Roman Forum, the [[Temple of Divus Augustus]], which was dedicated to Minerva when it was rebuilt under Emperor Domitian's orders.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hülsen |first=Christian |author-link=Christian Hülsen |date=1909 |title=The Roman forum: its history and its monuments |edition=2nd |translator=Jesse Benedict Carter |translator-link=Jesse Benedict Carter |location=Rome / New York City |publisher=Loescher & C. / Stechert & Co |page=117 |url=https://dn760004.eu.archive.org/0/items/romanforumitshis00hulsiala/romanforumitshis00hulsiala.pdf }}</ref> By the fall of the Western Roman Empire, the city of Rome had more than two dozen public libraries.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Boyd |first=Clarence E. |date=2008 |orig-date=1915 |title=Public Libraries and Literary Culture in Ancient Rome |publisher=[[Kessinger Publishing]] |isbn=9781437035117 }}</ref> As the Roman Empire spread, public libraries were established in other major cities and cultural centres including Ephesos, Athens, and [[Timgad]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cartwright |first=Mark |date=23 July 2019 |title=Libraries in the Ancient World |website=World History Encyclopedia |access-date=29 November 2023 |url=https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1428/libraries-in-the-ancient-world/ }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pfeiffer |first=Homer F. |date=1931 |title=The Roman Library at Timgad |journal=Memoirs of the American Academy in Rome |volume=9 |pages=157–165 |doi=10.2307/4238558 |jstor=4238558 |issn=0065-6801 |url-access=registration |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4238558 }}</ref>

=== Cuisine ===
{{Main|Ancient Roman cuisine|Ancient Rome and wine|Food and dining in the Roman Empire}}
[[File:Mosaico di un giovane come mese di giugno, III secolo dc..JPG|thumb|A boy with a platter of fruits and what may be a bucket of crabs, in a kitchen with fish and [[squid]], on the June panel from a 3rd-century mosaic depicting the months, in the [[Hermitage Museum]], [https://hermitagemuseum.org/digital-collection/973795?lng=en Antiquity Collection, room 101] in [[St Petersburg]], [[Russia]]<ref>{{cite book |last=Webster |first=James Carson |date=1938 |title=The Labors of the Months in Antique and Mediaeval Art to the End of the Twelfth Century |title-link=Labours of the Months |series=Studies in the Humanities 4 |publisher=[[Northwestern University Press]] |pages=[https://dn720407.ca.archive.org/0/items/labormonth00webs/labormonth00webs.pdf 18 ff., 122] }}</ref>]]
Ancient Roman cuisine changed over the long duration of this ancient civilisation. Dietary habits were affected by the influence of Greek culture, the political changes from [[Roman Kingdom|Kingdom]] to [[Roman Republic|Republic]] to [[Roman Empire|Empire]], and the Empire's enormous expansion, which exposed Romans to many new, provincial culinary habits and cooking techniques. In the beginning the differences between social classes were relatively small, but disparities evolved with the Empire's growth. Men and women drank wine with their meals.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Civitello |first=Linda |date=2011 |title=Cuisine and Culture: A History of Food and People |publisher=[[Wiley (publisher)|Wiley]] |isbn=9780470403716 |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=uaRl9ZUtBYkC&pg=PR9 IX] }}</ref>

The ancient Roman diet included many items that are staples of [[Italian cuisine|modern Italian cooking]]. [[Pliny the Elder]] discussed more than 30 varieties of [[olive]], 40 kinds of pear, [[Ficus|figs]] (native and imported from Africa and the eastern provinces), and a wide variety of vegetables, including carrots (of different colours, but not orange{{sfnp|Pray Bober|1999|p=[https://archive.org/details/artculturecuisin0000bobe/page/118/mode/1up?q=carrot 118]}}) as well as [[celery]], garlic, some [[flower bulb]]s, [[cabbage]] and other [[brassica]]s (such as [[kale]] and [[broccoli]]), lettuce, [[endive]], onion, [[leek]], [[asparagus]], [[radish]]es, [[turnip]]s, [[parsnip]]s, [[beet]]s, [[green peas]], [[chard]], [[cardoon]]s, olives, and [[cucumber]].{{r|n=Faas2005_209|r={{cite book |last=Faas |first=Patrick |date=2005 |orig-date=1994 |title=Around the Roman Table: Food and Feasting in Ancient Rome |translator=Shaun Whiteside |publisher=[[University of Chicago Press]] |page=209 |isbn=9780226233475 }}}}

However, some foods now considered characteristic of modern Italian cuisine were not used.{{r|n=Pray1999_187|r={{harvp|Pray Bober|1999|p=[https://archive.org/details/artculturecuisin0000bobe/page/187/mode/1up?q=capsicum 187]}}.}} In particular, [[spinach]] and [[eggplant]] (aubergine) were introduced later from the [[Arab world]], and tomatoes, potatoes, [[capsicum]] peppers, and maize (the modern source of [[polenta]]){{r|Faas2005_209}} only appeared in Europe following the discovery of the [[New World]] and the [[Columbian Exchange]].{{r|Pray1999_187}} The Romans knew of rice, but it was very rarely available to them. There were also few [[citrus]] fruits.{{sfnp|Pray Bober|1999|p=[https://archive.org/details/artculturecuisin0000bobe/page/184/mode/1up?q=Neuss 184]}}

Butcher's meat such as beef was an uncommon luxury. The most popular meat was pork, especially [[sausage]]s.<ref>{{cite book |last=Toussaint-Samat |first=Maguelonne |date=2009 |title=A History of Food |publisher=[[Wiley-Blackwell]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=QmevzbQ0AsIC&pg=PA93 93] |isbn=9781405181198 }}</ref> Fish was more common than meat, with a sophisticated [[aquaculture]] and large-scale industries devoted to [[oyster farming]]. The Romans also engaged in [[snail farming]] and oak grub farming. Some fish were greatly esteemed and fetched high prices, such as [[mullet (fish)|mullet]] raised in the fishery at [[Cosa]], and "elaborate means were invented to assure its freshness".<ref>{{cite book |last=Stambaugh |first=John E. |author-link=John E. Stambaugh |date=1988 |title=The Ancient Roman City |publisher=[[Johns Hopkins University Press|JHU Press]] |page=[https://archive.org/details/ancientromancity0000stam_j8j5/page/148/mode/1up?q=mullet 148] |isbn=0801836921 }}</ref>

Traditionally, a breakfast called {{lang|la|ientaculum}}{{sfnp|Artman|1991|p=26}} was served at dawn. At mid-day to early afternoon, Romans ate {{lang|la|[[cena]]}},{{sfnp|Artman|1991|p=26}} the main meal of the day, and at nightfall a light supper called {{lang|la|vesperna}}.{{sfnp|Artman|1991|p=26}} With the increased importation of foreign foods, the {{lang|la|cena}} grew larger in size and included a wider range of foods. Thus, it gradually shifted to the evening, while the {{lang|la|vesperna}}{{sfnp|Artman|1991|p=26}} was abandoned completely over the course of the years. The mid-day meal {{lang|la|prandium}} became a light meal to hold one over until {{lang|la|cena}}.{{sfnp|Artman|1991|p=26}}

=== Fashion ===
{{See also|Clothing in ancient Rome}}
[[File:Mosaico di cristo in trono tra gli apostoli e le ss. prudenziana e prassede, 410 dc ca. 06.jpg|thumb|upright=1.8|Detail of a [[Early Christian art and architecture|Paleochristian]] Roman mosaic from the basilica of [[Santa Pudenziana]] in Rome, c.&nbsp;410&nbsp;AD, depicting Saint [[Pudentiana]]]]

The [[toga]], a common garment during the era of Julius Caesar, was gradually abandoned by all social classes of the Empire. At the early 4th century, the toga had become just a garment worn by senators in Senate and ceremonial events. At the 4th century, the toga was replaced by the {{lang|la|[[paenula]]}} (a garment similar to a poncho) as the everyday garment of the Romans, from the lower classes to the upper classes. Another garment that was popular among the Romans in the later years of the [[Western Roman Empire]] was the {{lang|la|[[Pallium (Roman cloak)|pallium]]}}, which was mostly worn by philosophers and scholars in general. Due to external influences, mainly from the Germanic peoples, the Romans adopted [[tunic]]s very similar to those used by the Germanic peoples with whom they interacted in the final years of the Western Empire, also adopted trousers and hats like the {{lang|la|[[Pileus (hat)|pileus pannonicus]]}}. During the Late Empire, the {{lang|la|[[paludamentum]]}} (a type of military clothing) was used only by the Emperor of Rome (since the reign of Augustus, the first emperor) while the [[dalmatic]] (also used by the Christian clergy) began to spread throughout the empire.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dalmatica |language=it |website=[[Treccani|Treccani Encyclopedia Online]] |access-date=12 August 2023 |url=https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/dalmatica/ }}</ref>

=== Games and recreation ===
{{See also|History of physical training and fitness}}
[[File:Nennig Roman Villa and Mosaics - 51134391753.jpg|thumb|[[Gladiator]] combat was strictly a spectator sport. This [[Roman mosaic|mosaic]] shows combatants and referee, from the [[Roman villa|villa]] at [[Nennig]], Germany, {{Circa|2nd}}–3rd century AD.]]
[[File:Villa romana bikini girls.JPG|right|thumb|The "[[bikini]] girls" [[mosaic]], showing women playing sports, from the [[Villa Romana del Casale]], Italy, Roman province of [[Sicilia (Roman province)|Sicilia]], 4th century AD]]
The youth of Rome had several forms of athletic play and exercise. Play for boys was supposed to prepare them for active military service, such as [[jumping]], [[wrestling]], [[boxing]], and [[racing]].{{r|n=Casson1998_98108|r={{harvp|Casson|1998|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=8UoqKfh2azIC&pg=PA98 98–108]}}.}} In the countryside, pastimes for the wealthy also included fishing and hunting.<ref name="SPQR Online-1998">{{Cite web |title=Daily Life: Entertainment |website=SPQR Online |date=1998 |url=http://library.thinkquest.org/26602/entertainment.htm#leisure |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070430025620/http://library.thinkquest.org/26602/entertainment.htm |archive-date=30 April 2007 }}</ref> The Romans also had several forms of ball playing, including one resembling [[American handball|handball]].{{r|Casson1998_98108}} [[Dice game]]s, [[board game]]s, and [[gamble games]] were popular pastimes.{{r|Casson1998_98108}} For the wealthy, dinner parties presented an opportunity for entertainment, sometimes featuring music, dancing, and poetry readings.{{r|AdkinsAdkins1998_3502}} The majority, less well-off, sometimes enjoyed similar parties through clubs or associations, but for most Romans, recreational dining usually meant patronising [[tavern]]s.{{r|AdkinsAdkins1998_3502}} Children entertained themselves with toys and such games as [[leapfrog]].<ref name="SPQR Online-1998" />{{r|AdkinsAdkins1998_3502}}

Public games and spectacles were sponsored by leading Romans who wished to advertise their generosity and court popular approval; in Rome or its provinces, this usually meant the emperor or his governors. Venues in Rome and the provinces were developed specifically for public games. Rome's [[Colosseum]] was built in 70 AD under the Roman emperor Vespasian and opened in 80 AD to host other events and [[gladiator]]ial combats. Gladiators sometimes fought to the death, but more often to an adjudicated victory, usually in keeping with the mood of the watching crowd. Shows of exotic animals were popular in their own right; but sometimes animals were pitted against human beings, either armed professionals or unarmed criminals who had been condemned to public death.

[[Chariot racing]] was extremely popular among all classes. In Rome, these races were usually held at the [[Circus Maximus]], which had been purpose-built for chariot and horse-racing and, as Rome's largest public place, was also used for festivals and animal shows.<ref>{{cite web |title=Encyclopedia Romana - Circus Maximus |website=University of Chicago |access-date=19 April 2007 |url=http://penelope.uchicago.edu/~grout/encyclopaedia_romana/circusmaximus/circusmaximus.html }}</ref> It could seat around 150,000 people.<ref>{{cite book |last=Humphrey |first=John H. |date=1986  |title=Roman circuses: arenas for chariot racing |publisher=[[University of California Press]] |page=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=couetXBQO9AC&pg=PA216 216] |isbn=0520049217 }}</ref>

== Technology ==
{{Main|Ancient Roman technology}}
[[File:Pont du Gard 3.jpg|thumb|right|[[Pont du Gard]] in France is a [[Roman aqueduct]] built in c.&nbsp;19&nbsp;BC. It is a [[World Heritage Site]].]]
Ancient Rome boasted impressive technological feats, using many advancements that were lost in the [[Middle Ages]] and not rivalled again until the 19th and 20th centuries. An example of this is [[insulated glazing]], which was not invented again until the 1930s. Many practical Roman innovations were adopted from earlier Greek designs. Advancements were often divided and based on craft. [[trade (profession)|Artisans]] guarded technologies as [[trade secret]]s.{{efn|Ancient Roman laws protected against a person corrupting slaves to obtain secrets about the master's arts.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Zeidman |first=Bob |date=2011 |title=The Software IP Detective's Handbook: Measurement, Comparison, and Infringement Detection |publisher=[[Prentice Hall]] |isbn=9780137035335 |page=103 }}</ref>}}

[[Ancient Roman engineering|Roman civil engineering]] and [[Roman military engineering|military engineering]] constituted a large part of Rome's technological superiority and legacy, and contributed to the construction of hundreds of [[Roman road|roads]], [[Roman bridge|bridges]], [[Roman aqueduct|aqueducts]], [[Thermae|public baths]], [[Roman theatre (structure)|theatres]] and [[Roman amphitheatre|arenas]]. Many monuments, such as the [[Colosseum]], [[Pont du Gard]], and [[Pantheon, Rome|Pantheon]], remain as testaments to Roman engineering and culture.

The Romans were renowned for their [[Roman architecture|architecture]], which is grouped with Greek traditions into "[[Classical architecture]]". Although there were many differences from [[Greek architecture]], Rome borrowed heavily from Greece in adhering to strict, formulaic building designs and proportions. Aside from two new [[classical order|orders]] of columns, [[composite order|composite]] and [[Tuscan order|Tuscan]], and from the [[dome]], which was derived from the [[Etruscan civilization|Etruscan]] [[arch]], Rome had relatively few architectural innovations until the end of the Republic.

In the 1st century BC, Romans started to use [[Roman concrete]] widely. Concrete was [[Roman architectural revolution|invented]] in the late 3rd century BC. It was a powerful cement derived from [[pozzolana]], and soon supplanted [[marble]] as the chief Roman building material and allowed many daring architectural forms.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Winter |first=Thomas Nelson |author-link=Thomas Nelson Winter |date=1979 |title=Roman Concrete: The Ascent, Summit, and Decline of an Art |journal=Transactions of the Nebraska Academy of Sciences |volume=7 |pages=137–143 |url=http://digitalcommons.unl.edu/classicsfacpub/1}}</ref> Also in the 1st century BC, [[Vitruvius]] wrote {{lang|la|[[De architectura]]}}, possibly the first complete treatise on architecture in history.

The Romans also largely built using timber, causing a rapid decline of the woodlands surrounding Rome.
