Textiles can be [[felt]] or [[Spinning (textiles)|spun]] [[fibre|fibers]] made into [[yarn]] and subsequently [[net (textile)|netted]], looped, [[knitting|knit]] or [[weaving|woven]] to make fabrics which appeared in the Middle East during the late [[Stone Age]].<ref>[http://www.textileinstitutebooks.com/Merchant2/merchant.mv?Screen=PROD&Store_Code=TI&Product_Code=1870372557CD-ROM&Category_Code=History Creativity In The Textile Industries: A Story From Pre-History To The 21st century] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080509152332/http://www.textileinstitutebooks.com/Merchant2/merchant.mv?Screen=PROD&Store_Code=TI&Product_Code=1870372557CD-ROM&Category_Code=History |date=9 May 2008 }}. Textileinstitutebooks.com. Retrieved on 1 January 2012.</ref> From ancient times to the present day, methods of [[textile]] production have continually evolved, and the choices of textiles available have influenced how people carry their possessions, [[clothing|clothed]] themselves, and decorated their surroundings.{{sfnp|Jenkins|2003|p=1–6}}

Sources available for the study of clothing and textiles include material remains discovered via [[archaeology]];<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Andersson Strand, E., Frei, K., Gleba, M., Mannering, U., Nosch, M. and Skals, I. |date=2010 |title=Old textiles new possibilities |url=https://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/library/browse/details.xhtml?recordId=3029185&recordType=Journal |journal=Journal of European Archaeology |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=149–173 |doi=10.1177/1461957110365513 |via=Archaeological Data Service (ADS)|hdl=109.1.5/1a4d780a-d34d-4c38-a27a-b565be556c93 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> representation of textiles and their manufacture in art; and documents concerning the manufacture, acquisition, use, and trade of fabrics, tools, and finished garments. Scholarship of textile history, especially its earlier stages, is part of [[material culture]] studies.

==Prehistoric development==
{{See also|Prehistory of nakedness and clothing}}
{{Human timeline}}
[[File:Clothes 3 - Sungir - Vladimir Palaty.jpg|thumb|[[Sungir]] boy clothes reconstruction, about 30,000 years ago.]]
The development of textile and clothing in prehistory has been the subject of a number of scholarly studies since the late 20th century.<ref name=barber1992/><ref name=barber1995/> These sources have helped to provide a coherent history of these prehistoric developments. Nonetheless, scientists have never agreed on when humans began wearing clothes and the estimates suggested by various experts have ranged greatly, from 40,000 to as many as 3 million years ago.

Recent studies by Ralf Kittler, Manfred Kayser and Mark Stoneking—[[Anthropology|anthropologists]] at the [[Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology]]—have attempted to constrain the most recent date of the introduction of clothing with an indirect method relying on [[Louse|lice]]. The rationale for this method of dating stems from the fact that the human body louse (''[[Body louse|P. humanus corporus]]'') cannot live outside of clothing, dying after only a few hours without shelter. This strongly implies that the date of the body louse's speciation from its parent, the human louse (''[[Pediculus humanus]]''), can have taken place no earlier than the earliest human adoption of clothing. This date, at which the body louse  diverged from both its parent species and its sibling subspecies, the head louse (''[[Head louse|P. humanus capitus]]''), can be determined by the number of mutations each has developed during the intervening time. Such mutations occur at a known rate and the date of last-common-ancestor for two species can therefore be estimated from the difference in number of their respective mutations. These studies have produced dates ranging from 40,000 to 170,000 years ago, with a 2003 study speculating a date of 107,000 years ago, and a 2011 study confirming the most likely time of 170,000 years ago.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Priest |first=Tyler |date=26 January 2018 |title=How shall we save the planet? |journal=Science |volume=359 |issue=6374 |page=399 |doi=10.1126/science.aar2447 |bibcode=2018Sci...359..399P |s2cid=13685833 |issn=0036-8075}}</ref>

Kittler, Kayser and Stoneking suggest that the invention of clothing may have coincided with the northward migration of modern ''[[Homo sapiens]]'' away from the warm [[climate]] of [[Africa]], which is thought to have begun between 100,000 and 50,000 years ago. A second group of researchers, also relying on the genetic clock, estimate that clothing originated between 30,000 and 114,000 years ago.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Reed |display-authors=et al |year=2004 |title=Genetic Analysis of Lice Supports Direct Contact between Modern and Archaic Humans |journal=PLOS Biology |volume=2 |issue=11 |article-number=e340 |doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.0020340 |pmc=521174 |pmid=15502871 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Some of these estimates predate the first known [[History of human migration#Pre-modern migrations|human exodus from Africa]]. However, other [[Hominidae]] species, now extinct, may have also worn clothes and appear to have migrated earlier.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Toups|first1=M. A.|last2=Kitchen|first2=A.|last3=Light|first3=J. E.|last4=Reed|first4=D. L.|title=Origin of Clothing Lice Indicates Early Clothing Use by Anatomically Modern Humans in Africa|journal=Molecular Biology and Evolution|volume=28|issue=1|year=2010|pages=29–32|issn=0737-4038|doi=10.1093/molbev/msq234| pmid=20823373|pmc=3002236}}</ref> It follows that the lice which presently infest human clothing may have first been acquired by ''Homo sapiens'' in colder climates from the bodies or discarded clothing of these cousin [[Hominini|hominins]].

Dating with direct archeological evidence produces dates consistent with those hinted at by lice. In September 2021, scientists reported evidence of clothes being made from 90,000 to 120,000 years ago based on findings in deposits in [[Morocco]].<ref name="iSC-202109162">{{cite journal |author=Hallett, Emily Y. |display-authors=et al. |date=16 September 2021 |title=A worked bone assemblage from 120,000–90,000 year old deposits at Contrebandiers Cave, Atlantic Coast, Morocco |journal=[[iScience]] |volume=24 |issue=9 |article-number=102988 |bibcode=2021iSci...24j2988H |doi=10.1016/j.isci.2021.102988 |pmc=8478944 |pmid=34622180 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="TG-20210916">{{cite news |last=Davis |first=Nicola |date=16 September 2021 |title=Scientists find evidence of humans making clothes 120,000 years ago - Tools and bones in Moroccan cave could be some of earliest evidence of the hallmark human behaviour |work=[[The Guardian]] |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2021/sep/16/scientists-find-evidence-of-humans-making-clothes-120000-years-ago |url-status=live |access-date=16 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211228095707/https://www.theguardian.com/science/2021/sep/16/scientists-find-evidence-of-humans-making-clothes-120000-years-ago |archive-date=28 December 2021}}</ref> However, despite these archaeological indications and genetic evidence, there is no single estimate that is widely accepted.<ref>{{Citation |author=Ralf Kittler, Manfred Kayser & Mark Stoneking |title=Molecular evolution of ''Pediculus humanus'' and the origin of clothing |journal=[[Current Biology]] |volume=13 |issue=16 |pages=1414–1417 |year=2003 |doi=10.1016/S0960-9822(03)00507-4 |pmid=12932325 |s2cid=15277254 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2003CBio...13.1414K }}</ref><ref name="Stoneking">{{cite journal |last1=Kittler |first1=Ralf |last2=Kayser |first2=Manfred |last3=Stoneking |first3=Mark |year=2004 |title=Molecular Evolution of Pediculus humanus and the Origin of Clothing |journal=Current Biology |volume=14 |issue=24 |pages=P2309 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2004.12.024 |pmid=<!--none--> |doi-access=free|bibcode=2004CBio...14.2309K }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Toups |first1=Melissa A. |display-authors=et al |date=January 2011 |title=Origin of Clothing Lice Indicates Early Clothing Use by Anatomically Modern Humans in Africa |journal=Molecular Biology and Evolution |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=29–32 |doi=10.1093/molbev/msq234 |pmc=3002236 |pmid=20823373}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Reed |first=David |display-authors=et al. |year=2007 |title=Pair of lice lost or parasites regained: The evolutionary history of Anthropoid primate lice |journal=BMC Biology |volume=5 |issue=7 |article-number=7 |doi=10.1186/1741-7007-5-7 |pmc=1828715 |pmid=17343749 |bibcode=2007BMCB....5....7R |doi-access=free }}</ref>

[[Cave painting]]s and pictorial evidence suggest the existence of dress in the [[Paleolithic]] period, around 30,000 years ago, though these were skin [[Draped garment|drapes]]. Textile clothing came to notice around 27,000 years ago, while actual textile fragments from 7000 B.C. have been discovered by archeologists.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Tortora|first=Phyllis G.|url=https://archive.org/details/surveyofhistoric0000tort_b0e3|title=Survey of historic costume: a history of Western dress|date=1998|publisher=New York : Fairchild Publications|others=Internet Archive|isbn=978-1-56367-142-5}}</ref>{{Rp|1}}<ref>{{Cite web|title=Archive Report 2013 {{!}} Conservation And Restoration {{!}} Archaeology|url=https://www.scribd.com/document/206552281/Archive-Report-2013|access-date=16 July 2021|website=Scribd|language=en}}</ref>

===Early adoption of apparel===
[[Sewing needles]] have been dated to at least 50,000 years ago ([[Denisova Cave]], Siberia)—and are likely to have been made by ''[[homo denisovan|H. Longi]]'', about 10,000 years before the arrival of [[Neanderthal]] and [[human]] groups in the cave. The oldest possible example is 60,000 years ago, a needlepoint (missing stem and eye) found in [[Sibudu Cave]], [[South Africa]]. Other early examples of needles dating from 41,000 to 15,000 years ago are found in multiple locations, e.g. Slovenia, Russia, China, Spain, and France.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/found-the-worlds-oldest-sewing-needle|title=Found: The World's Oldest Sewing Needle|date=24 August 2016}}</ref>

The earliest dyed [[flax]] fibers have been found in a prehistoric cave in the [[Republic of Georgia]] and date back to 36,000.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2009/09/090910142352.htm |title=Archaeologists Discover Oldest-known Fiber Materials Used By Early Humans |access-date=31 December 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180101030416/https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2009/09/090910142352.htm |archive-date=1 January 2018}}</ref>

The 25,000-year-old [[Venus figurines|Venus Figurine]] "[[Venus of Lespugue]]", found in southern France in the [[Pyrenees]], depicts a cloth or twisted fiber skirt. Some other Western Europe figurines were adorned with basket hats or caps, belts were worn at the waist, and a strap of cloth wrapped around the body right above the breast. Eastern European figurines wore [[Belt (clothing)|belt]]s, hung low on the hips and sometimes string skirts. However, according to archeologists [[James M. Adovasio]], Soffer and Hyland, the garments are more likely ritual wear, real or imagined, which served as a signifier of distinct social categories.{{citation needed|date=March 2024}}

Archaeologists have discovered artifacts from later which appear to have been used in the textile arts: net gauges from 5000 B.C., spindle needles, and weaving sticks.{{citation needed|date=February 2021}}

==Ancient textiles and clothing==
{{See also|Clothing in the ancient world}}
Knowledge of ancient textiles and clothing has expanded in the recent past due to modern technological developments.<ref>[http://researchnews.osu.edu/archive/textiles.htm Forensic Photography Brings Color Back To Ancient Textiles] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070923030804/http://researchnews.osu.edu/archive/textiles.htm|date=23 September 2007}}. Researchnews.osu.edu. Retrieved on 1 January 2012.</ref> One of the earliest fabrics - after the initial use of animal-skin textiles - may have been [[felt]].<ref>
{{cite book
 |last1                = Snodgrass
 |first1               = Mary Ellen
 |author-link1         = Mary Ellen Snodgrass
 |date                 = 17 March 2015
 |orig-date            = 2014
 |chapter              = Felt
 |title                = World Clothing and Fashion: An Encyclopedia of History, Culture, and Social Influence
 |url                  = https://books.google.com/books?id=gO9nBwAAQBAJ
 |volume               = 1 - 2
 |edition              = reprint
 |publication-place    = London
 |publisher            = Routledge
 |page                 = 251
 |isbn                 = 9781317451679
 |access-date          = 8 March 2026
 |quote                = A light, flexible, matted fabric made from tangled hair, felt may be humankind's oldest clothing material. The felting process developed around 6000 B.C.E. across Asia and Europe from the layering, dampening, shrinkage, rubbing, pounding and compacting of beaver fur and sheep, goat, and camel hair into a tough and interlinking fiber. [...] Faster and less meticulous than weaving, felting produced a durable cold-weather fabric for socks and sweaterss long before the invention of knitting. The prehistoric felting process influenced Chinese, Indian, and Greek apparel, but did not extend to Africa or the Americas.
}}
</ref>
The earliest known plant-based textile from South America was discovered in [[Guitarrero Cave]] in [[Peru]]. It was woven out of [[vegetable fiber]] and dates back to 8,000 B.C.E.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Adovasio |first1=James M. |last2=Lynch |first2=Thomas F. |date=1973 |title=Preceramic Textiles and Cordage from Guitarrero Cave, Peru |journal=American Antiquity |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=84–90 |doi=10.2307/279313 |jstor=279313 |s2cid=162233999 |issn=0002-7316 | quote = It appears that twining in South America as well as North America is the basic textile technique from which most of the others are derived, and that it has a similar antiquity in both continents. Spiral interlinking and cross-knit looping are also represented in the early deposits, and there is a possibility that simple loom weaving may have a longer history in Peru than previously supposed.}}</ref> Surviving examples of [[nålebinding]], another textile method emerging after animal-skin textile usage, have been found in Israel; they date from 6500 B.C.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dupernex |first=Alison |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wmTIDwAAQBAJ&q=Nehal+Hemar+cave+textile&pg=PT17 |title=Machine Knitting: Designing with Colour |date=24 February 2020|publisher=The Crowood Press|isbn=978-1-78500-686-9|language=en}}</ref>

=== Looms ===
{{Main|Loom}}

[[File:Warp-weighted loom twill.jpg|thumb|Warp-weighted loom configured for [[twill weave]] fabric.]]
A loom is a device or machine used for weaving cloth.<ref>{{Cite web |title =Looms: 12 Types of looms and Uses you should want to know |date =June 2023 |url =https://textilementor.com/looms-12-types-of-looms-and-uses-you-want-know/}}</ref> From prehistory through the early Middle Ages, for most of Europe, the Near East and North Africa, two main types of loom dominated textile production: the [[warp-weighted loom]] and the two-beam loom. The length of the beam determined the width of the cloth woven upon the loom; it could extend to 2 to 3 meters.{{sfnp|Jenkins|2003|p=13}} Early woven clothing was often made of full loom widths draped, tied, or pinned in place.  Large-scale fabrics for clothes were most likely produced on the warp-weighted loom in Central European prehistory: this is evidenced by the numerous finds of loom weights from prehistoric settlements. Even small fragments of large textiles produced on the warp-weighted loom can be identified by their starting border.<ref>{{cite book |last1 =Grömer |first1 =Karina |title =The Art of Prehistoric Textile Making: The development of craft traditions and clothing in Central Europe |date=2016 |publisher =Naturhistorisches Museum Wien |isbn=978-3-902421-94-4 |page=92 |url =https://directory.doabooks.org/handle/20.500.12854/39554 |access-date=30 April 2025}}</ref>

=== Preservation ===
Knowledge of ancient cultures varies greatly with the climatic conditions to which archeological deposits are exposed; the Middle East, South America and the arid fringes of [[China]] have provided many very early samples in good condition, along with textile impressions in clay, and graphic portrayals. In northern [[Eurasia]], [[peat bog]]s, rock-salt mines, oak coffins, and [[permafrost]] also preserved textiles, with whole [[Neolithic]] garments surviving (some of the most famous are those associated with [[Ötzi#Clothes and shoes|Ötzi ("the Iceman")]]), along with artifacts associated with textile production.<ref>{{Cite web |date=15 January 2017 |title=Woven and twined textiles in prehistoric Europe |url=https://richlyadorned.wordpress.com/2017/01/15/woven-and-twined-textiles-in-prehistoric-europe/ |access-date=24 September 2021 |website=Richly Adorned |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last =Grömer |first =Karina |author-link=Karina Grömer |url =https://library.oapen.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.12657/32825/604250.pdf;jsessionid=37D9202E700CC21BD4B72696B268BE4E?sequence=1 |title=The Art of Prehistoric Textile Making - The development of craft traditions and clothing in Central Europe |publisher =Natural History Museum Vienna |year =2016 |isbn =978-3-902421-94-4}}</ref> Early development of textiles in the [[Indian subcontinent]], [[sub-Saharan Africa]] and other moist parts of the world remains unclear.

===Textile trade in the ancient world===

{{Main|Silk Road}}

Throughout the [[Neolithic]] and Bronze Ages, the fertile grounds of the [[Eurasian Steppe]] provided a setting for a network of nomadic communities to develop and interact. The [[Steppe Route]] has long connected regions of the Asian continent with trade and transmission of culture, including clothing.

Around 114 B.C., the [[Han dynasty]],<ref>Elisseeff, Vadime, ''The Silk Roads: Highways of Culture and Commerce'', UNESCO Publishing / Berghahn Books, 2001, {{ISBN|978-92-3-103652-1}}</ref> initiated the [[Silk Road]] trade-route. Geographically, the Silk Road or Silk Route is an interconnected series of ancient trade routes between [[Chang'an]] (present-day [[Xi'an]]) in China, [[Asia Minor]] and the Mediterranean, extending over {{convert|8000|km|mi|abbr=on}} on land and sea. Trade on the Silk Road was a significant factor{{citation needed|date=March 2026}} in the development of the great [[civilization]]s of China, Egypt, [[Mesopotamia]], [[Persia]], the Indian subcontinent, and [[Ancient Rome|Rome]], and helped to lay the foundations for the modern world. The exchange of luxury textiles was predominant on the [[Silk Road]], which linked traders, merchants, [[pilgrim]]s, [[monk]]s, soldiers, [[nomad]]s and urban dwellers from China to the [[Mediterranean Sea]] during various periods.

===Ancient Near East===
The earliest known woven textiles of the [[Near East]] may be [[flax]] fabrics used to wrap the dead; these have been excavated at [[Çatalhöyük]] in [[Anatolia]]. Found in a [[Neolithic]] grave, and "protected by several layers of clay/plaster, in an anaerobic milieu [...] They were 'baked', or 'steam cooked' ({{lang|fr|une cuisson à l'étouffée}})<!-- in  the report, this seemed to be a translated quote from field excavation notes that were originally in French. -->" in a fire. Because of the absence of flax seeds at or near the site, the textile may have been imported from the Levant.<ref>{{Cite report |title=Çatalhöyük 2013 Archive Report |url =https://www.scribd.com/document/206552281/Archive-Report-2013|pages=13–14 (pdf 17–18) |quote=The materials of the grave, protected by several layers of clay/plaster, in an anaerobic milieu, were not directly affected by the fire. They were 'baked', or 'steam cooked' (une cuisson à l'étouffée). Some organic remains were thus preserved: textile, wood, [...] Specialists were able to identify linen/flax for the first time on the site. Because seeds of flax are absent at Çatalhöyük, the hypothesis of an imported textile from the Levant is plausible yet has to be tested.}}</ref> Evidence exists of [[flax]] cultivation from {{circa|8000 BC}} in the Near East, but the breeding of sheep with a wooly [[Wool|fleece]] rather than hair occurs much later, {{circa|3000 BC}}.{{sfnp|Jenkins|2003|pp=39–47}} Well-preserved linen textiles found in the [[Cave of the Warrior]] in Judea date from around 3200 BC.

In [[Mesopotamia]], the clothing of a regular [[Sumer]]ian was very simple, especially in summer. Winter clothes were made of sheep fur. Even wealthy men were depicted with naked torsos, wearing only short skirts, known as ''[[kaunakes]]'', while women wore long dresses to their ankles. The king wore a tunic and a coat that reached to his knees, with a belt in the middle. Over time, the development of the craft of [[wool]] weaving in Mesopotamia led to a great variety in clothing. Thus, towards the end of the 3rd millennium BC and later men wore tunics with short sleeves and even over the knees, with a belt (over which the rich wore a wool cloak). Women's dresses featured more varied designs: with or without sleeves, narrow or wide, usually long and without highlighting the body<ref>{{cite book |last1=Drimba |first1=Ovidiu |title= Istoria Culturii și Civilizației |date=1985 |publisher=Editura științifică și enciclopedică |page=79 |language=ro}}</ref>

The loin-cloth has become recognizably a skirt and the twisted tufts have shrunk to a fringe<ref>{{cite book |last1 =Laver |first1=James |title=Costume and Fashion A Concise History| date=2020 |publisher=Thames & Hudson |page=14 |isbn=978-0-500-20449-8 |language=en}}</ref>

===Ancient India===
{{Main|History of clothing in India}}

Excavations of sites of the [[Indus Valley]] civilization to date have yielded a few twisted cotton threads, in the context of a connecting cord for a bead necklace.<ref>{{Cite web |title=First Evidence of cotton at Neolithic Mehrgarh, Pakistan: Analysis of Mineralized Fibres from a Copper Bead {{!}} Request PDF |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/229411804 |access-date=20 July 2020 |website=ResearchGate |language=en}}</ref> However, terracotta figurines uncovered at Mehrgarh show a male figure wearing what is commonly interpreted as a turban. A figurine from the site of [[Mohenjo-daro]], and labeled the "Priest King" depicts the wearing of a shawl with floral patterns. So far, this is the only sculpture from the Indus Valley to show clothing in such explicit detail. Other sculptures of [[Dancing Girl (prehistoric sculpture)|dancing girls]], excavated from Mohenjo-daro, only show the wearing of bangles and other jewelry.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lal |first1=Braj Basi |url=https://searchworks.stanford.edu/view/8301806 |title=How deep are the roots of Indian civilization?: archaeology answers in SearchWorks catalog |year=2009 |publisher=Aryan Books International |isbn=978-81-7305-376-4 |access-date=8 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180508123647/https://searchworks.stanford.edu/view/8301806 |archive-date=8 May 2018 |url-status=live}}</ref> However, the figurines do not provide any concrete proof to legitimize the history of clothing in the Harappan times.

[[Harappan script|Harappans]] may have used natural colors to dye their fabric. Research shows that the cultivation of indigo plants (genus: '''''[[Indigofera]]''''') was prevalent.

[[Herodotus]], an ancient Greek historian, mentions [[Indian subcontinent|Indian]] cotton in the 5th century BCE as "a wool exceeding in beauty and goodness that of sheep". When [[Alexander the Great]] invaded [[Indian campaign of Alexander the Great|India in 327 BCE]], his troops started wearing cotton clothes that were more comfortable than their previous [[wool]]en ones.<ref name=Facts>{{cite encyclopedia |title = cotton |author = Volti, Rudi |encyclopedia = The Facts On File Encyclopedia of Science, Technology, and Society |year = 1999 |url = http://www.fofweb.com/activelink2.asp?ItemID=WE49\&iPin=ffests0220}}</ref> [[Strabo]], a Greek geographer, mentioned the vividness of Indian fabrics,{{citation needed|date=March 2026}} and [[Arrian]] told of Indian–Arab trade of cotton fabrics in 130 CE.<ref name=Fabric>{{cite book |title = The Fragile Fabric of Union: Cotton, Federal Politics, and the Global Origins of the Civil War |url = https://archive.org/details/fragilefabricuni00scho |url-access = limited |author = Schoen, Brian |publisher = Johns Hopkins University Press |year = 2009 |pages = [https://archive.org/details/fragilefabricuni00scho/page/n40 26]–31 |isbn=978-0-8018-9303-2}}</ref>

===Ancient Egypt===
{{Main|Clothing in ancient Egypt}}

Evidence exists for the production of [[linen cloth]] in [[Ancient Egypt]] in the Neolithic period, {{circa |  5500 BC}}. Cultivation of domesticated wild [[flax]], probably an import from the [[Levant]], is documented as early as {{circa |  6000 BC}}. Other [[bast fiber]]s including [[Juncaceae|rush]], [[Reed (plant)|reed]], [[Palm tree|palm]], and [[papyrus]] were used alone or with [[linen]] to make rope and other textiles. Evidence for [[wool]] production in Egypt is scanty at this period, although there are examples of wool tunics from [[Greco-Roman Egypt]] in [[late antiquity]].{{sfnp|Jenkins|2003|pp =30–39}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last =Eiland |first =Murray |date =2007 |title=Late Antique Textiles from Egypt |url =https://www.academia.edu/8078335 |journal =Athena Review |volume=4 |issue=4 |pages=92–94}}</ref>

Ancient Egyptian spinning techniques included the drop spindle, hand-to-hand spinning, and rolling on the thigh; yarn was also spliced.{{sfnp|Jenkins|2003|pp=30–39}} A horizontal ground loom was used prior to the [[New Kingdom of Egypt|New Kingdom]] (16th to 11th centuries BCE), when a vertical two-beam loom was introduced, probably from Asia.

The [[Ancient Egyptian burial customs|Ancient Egyptian burial custom]] of [[mummy|mummification]] used linen bandages, and [[Art of ancient Egypt|art]] depicts Egyptian men wearing linen [[kilt]]s and women in narrow dresses with various forms of shirts and jackets, often of [[Sheer fabric|sheer]] pleated fabric.{{sfnp|Jenkins|2003|pp=30–39}}

===Ancient China===
{{Main|History of silk|Hanfu}}

The earliest known evidence of silk production in China occurs at the sites of [[Yangshao culture]] in Xia, [[Shanxi]], where a [[Cocoon (silk)|cocoon]] of [[bombyx mori]], the domesticated silkworm, cut in half by a sharp knife, dates from between 5000 and 3000 BC. Fragments of primitive looms are also seen from the sites of [[Hemudu culture]] in [[Yuyao|Yuyao, Zhejiang]], dated to about 4000 BC. Scraps of silk have been found in a [[Liangzhu culture]] site at Qianshanyang in [[Huzhou|Huzhou, Zhejiang]], dating back to 2700 BC.<ref>Tang, Chi and Miao, Liangyun, [http://203.72.198.245/web/Content.asp?ID=27524&Query=1 "Zhongguo Sichoushi" ("History of Silks in China")] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071123095921/http://203.72.198.245/web/Content.asp?ID=27524&Query=1 |date=23 November 2007 }}. ''[[Encyclopedia of China]]'', 1st ed.</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.asianart.com/textiles/intro.html |title=Textile Exhibition: Introduction |access-date=2 August 2006 |publisher=Asian art |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070908231937/http://www.asianart.com/textiles/intro.html |archive-date=8 September 2007}}</ref> Other fragments have been recovered from royal tombs of the [Shang Dynasty] ({{circa |  1600}} to {{circa | 1046 BC}}).<ref name=Meyer>{{in lang|fr}} Charles Meyer, ''Des mûriers dans le jardine du mandarin'', ''Historia'', no. 648, December 2000.</ref>

Under the Shang Dynasty, [[Han Chinese]] clothing or [[Hanfu]] consisted of a ''yi'', a narrow-cuffed, knee-length tunic tied with a sash, and a narrow, ankle-length skirt, called ''shang'', worn with a [[Bixi (clothing)|''bixi'']], a length of fabric that reached the knees. Clothing of the élite was made of silk in vivid primary colours.
