==Identity==
{{See also|Names of the Greeks|Achaeans (Homer)}}
[[File:Elephant or Hippopotamus Tooth Warrior Head Wearing Boar Tusk Helmets (3404330867).jpg|thumb|left|Warrior wearing a [[boar's tusk helmet]], from a Mycenaean chamber tomb in the [[Acropolis of Athens]], 14th–13th century BC.|256x256px]]

The [[decipherment]] of the Mycenaean [[Linear B]] script, a writing system adapted for the use of the ([[Indo-European languages|Indo-European]]) [[Mycenaean Greek|Greek language of the Late Bronze Age]],<ref>{{harvnb|Chadwick|1976|p=617}}.</ref> demonstrated the continuity of [[Greek language|Greek speech]] from the second millennium BC into the eighth century BC when a new [[Phoenician alphabet|Phoenician-derived]] [[Greek alphabet|alphabetic script]] emerged.<ref>{{harvnb|Latacz|2004|pp=159, 165, 208–209}}.</ref> Moreover, it revealed that the bearers of Mycenaean culture were ethnically connected with [[Greeks|the populations]] that resided in the Greek peninsula after the end of this cultural period.<ref>{{harvnb|Latacz|2004|pp=159, 165}}.</ref> Finally, the script records the advent of an [[Indo-European migrations|Indo-European]] language in the Aegean region in contrast to unrelated prior languages spoken in adjoining areas.<ref>{{harvnb|Beckwith|2009|p=43}}.</ref> Various collective terms for the inhabitants of Mycenaean Greece were used by Homer in his 8th-century BC epic the ''[[Iliad]]'' in reference to the [[Trojan War]].<ref name="Latacz120">{{harvnb|Latacz|2004|p=120}}.</ref>

Homer interchangeably used the [[ethnonym]]s ''Achaeans'', ''Danaans'', and ''Argives'' to refer to the besiegers,<ref name=Latacz120/> and these names appear to have passed down from the time they were in use to the time when Homer applied them as collective terms in his ''Iliad''.<ref>{{harvnb|Latacz|2004|p=138}}.</ref> There is an isolated reference to ''a-ka-wi-ja-de'' in the Linear B records in [[Knossos]], Crete dated to {{Circa|1400 BC}}, which presumably refers to a Mycenaean (Achaean) state on the Greek mainland.<ref>{{harvnb|Hajnal|Posch|2009|pp=1–2}}.</ref>

Egyptian records mention a ''T(D)-n-j'' or ''Danaya'' (''Tanaju'') land for the first time {{Circa|1437 BC}}, during the reign of [[Pharaoh]] [[Thutmoses III]] (r. 1479–1425 BC). This land is geographically defined in an inscription from the reign of [[Amenhotep III]] (r. {{Circa|1390}}–1352 BC), where a number of Danaya cities are mentioned, which cover the largest part of southern mainland Greece.<ref name="Kelder4647">{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|pp=46–47}}.</ref> Among them, cities such as Mycenae, Nauplion, and Thebes have been identified with certainty. Danaya has been equated with the [[ethnonym]] ''Danaoi'' ({{langx|el|Δαναοί}}), the name of the [[Danaoi|mythical dynasty]] that ruled in the region of Argos, also used as an ethnonym for the Greek people by Homer.<ref name="Kelder4647" /><ref>{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|pp=37–38}}; {{harvnb|Latacz|2004|p=159}}.</ref>

In the official records of another Bronze Age empire, that of the [[Hittites]] in [[Anatolia]], various references from {{Circa|1400 BC}} to 1220 BC mention a country named ''[[Ahhiyawa]]''.<ref name="BeckmanBryceCline4"/><ref>{{harvnb|Latacz|2004|p=123}}.</ref> Recent scholarship, based on textual evidence, new interpretations of the Hittite inscriptions, and recent surveys of archaeological evidence about Mycenaean–Anatolian contacts during this period, concludes that the term ''Ahhiyawa'' must have been used in reference to the Mycenaean world (land of the Achaeans), or at least to a part of it.<ref name="Bryce58">{{harvnb|Bryce|2005|p=58}}.</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Latacz|2004|p=122}}.</ref> This term may have also had broader connotations in some texts, possibly referring to all regions settled by Mycenaeans or regions under direct Mycenaean political control.<ref name="BeckmanBryceCline4">{{harvnb|Beckman|Bryce|Cline|2012|p=4}}.</ref> Another similar ethnonym, ''[[Ekwesh]],'' in twelfth century BC Egyptian inscriptions has been commonly identified with the Ahhiyawans. These Ekwesh were mentioned as a group of the [[Sea People]].<ref>{{harvnb|Bryce|2005|p=357}}.</ref>

==History==

===Early Mycenaean period and Shaft Grave era (c. 1750–1400 BC)===
[[File:Athens — Mask of Agamemnon.jpg|thumb|Death mask, known as the [[Mask of Agamemnon]], [[Grave Circle A, Mycenae|Grave Circle A]], Mycenae, 16th century BC, probably the most famous artifact of Mycenaean Greece.<ref>{{harvnb|Burns|2010|p=92: "The most famous object from Shaft Grave V, if not all of Mycenaean Greece, is the gold mask popularly known as the 'mask of Agamemnon'."}}</ref>]]

Scholars have proposed different theories on the origins of the Mycenaeans.<ref name="Lazaridis2017-Supplementary" /> According to one theory, Mycenaean civilization reflected the exogenous imposition of archaic [[Indo-European migrations|Indo-Europeans]] from the [[Eurasian steppe]] onto the pre-Mycenaean local population.<ref name="Lazaridis2017-Supplementary" /> An issue with this theory, however, is the very tenuous material and cultural relationship between Aegean and northern steppe populations during the Bronze Age.<ref name="Lazaridis2017-Supplementary" /> Another theory proposes that Mycenaean culture in Greece dates back to circa 3000 BC with Indo-European migrants entering a mainly-depopulated area; other hypotheses argue for a date as early as the seventh millennium BC (with the [[Neolithic Revolution|spread of agriculture]]) and as late as 1600 BC (with the spread of [[Chariot|chariot technology]]).<ref name="Lazaridis2017-Supplementary" /> A 2017 genetic study conducted by Lazaridis et al. found: "the Minoans and Mycenaeans were genetically similar, [but] the Mycenaeans differed from Minoans in deriving additional ancestry from an ultimate source related to the hunter–gatherers of eastern Europe and Siberia, introduced via a proximal source related to the inhabitants of either the Eurasian steppe or Armenia."<ref name="Lazaridis2017-Supplementary" /> However, Lazaridis et al. admit that their research "does not settle th[e] debate" on Mycenaean origins.<ref name="Lazaridis2017-Supplementary" /> Historian [[Bernard Sergent]] notes that archaeology alone is not able to solve the issue and that the majority of Hellenists believed Mycenaeans spoke a non-Indo-European [[Minoan language]] before [[Linear B]] was deciphered in 1952.{{Sfn|Sergent|1982|p=672}}

[[File:NAMA 1428 - Stele of Grave Circle A Mycenae.jpg|thumb|Stone stele from [[Grave Circle A, Mycenae|Grave Circle A]]|left|298x298px]]

Notwithstanding the above academic disputes, the mainstream consensus among [[Mycenology|modern Mycenologists]] is that Mycenaean civilization began around 1750 BC,<ref name=Knodell/> earlier than the Shaft Graves,<ref>{{harvnb|Wright|2008|p=230: "Scholars during much of the twentieth century CE argued for a break between the Early and Middle Bronze Ages, theorizing in particular the arrival of Indo-European speaking peoples at this time. Research in the past thirty years, though, shows that despite destruction and abandonment of some settlements after EH II and EH III, the transition between these periods shows many signs of continuity [...] Furthermore, the succeeding transition between EH III and MH I seems to have been less abrupt than previously thought, with evidence of continuity in some of the ceramics and lithic traditions at Lerna [...] Likewise, it was thought through the 1970s that the shaft graves at Mycenae announced a dramatic cultural change beginning in LH I (with some scholars even arguing that Indo-European Greek speakers arrived at this time), but this view no longer prevails. We often cannot distinguish MH III from LH I, and frequently refer to assemblages as MH III/LH I, because the society that was developing into what we commonly refer to as Mycenaean civilization had deep roots in the indigenous Middle Helladic cultural forms [...]"}}</ref> originating and evolving from the local socio-cultural landscape of the [[Helladic period|Early and Middle Bronze Age in mainland Greece]] with influences from [[Minoan civilization|Minoan Crete]].<ref name=Dickinson>{{harvnb|Dickinson|1977|pp=32, 53, 107–108}}; {{harvnb|Dickinson|1999|pp=97–107}}.</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Littauer|Crouwel|1996|loc=p. 299: "The Shaft Graves of Mycenae themselves do not mark a new dynasty imposed from outside, as Drews and other scholars would have it; nor do they represent a sudden clear break with the Middle Helladic past. The tombs indicate the rise of vigorous local chieftains who became a warrior élite."}}</ref> Towards the end of the Middle Bronze Age ({{Circa|1700}}/1675 BC),<ref name=Knodell/> a significant increase in the population and the number of settlements occurred.<ref name="Schofield31" /> A number of centers of power emerged in southern mainland Greece dominated by a warrior elite society;<ref name="Fields-2004-10" /><ref name="Dickinson" /> while the typical dwellings of that era were an early type of [[megaron]] buildings, some more complex structures are classified as forerunners of the later palaces. In a number of sites, defensive walls were also erected.<ref>{{harvnb|Schofield|2006|p=51}}.</ref>

Meanwhile, new types of burials and more imposing ones have been unearthed, which display a great variety of luxurious objects.<ref name="Schofield31" /><ref>{{harvnb|Schofield|2006|p=48}}.</ref> Among the various burial types, the [[shaft grave]] became the most common form of elite burial, a feature that gave the name to the early period of Mycenaean Greece.<ref name="Schofield31">{{harvnb|Schofield|2006|p=31}}.</ref> Among the Mycenaean elite, deceased men were usually laid to rest in gold masks and funerary armor, and women in gold crowns and clothes gleaming with gold ornaments.<ref>{{harvnb|Schofield|2006|p=32}}.</ref> The royal shaft graves next to the acropolis of Mycenae, in particular the Grave Circles [[Grave Circle A|A]] and [[Grave Circle B|B]], signified the elevation of a native Greek-speaking royal dynasty whose economic power depended on long-distance sea trade.<ref>{{harvnb|Dickinson|1977|pp=53, 107}}; {{harvnb|Littauer|Crouwel|1996|pp=297–305}}.</ref>

During this period, the Mycenaean centers witnessed increased contact with the outside world, especially with the [[Cyclades]] and the Minoan centers on the island of [[Crete]].<ref name=Fields-2004-10/><ref name=Schofield31/> Mycenaean presence appears to be also depicted in a fresco at [[Akrotiri (prehistoric city)|Akrotiri]], on [[Thera]] island, which possibly displays many warriors in [[boar's tusk helmet]]s, a feature typical of Mycenaean warfare.<ref>{{harvnb|Schofield|2006|p=67}}.</ref> In the 16th and early 15th century BC, commerce intensified, with [[Mycenaean pottery]] having been found in the southern Italian islands of [[Lipari]] and [[Vivara]], the western and southern coasts of [[Asia Minor]] (including [[Miletus]], [[Troy]], and [[Aulae (Cilicia)|Aulae]]), [[Agia Eirini, Kyrenia|Agia Eirini]] in [[Cyprus]], [[Tel Lachish]] and [[Tell el-Ajjul]] in [[Palestine (region)|Palestine]], [[Byblos]] in [[Lebanon]], and [[Saqqara]] and [[Gurob]] in [[Ancient Egypt|Egypt]].<ref>{{harvnb|Schofield|2006|pp=64–68}}: "Small quantities of Mycenaean pottery from the sixteenth century (LHI) have also been found further afield, for example to the west on the Aeolian island of Lipari and the island of Vivara opposite Naples, and to the east at Miletos on the coast of Asia Minor. Later in the Shaft Grave Era, in the first half of the fifteenth century (LHIIA), Mycenaean pottery also reached such sites as Troy and Kazanli in Asia Minor, Ayia Irini on the island of Cyprus, Lachish and Tell Ajjul in Palestine, Byblos in the Lebanon and Saqqara and Gurob in Egypt."</ref>

Early Mycenaean civilization from the Shaft Grave period generally showcases heavy influence from Minoan Crete in regards to e.g. art, infrastructure and symbols, while also maintaining some Helladic elements as well as some innovations, and some West Asian influences. A difference between Mycenaean and Minoan civilizations is complexity and monumentality; Mycenaean craftmanship and architecture are more simplified versions of Minoan ones, but are more monumental in size. Later phases of the Mycenaean civilization showcase more sophistication, eventually coming to surpass Minoan Crete after a few centuries.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Higgins |first=Reynold Alleyne |title=Minoan and Mycenaean art |date=1997 |publisher=Thames and Hudson |isbn=978-0-500-20303-3 |edition=New rev. |series=World of art |location=London}}</ref>

At the end of the Shaft Grave era, a new and more imposing type of elite burial emerged, the [[Beehive tomb#Greece|tholos]]: large circular burial chambers with high vaulted roofs and a straight entry passage lined with stone.<ref>{{harvnb|Castleden|2005|p=97}}; {{harvnb|Schofield|2006|p=55}}.</ref>

===Koine era or Palatial Bronze Age (c. 1400–1200 BC)===
[[File:La Dame de Mycènes, fresco.jpg|thumb|Fresco depicting a female figure in the acropolis of Mycenae, 13th century BC]]
Starting in the 15th century BC, the Mycenaeans began to spread their influence throughout the Aegean and Western Anatolia. By {{Circa|1450 BC}}, the palace of [[Knossos]] was ruled by a Mycenaean elite who formed a hybrid Minoan-Mycenaean culture. Mycenaeans also colonized several other Aegean islands, reaching as far as [[Rhodes]].<ref>{{harvnb|Tartaron|2013|p=28}}.</ref><ref name=Schofield7172/> The Mycenaeans became the dominant power of the region, marking the beginning of the Mycenaean 'Koine' era (from {{langx|el|Κοινή}}, common), a highly uniform culture that spread in mainland Greece and the Aegean.<ref>{{harvnb|Schofield|2006|p=75}}.</ref>

From the early 14th century BC, Mycenaean trade began to take advantage of the new commercial opportunities in the Mediterranean after the Minoan collapse.<ref name=Schofield7172>{{harvnb|Schofield|2006|pp=71–72}}.</ref> The trade routes were expanded further, reaching [[Cyprus]], [[Amman]] in the Near East, [[Apulia]] in Italy and [[Spain]].<ref name=Schofield7172/> From that time period ({{Circa|1400 BC}}), the palace of Knossos has yielded the earliest records of the Greek [[Linear B]] script, based on the previous [[Linear A]] of the Minoans. The use of the new script spread in mainland Greece and offers valuable insight into the administrative network of the palatial centers. However, the unearthed records are too fragmentary for a political reconstruction of Bronze Age Greece.<ref name="Kelder8"/>

[[File:Πανοπλία των Δέντρων 8005.jpg|thumb|upright|left|Mycenaean [[Dendra panoply|panoply]], found in Dendra, Argolid, {{circa}} 1400 BC]]

Excavations at Miletus, southwest [[Asia Minor]], indicate the existence of a Mycenaean settlement there already from {{Circa|1450 BC}}, replacing the previous Minoan installations.<ref>{{harvnb|Tartaron|2013|p=21}}.</ref> This site became a sizable and prosperous Mycenaean center until the 12th century BC.<ref>{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|pp=50, 52}}.</ref> Apart from the archaeological evidence, this is also attested in Hittite records, which indicate that Miletos (Milawata in Hittite) was the most important base for Mycenaean activity in Asia Minor.<ref name="Bryce 2005 361">{{harvnb|Bryce|2005|p=361}}.</ref> Mycenaean presence also reached the adjacent sites of [[Iasos|Iasus]] and [[Ephesus]].<ref>{{harvnb|Castleden|2005|loc=p. 194: "The Mycenaean colonies in Anatolia were emphatically confined to a narrow coastal strip in the west. There were community-colonies at Ephesus, Iasos and Miletus, but they had little effect on the interior..."}}</ref>

Meanwhile, imposing palaces were built in the main Mycenaean centers of the mainland. The earliest palace structures were megaron-type buildings, such as the Menelaion in [[Sparta]], [[Lakonia]].<ref name="Kelder107"/> Palaces proper are datable from {{Circa|1400 BC}}, when [[Cyclopean masonry|Cyclopean fortifications]] were erected at Mycenae and nearby [[Tiryns]].<ref name=Fields-2004-10/> Additional palaces were built in [[Midea (Argolid)|Midea]] and [[Pylos]] in [[Peloponnese]], [[Athens]], [[Eleusis]], [[Thebes, Greece|Thebes]] and [[Orchomenus (Boeotia)|Orchomenos]] in [[Central Greece (geographic region)|Central Greece]] and [[Iolcos]], in [[Thessaly]], the latter being the northernmost Mycenaean center. Knossos in Crete also became a Mycenaean center, where the former Minoan complex underwent a number of adjustments, including the addition of a [[Throne Room, Knossos|throne room]].<ref>{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|pp=108–109}}.</ref> These centers were based on a rigid network of bureaucracy where administrative competencies were classified into various sections and offices according to specialization of work and trades. At the head of this society was the king, known as ''[[anax|wanax]]'' (Linear B: wa-na-ka) in [[Mycenaean Greek]]. All powers were vested in him, as the main landlord and spiritual and military leader. At the same time he was an entrepreneur and trader and was aided by a network of high officials.<ref>{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|p=11}}; {{harvnb|Fields|2004|p=53}}.</ref>

====Involvement in Asia Minor====
[[File:Mycenaean_and_Mycenaeanizing_features_in_Western_Anatolia_(c._1400-1200BC).png|thumb|400x400px|Mycenaean and Mycenaeanizing features in western Anatolia, {{c.|1400–1200 BC}}]]
The presence of ''Ahhiyawa'' in western Anatolia is mentioned in various Hittite accounts from {{Circa|1400}} to {{Circa|1220 BC}}.<ref name="Bryce 2005 361"/> ''Ahhiyawa'' is generally accepted as a Hittite term for Mycenaean Greece (''Achaeans'' in Homeric Greek), but a precise geographical definition of the term cannot be drawn from the texts.<ref name="BeckmanBryceCline6"/> During this time, the kings of Ahhiyawa were evidently capable of dealing with their Hittite counterparts both on a diplomatic and military level.<ref>{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|pp=119–120}}.</ref> Moreover, Ahhiyawa achieved considerable political influence in parts of Western Anatolia, typically by encouraging anti-Hittite uprisings and collaborating with local vassal rulers.<ref>{{harvnb|Bryce|2005|p=59}}; {{harvnb|Kelder|2010|p=23}}.</ref>

In {{Circa|1400 BC}}, Hittite records mention the military activities of an Ahhiyawan warlord, [[Attarsiya]], possibly related to the mythic character of [[Atreus]]. Attarsiya attacked Hittite vassals in western Anatolia including [[Madduwatta]].<ref>{{harvnb|Bryce|2005|pp=129, 368}}.</ref> Later, in c. 1315 BC, an anti-Hittite rebellion headed by [[Arzawa]], a Hittite vassal state, received support from Ahhiyawa.<ref>{{harvnb|Bryce|2005|p=193}}.</ref> Meanwhile, Ahhiyawa appears to be in control of a number of islands in the Aegean, an impression also supported by archaeological evidence.<ref>{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|p=26}}.</ref> During the reign of the Hittite king [[Hattusili III]] (c. 1267–1237 BC), the king of Ahhiyawa is recognized as a "Great King" and of equal status with the other contemporary great Bronze Age rulers: the kings of [[New Kingdom of Egypt|Egypt]], [[Kassites|Babylonia]] and [[Middle Assyrian period#Middle Assyrian Empire 1392-1056 BC|Assyria]].<ref>{{harvnb|Bryce|2005|p=58}}; {{harvnb|Kelder|2010|pp=119–120}}.</ref> At that time, another anti-Hittite movement, led by [[Piyama-Radu]], broke out and was supported by the king of Ahhiyawa.<ref>{{harvnb|Bryce|2005|p=224}}.</ref> Piyama-Radu caused major unrest which may have extended to the region of [[Wilusa]], and later invaded the island of [[Lesbos]], which then passed into Ahhiyawan control.<ref name="Kelder27">{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|p=27}}.</ref>

Scholars have speculated that the mythic tradition of the [[Trojan War]] could have a [[Historicity of the Iliad|historical basis]] in the political turmoil of this era.<ref>{{harvnb|Bryce|2005|pp=361, 364}}.</ref> As a result of this instability, the Hittite king initiated [[Tawagalawa letter|correspondence]] in order to convince his Ahhiyawan counterpart to restore peace in the region. The Hittite record mentions a certain [[Tawagalawa]], a possible Hittite rendering of the Greek name [[Eteocles]], as brother of the king of Ahhiyawa.<ref name="Kelder27" /><ref>{{harvnb|Bryce|2005|p=290}}.</ref>

===Collapse or Postpalatial Bronze Age (c. 1200–1050 BC)===

====Initial decline and revival====
[[File:Large Krater with Armored Men Departing for Battle, Mycenae acropolis, 12th century BC (3402016857).jpg|thumb|left|Marching soldiers on the [[Warrior Vase]], {{Circa|1200 BC}}, a [[krater]] from Mycenae]]
In {{circa}} 1250 BC, the first wave of destruction apparently occurred in various centres of mainland Greece for reasons that cannot be identified by archaeologists. In [[Boeotia]], [[Thebes, Greece|Thebes]] was burned to the ground, around that year or slightly later.<ref name="Kelder 2010 34">{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|p=34}}.</ref> Nearby [[Orchomenus (Boeotia)|Orchomenos]] was not destroyed at this time but was abandoned, while the Boeotian fortifications of [[Gla]] displays evidence for a targeted destruction as only the four gates and the monumental building, called the Melathron, were burned before the site was abandoned.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Millek |first=Jesse |title=Destruction and Its Impact on Ancient Societies at the End of the Bronze Age |publisher=Lockwood Press |year=2023 |isbn=978-1-948488-84-6 |pages=74–75, 139–142}}</ref> In the Peloponnese, a number of buildings surrounding the citadel of Mycenae were attacked and burned.<ref name="Cline 2014 130">{{harvnb|Cline|2014|p=130}}.</ref>

These incidents appear to have prompted the massive strengthening and expansion of the fortifications in various sites. In some cases, arrangements were also made for the creation of subterranean passages which led to underground cisterns. Tiryns, Midea and Athens expanded their defences with new cyclopean-style walls.<ref name="Castleden219">{{harvnb|Castleden|2005|p=219}}.</ref> The extension program in Mycenae almost doubled the fortified area of the citadel. To this phase of extension belongs the impressive [[Lion Gate]], the main entrance into the Mycenaean acropolis.<ref name="Castleden219" />

It appears that after this first wave of destruction a short-lived revival of Mycenaean culture followed.<ref name="Freeman126" /> Mycenaean Greece continues to be mentioned in international affairs, particularly in Hittite records. In {{Circa|1220 BC}}, the king of Ahhiyawa is again reported to have been involved in an anti-Hittite uprising in western Anatolia.<ref name="Kelder33">{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|p=33}}.</ref> Another contemporary Hittite account reports that Ahhiyawan ships should avoid [[Middle Assyrian Empire|Assyrian]]-controlled harbors, as part of a trade embargo imposed on Assyria.<ref>{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|p=32}}.</ref> In general, in the second half of 13th century BC, trade was in decline in the Eastern Mediterranean, most probably due to the unstable political environment there.<ref>{{harvnb|Tartaron|2013|p=20}}.</ref>

====Final collapse and differing trajectories====
[[File:Invasions, destructions and possible population movements during the Bronze Age Collapse, ca. 1200 BC.png|thumb|upright=1.35|Invasions, destructions, and possible population movements during the [[Late Bronze Age collapse]], {{Circa|1200 BC}}]]
None of the defence measures appear to have prevented the final destruction and collapse of the Mycenaean states. A second destruction struck [[Mycenae]] in c. 1190 BC or shortly thereafter. This event marked the end of Mycenae as a major power. The site was then reoccupied, but on a smaller scale.<ref name="Cline 2014 130" /> A recent study suggests that neither of the palaces at Tiryns or Midea were destroyed by an earthquake,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hinzen |first1=Klaus-G. |last2=Maran |first2=Joseph |last3=Hinojosa-Prieto |first3=Hector |last4=Damm-Meinhardt |first4=Ursula |last5=Reamer |first5=Sharon K. |last6=Tzislakis |first6=Jana |last7=Kemna |first7=Kilian |last8=Schweppe |first8=Gregor |last9=Fleischer |first9=Claus |last10=Demakopoulou |first10=Katie |date=2018-03-27 |title=Reassessing the Mycenaean Earthquake Hypothesis: Results of the HERACLES Project from Tiryns and Midea, Greece |journal=Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America |volume=108 |issue=3A |pages=1046–1070 |doi=10.1785/0120170348 |bibcode=2018BuSSA.108.1046H |issn=0037-1106}}</ref> and further studies have shown that upwards of fifty arrowheads were found scattered in the destruction debris at Midea perhaps indicating that the destruction was caused by an assault.<ref>Millek 2023, pp. 147–156.</ref> The palace of [[Pylos]], in the southwestern Peloponnese, was destroyed in c. 1180 BC.<ref>{{harvnb|Cline|2014|p=129}}.</ref><ref name="Tartaron18">{{harvnb|Tartaron|2013|p=18}}.</ref> The Linear B archives found there, preserved by the heat of the fire that destroyed the palace, mention hasty defence preparations due to an imminent attack without giving any detail about the attacking force.<ref name="Freeman126">{{harvnb|Freeman|2014|p=126}}.</ref>

As a result of this turmoil, specific regions in mainland Greece witnessed a dramatic population decrease, especially Boeotia, Argolis and [[Messenia]].<ref name="Freeman126" /> Mycenaean refugees migrated to [[Cyprus]] and the [[Levant]]ine coast.<ref name="Tartaron18" /> Nevertheless, other regions on the edge of the Mycenaean world prospered, such as the [[Ionian islands]], the northwestern Peloponnese, parts of [[Attica]] and a number of Aegean islands.<ref name="Freeman126" /> The [[acropolis of Athens]], oddly, appears to have avoided destruction.<ref name="Freeman126" />

Athens and the eastern coast of Attica were still occupied in the 12th century BC, and were not destroyed or abandoned; this points to the existence of new decentralized coastal and maritime networks there. It is attested by the cemetery of Perati that lasted a century and showed imports from [[Cyclades]], [[Dodecanese]], Crete, Cyprus, Egypt and Syria, as well as by the Late Helladic IIIC ({{Circa|1210}}–1040 BC) cemetery of Drivlia at [[Porto Rafti]]; located 2&nbsp;km west of Perati. This indicates that Attica participated in long-distance trade, and was also incorporated in a mainland-looking network.<ref>{{cite web|last=Salavoura|first=Eleni|year=2021|title=New opportunities in turbulent times: Attica in the 12th c. BC|website=EAA 2021, Widening Horizons, 8–11 September, Kiel|url=https://submissions.e-a-a.org/eaa2021/repository/preview.php?Abstract=2227}}</ref>

The site of Mycenae experienced a gradual loss of political and economic status, while [[Tiryns]], also in the [[Argolid]] region, expanded its settlement and became the largest local center during the post-palatial period, in Late Helladic IIIC, c. 1200–1050 BC.<ref>{{cite web|last=Zeman|first=Piotr|year=2021|title=Differing trajectories of collapse in the Late Bronze Age Argolid: Mycenae and Tiryns from 1250 BC to 1100 BC|website=EAA 2021, Widening Horizons, 8–11 September, Kiel|url=https://submissions.e-a-a.org/eaa2021/repository/preview.php?Abstract=3840}}</ref>

====Hypotheses for the collapse====
{{See also|Late Bronze Age collapse|Dorian invasion}}[[File:14 century BC Eastern Mediterranean and the Middle East.png|thumb|upright=1.35|Eastern Mediterranean and the Middle East during the 14th century BC; Mycenaean Greece in purple]]

The reasons for the end of the Mycenaean culture have been hotly debated among scholars. At present, there is no satisfactory explanation for the collapse of the Mycenaean palace systems. The two most common theories are population movement and internal conflict. The first attributes the destruction of Mycenaean sites to invaders.<ref>{{harvnb|Mylonas|1966|pp=227–228}}.</ref>

The hypothesis of a [[Dorian invasion]], known as such in [[Ancient Greek Mythology|Ancient Greek tradition]], that led to the end of Mycenaean Greece, is supported by sporadic archaeological evidence such as new types of burials, in particular cist graves, and the use of a new dialect of Greek, the [[Doric Greek|Doric]] one. It appears that the Dorians moved southward gradually over a number of years and devastated the territory, until they managed to establish themselves in the Mycenaean centers.<ref>{{harvnb|Mylonas|1966|pp=231–232}}.</ref> A new type of ceramic also appeared, called "Barbarian Ware" because it was attributed to invaders from the north.<ref name=Freeman126/> On the other hand, the collapse of Mycenaean Greece coincides with the activity of the [[Sea Peoples]] in the Eastern Mediterranean. They caused widespread destruction in Anatolia and the Levant and were finally [[Battle of the Delta|defeated]] by Pharaoh [[Ramesses III]] in c. 1175 BC. One of the ethnic groups that comprised these people were the ''Eqwesh'', a name that appears to be linked with the Ahhiyawa of the Hittite inscriptions.<ref>{{harvnb|Drews|1993|p=49}}.</ref>

Alternative scenarios propose that the fall of Mycenaean Greece was a result of internal disturbances which led to internecine warfare among the Mycenaean states or civil unrest in a number of states, as a result of the strict hierarchical social system and the ideology of the wanax.<ref name=Tartaron19/> In general, due to the obscure archaeological picture in 12th–11th century BC Greece, there is a continuing controversy among scholars over whether the impoverished societies that succeeded the Mycenaean palatial states were newcomers or populations that already resided in Mycenaean Greece. Recent archaeological findings tend to favor the latter scenario.<ref name=Freeman126/> Additional theories, concerning [[Late Bronze Age collapse#Environmental|natural factors]], such as climate change, droughts, or earthquakes have also been proposed.<ref name=Tartaron19>{{harvnb|Tartaron|2013|p=19}}.</ref> Another theory considers the decline of the Mycenaean civilization as a manifestation of a common pattern for the decline of many ancient civilizations: the Minoan, the [[Indus Civilization|Harappan]] and the Western Roman Empire; the reason for the decline is migration due to overpopulation.<ref>{{harvnb|Alexakha|2016|pp=164–169}}.</ref> The period following the end of Mycenaean Greece, c. 1100–800 BC, is generally termed the "[[Greek Dark Ages]]".<ref>{{harvnb|Freeman|2014|p=127}}.</ref>

==Political organization==
[[File:Mycenaean Palace States.svg|thumb|upright=1.45|Reconstruction of the political landscape in mainland southern Greece, {{Circa|1400–1250 BC}}]]

===Palatial states===
Mycenaean palatial states, or centrally organized palace-operating polities, are recorded in ancient [[Greek literature]] and [[Greek mythology|mythology]] (e.g., ''Iliad'', [[Catalogue of Ships]]) and confirmed by discoveries made by modern archaeologists such as [[Heinrich Schliemann]]. Each Mycenaean kingdom was governed from the palace, which exercised control over most, if not all, industries within its realm. The palatial territory was divided into several sub-regions, each headed by its provincial center. Each province was further divided in smaller districts, the ''damoi''.<ref name=Kelder9/> A number of palaces and fortifications appear to be part of a wider kingdom. For instance, [[Gla]], located in the region of Boeotia, belonged to the state of nearby Orchomenos.<ref name="Kelder 2010 34"/> Moreover, the palace of Mycenae appeared to have ruled over a territory two to three times the size of the other palatial states in Bronze Age Greece. Its territory would have also included adjacent centers, including [[Tiryns]] and [[Nafplio|Nauplion]], which could plausibly be ruled by a member of Mycenae's ruling dynasty.<ref>{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|p=97}}.</ref>

The unearthed Linear B texts are too fragmentary for the reconstruction of the political landscape in Mycenaean Greece and they do not support nor deny the existence of a larger Mycenaean state.<ref name=BeckmanBryceCline6>{{harvnb|Beckman|Bryce|Cline|2012|p=6}}.</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|pp=8–9}}.</ref> On the other hand, contemporary Hittite and Egyptian records suggest the presence of a single state under a "Great King".<ref>{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|pp=45, 86, 107}}.</ref> Alternatively, based on archaeological data, some sort of confederation among a number of palatial states appears to be possible.<ref name=BeckmanBryceCline6/> If some kind of united political entity existed, the dominant center was probably located in Thebes or in Mycenae, with the latter state being the most probable center of power.<ref>{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|pp=86–87}}.</ref>

===Society and administration===

The Neolithic agrarian village (6000 BC) constituted the foundation of Bronze Age political culture in Greece.<ref>{{harvnb|Thomas|1995|p=350}}.</ref> The vast majority of the preserved Linear B records deal with administrative issues and give the impression that Mycenaean palatial administration was highly systematized, featuring thoroughly consistent language, terminology, tax calculations, and distribution logistics.<ref name=Kelder8>{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|p=8}}.</ref><ref name=Kelder9>{{harvnb|Kelder|2010|p=9}}.</ref> Considering this sense of uniformity, the [[Pylos]] archive, which is the best preserved one in the Mycenaean world, is generally taken as a representative one.<ref name=Kelder8/>

{{multiple image
| align = left
| total_width = 320
| footer = Two Mycenaean chariot warriors on a fresco from [[Pylos]] (about 1350 BC; left) and two female charioteers from [[Tiryns]] (1200&nbsp;BC; right)
| image1 = Two Mycenaean chariot warriors on a fresco from Pylos about 1350 BC.jpg
| image2 = Fresco of two female charioteers from Tiryns 1200 BC.jpg
| width1 = 250
| height1 = 289
