Ardashir established the [[Sasanian Empire]], which ruled Iran and much of the Near East until the [[Early Muslim conquests|Muslim conquests]] of the 7th century AD, although the Arsacid dynasty lived on through branches of the family that ruled [[Arsacid dynasty of Armenia|Armenia]], [[Arsacid dynasty of Iberia|Caucasian Iberia]], and [[Arsacid dynasty of Caucasian Albania|Caucasian Albania]].

Native Parthian sources, written in [[Parthian language|Parthian]], [[Koine Greek|Greek]] and other languages, are scarce when compared to [[Sasanian Empire|Sasanian]] and even earlier [[Achaemenid Empire|Achaemenid]] sources. Aside from scattered [[cuneiform]] tablets, fragmentary [[ostraca]], rock inscriptions, [[Ancient drachma|drachma]] coins, and the chance survival of some [[parchment]] documents, much of Parthian history is only known through external sources. These include mainly [[Greek historiography|Greek]] and [[Roman historiography|Roman histories]], but also [[Chinese historiography|Chinese histories]], prompted by the Han Chinese [[Han-Xiongnu War|desire to form alliances against the Xiongnu]].{{sfnp|Ball|2000|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=8Q2XxXx5ZdsC&pg=PA137 137]}} [[Parthian art]]work is a means of understanding aspects of society and culture that are otherwise absent in textual sources.

==History==
===Origins and establishment===
{{Further|Parni conquest of Parthia}}
[[File:Coin of Arsaces I (1), Nisa mint.jpg|thumb|The silver [[Ancient drachma|drachma]] of [[Arsaces I of Parthia|Arsaces I]] ({{reign|{{circa|247}}|211 BC}}) with the Greek language inscription ΑΡΣΑΚΟΥ "of Arsaces"|alt=Two sides of a silver coin. The one on the left bears the imprint of a man's head, while the one on the right a sitting individual.]]

Before [[Arsaces I of Parthia|Arsaces I]] founded the Arsacid dynasty, he was chieftain of the [[Parni]], an ancient [[Central Asia]]n tribe of [[Iranian peoples]] and one of several [[nomad]]ic tribes within the confederation of the [[Dahae]].<ref>{{harvp|Katouzian|2009|p=[https://archive.org/details/the-persians-ancient-mediaeval-and-modern-iran/page/41/mode/1up 41]}}; {{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|p=7}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=24–7}}.</ref>{{r|n=Brosius2006_834|r={{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/84/mode/1up 83–4]}}.}} The Parni most likely spoke an [[eastern Iranian language]], in contrast to the [[Western Iranian languages|northwestern Iranian language]] spoken at the time in [[Parthia]].{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=24}}{{r|Brosius2006_84}} The latter was a northeastern province, first under the [[Achaemenid Empire]], and then the [[Seleucid Empire]].{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=24–27}}{{r|Brosius2006_834}} After conquering the region, the Parni adopted [[Parthian language|Parthian]] as the official court language, speaking it alongside [[Middle Persian]], [[Aramaic language|Aramaic]], [[Greek language|Greek]], [[Akkadian language|Babylonian]], [[Sogdian language|Sogdian]] and other languages in the multilingual territories they would conquer.{{sfnp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|pp=7–8}}{{r|Brosius2006_834}} Some academics debate the ethnic origins of Arsaces I, such as Hashem Kazemi and Mostafa Dehpahlavan, who argue that he was a Parthian native rather than a member of the invading Parni.{{efn|Kazemi and Dehpahlavan, relying on archaeological findings and inferences from various textual primary sources, disagree with the ancient school of thought promoted by [[Apollodorus of Artemita]] and supported afterwards by [[Justin (historian)|Justin]] and [[Strabo]] that [[Arsaces I]] belonged to the [[Parni conquest of Parthia|invading Parni]]. They instead concur with [[Arrian]], [[Cassius Dio]], and [[Zosimus (historian)|Zosimus]], who suggested a native [[Parthia]]n origin for Arsaces I.{{sfnp|Kazemi|Dehpahlavan|2023|pp=1, 13, 15–9}}}}

Why the Arsacid court retroactively chose 247&nbsp;BC as the first year of the Arsacid era is uncertain. [[Adrian David Hugh Bivar|A. D. H. Bivar]] concludes that this was the year the Seleucids lost control of Parthia to [[Andragoras (3rd century BC)|Andragoras]], the appointed [[satrap]] who rebelled against them. Hence, Arsaces I "backdated his [[regnal year]]s" to the moment when Seleucid control over Parthia ceased.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=28–9}} However, Vesta Sarkhosh Curtis asserts that this was simply the year Arsaces was made chief of the Parni tribe.{{sfnp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|p=7}} Homa Katouzian{{r|n=katouzian2009_41|r={{harvp|Katouzian|2009|p=[https://archive.org/details/the-persians-ancient-mediaeval-and-modern-iran/page/41/mode/1up 41]}}.}} and Gene Ralph Garthwaite{{sfnp|Garthwaite|2005|p=[https://archive.org/details/persians0000gart/page/67/mode/1up 67]}} claim it was the year Arsaces conquered Parthia and expelled the Seleucid authorities, yet Curtis{{sfnp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|p=7}} and Maria Brosius{{r|n=Brosius2006_85|r={{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/85/mode/1up 85]}}.}} state that Andragoras was not [[Parni conquest of Parthia|overthrown by the Arsacids]] until 238&nbsp;BC.

It is unclear who immediately succeeded Arsaces I. Bivar{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=29–31}} and Katouzian{{r|katouzian2009_41}} affirm that it was his brother [[Tiridates I of Parthia]], who in turn was succeeded by his son [[Arsaces II of Parthia]] in 211&nbsp;BC. Yet Curtis{{sfnp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|p=8}} and Brosius{{r|n=Brosius2006_86|r={{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/86/mode/1up 86]}}.}} state that Arsaces II was the immediate successor of Arsaces I, with Curtis claiming the succession took place in 211&nbsp;BC, and Brosius in 217&nbsp;BC. Bivar insists that 138&nbsp;BC, the last regnal year of Mithridates I, is "the first precisely established regnal date of Parthian history."{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=36}} Due to these and other discrepancies, Bivar outlines [[List of Parthian kings|two distinct royal chronologies]] accepted by historians.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=98–9}} A fictitious claim was later made from the 2nd-century BC onwards by the Parthians, which represented them as descendants of the Achaemenid king of kings, [[Artaxerxes II of Persia]] ({{reign|404|358 BC}}).{{sfnp|Daryaee|2012|p=179}}

[[File:Rome-Seleucia-Parthia 200bc.jpg|thumb|left|upright=1.2|[[Parthia]], shaded yellow, alongside the [[Seleucid Empire]] (blue) and the [[Roman Republic]] (purple) around 200&nbsp;BC|alt=A map centered on the Mediterranean and Middle East showing the extent of the Roman Republic (Purple), Selucid Empire (Blue), and Parthia (Yellow) around 200&nbsp;BC.]]

For a time, Arsaces I consolidated his position in Parthia and [[Hyrcania]] by taking advantage of the invasion of Seleucid territory in the west by [[Ptolemy III Euergetes]] (''r''.&nbsp;246–222&nbsp;BC) of [[History of Ptolemaic Egypt|Egypt]]. This conflict with Ptolemy, the [[Syrian Wars#Third Syrian War (246-241 BC)|Third Syrian War]] (246–241&nbsp;BC), also allowed [[Diodotus I]] to rebel and form the [[Greco-Bactrian Kingdom]] in Central Asia.{{r|Brosius2006_85}} The latter's successor, [[Diodotus II]], formed an alliance with Arsaces I against the Seleucids, but Arsaces was temporarily driven from Parthia by the forces of [[Seleucus II Callinicus]] ({{reign|246|225 BC}}).{{r|n=Brosius2006_856|r={{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/85/mode/1up 85–6]}}.}} After spending some time in exile among the nomadic [[Apasiacae]] tribe, Arsaces I led a counterattack and recaptured Parthia. Seleucus II's successor, [[Antiochus III the Great]] ({{reign|222|187 BC}}), was unable to immediately retaliate because his troops were engaged in putting down the rebellion of [[Molon]] in [[Media (region)|Media]].{{r|Brosius2006_856}}

Antiochus III launched a massive campaign to retake Parthia and Bactria in 210 or 209&nbsp;BC. Despite some [[Battle of Mount Labus|victories]] he was unsuccessful, but did negotiate a peace settlement with Arsaces II. The latter was granted the title of king ([[Ancient Greek|Greek]]: ''[[basileus]]'') in return for his submission to Antiochus III as his superior.{{r|n=Bivar1983_29_kennedy1996_74|r={{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=29}}; {{harvp|Kennedy|1996|p=74}}.}}{{r|Brosius2006_86}} The Seleucids were unable to further intervene in Parthian affairs following increasing encroachment by the [[Roman Republic]] and the Seleucid [[Battle of Magnesia|defeat at Magnesia]] in 190&nbsp;BC.{{r|Bivar1983_29_kennedy1996_74}}{{r|Brosius2006_86}} [[Priapatius]] ({{reign|{{circa|191}}|176 BC}}) succeeded Arsaces II, and [[Phraates I]] ({{reign|{{circa| 176}}|171 BC}}) eventually ascended the Parthian throne. Phraates I ruled Parthia without further Seleucid interference.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=29–31}}{{r|Brosius2006_86}}

===Expansion and consolidation===
{{Main|Seleucid–Parthian wars}}

[[File:MithridatesIParthiaCoinHistoryofIran.jpg|thumb|[[Ancient drachma|Drachma]] of [[Mithridates I of Parthia|Mithridates I]], showing him wearing a beard and a royal [[diadem]] on his head. Reverse side: [[Heracles]]/[[Verethragna]], holding a club in his left hand and a cup in his right hand; Greek inscription reading ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ ΜΕΓΑΛΟΥ ΑΡΣΑΚΟΥ ΦΙΛΕΛΛΗΝΟΣ "of the Great King Arsaces the [[Philhellene]]"|alt=Two sides of a coin. The side on the left showing the head of a bearded man, while the right a standing individual.]]

Phraates I is recorded as expanding Parthia's control past the [[Gates of Alexander]] and occupied [[Apamea Ragiana]]. The locations of these are unknown.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=31}} Yet the greatest expansion of Parthian power and territory took place during the reign of his brother and successor [[Mithridates I of Parthia|Mithridates I]] (r. c.&nbsp;171–132 BC),{{r|Brosius2006_86}} whom Katouzian compares to [[Cyrus the Great]] (d. 530 BC), founder of the Achaemenid Empire.{{r|katouzian2009_41}}

Relations between Parthia and Greco-Bactria deteriorated after the death of Diodotus II, when forces under Mithridates I captured two [[Eparchy (disambiguation)|eparchies]] of the latter kingdom, then under [[Eucratides I]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;170–145&nbsp;BC).{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=33}}{{r|Brosius2006_86}} Turning his sights on the Seleucid realm, Mithridates I invaded Media and occupied [[Ecbatana]] in 148 or 147&nbsp;BC; the region had been destabilized by a recent Seleucid suppression of a rebellion there led by [[Timarchus]].<ref>{{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|pp=10–1}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=33}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=[https://archive.org/details/persians0000gart/page/76/mode/1up 76]}}.</ref> This victory was followed by the Parthian conquest of [[Babylonia]] in [[Mesopotamia]], where Mithridates I had coins minted at [[Seleucia]] in 141&nbsp;BC and held an official [[investiture]] ceremony.{{r|n=Sar2007_101_Biv1983_34_Gar2005_76|r={{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|pp=10–1}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=34}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=[https://archive.org/details/persians0000gart/page/76/mode/1up 76]}}.}}{{r|n=Brosius2006_867|r={{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/86/mode/1up 86–7]}}.}} While Mithridates I retired to Hyrcania, his forces subdued the kingdoms of [[Elymais]] and [[Characene]] and occupied [[Susa]].{{r|Sar2007_101_Biv1983_34_Gar2005_76}}{{r|Brosius2006_867}} By this time, Parthian authority extended as far east as the [[Indus River]].<ref>{{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=[https://archive.org/details/persians0000gart/page/76/mode/1up 76]}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=35}}.</ref>
[[File:Rodoguna, daughter of the Parthian king Mithridates II, marble from Nisa; National Museum of History, Ashgabat, Turkmenistan.jpg|alt=Two sides of a coin. The side on the left showing the head of a bearded man, while the right a standing individual.|thumb|Statue of a Parthian woman, marble from Nisa; National Museum of History, [[Ashgabat]], Turkmenistan]]
Whereas [[Hecatompylos]] had served as the first Parthian capital, Mithridates I established royal residences at Seleucia, Ecbatana, [[Ctesiphon]] and his newly founded city, Mithradatkert ([[Nisa, Turkmenistan|Nisa]]), where the tombs of the Arsacid kings were built and maintained.{{sfnp|Brosius|2006|pp=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/103/mode/1up 103], [https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/110/mode/1up 110–3]}} Ecbatana became the main summertime residence for the Arsacid royalty.<ref>{{harvp|Kennedy|1996|p=73}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=[https://archive.org/details/persians0000gart/page/77/mode/1up 77]}}.</ref> Ctesiphon may not have become the official capital until the reign of [[Gotarzes I]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;90–80&nbsp;BC).<ref>{{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=[https://archive.org/details/persians0000gart/page/77/mode/1up 77]}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=38–9}}.</ref> It became the site of the royal [[coronation]] ceremony and the representational city of the Arsacids, according to Brosius.{{r|n=Brosius2006_103|r={{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/103/mode/1up 103]}}.}}

The Seleucids were unable to retaliate immediately as general [[Diodotus Tryphon]] led a rebellion at the capital [[Antioch]] in 142 BC.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=34}} However, by 140&nbsp;BC [[Demetrius II Nicator]] was able to launch a counter-invasion against the Parthians in Mesopotamia. Despite early successes, the Seleucids were defeated and Demetrius himself was captured by Parthian forces and taken to Hyrcania. There Mithridates I treated his captive with great hospitality; he even married his daughter [[Rhodogune of Parthia]] to Demetrius.{{r|n=Brosius2006_89|r={{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/89/mode/1up 89]}}.}}<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=35}}; {{harvp|Shayegan|2003|pp=83–103}}.</ref>

[[Antiochus VII Sidetes]] (''r''.&nbsp;138–129&nbsp;BC), a brother of Demetrius, assumed the Seleucid throne and married the latter's wife [[Cleopatra Thea]]. After defeating Diodotus Tryphon, Antiochus initiated a campaign in 130&nbsp;BC to retake Mesopotamia, now under the rule of [[Phraates II]] (''r''.&nbsp;c.&nbsp;132–127&nbsp;BC). The Parthian general Indates was defeated along the [[Great Zab]], followed by a local uprising where the Parthian governor of Babylonia was killed. Antiochus conquered Babylonia and occupied Susa, where he minted coins.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=36–7}}; {{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|p=11}}; {{harvp|Shayegan|2011|pp=121–50}}.</ref> After Antiochus advanced his army into Media, the Parthians pushed for peace, which Antiochus refused to accept unless the Arsacids relinquished all lands to him except Parthia proper, paid heavy tribute, and released Demetrius from captivity. Arsaces released Demetrius and sent him to [[History of Syria|Syria]], but refused the other demands.<ref>{{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|pp=76–7}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=36–7}}; {{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|p=11}}.</ref> By spring 129&nbsp;BC, the Medes were in open revolt against Antiochus, whose army had exhausted the resources of the countryside during winter. While Antiochus attempted to put down the revolts, the main Parthian force swept into the region and killed Antiochus at the [[Battle of Ecbatana]] in 129 BC. His body was sent back to Syria in a silver coffin; his son Seleucus was made a Parthian hostage{{sfnp|Shayegan|2011|pp=145–50}} and a daughter joined Phraates' [[harem]].<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=37–38}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=[https://archive.org/details/persians0000gart/page/77/mode/1up 77]}}; see also {{harvp|Katouzian|2009|pp=41–2}}.</ref>{{r|n=Brosius2006_90|r={{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/90/mode/1up 90]}}.}}
[[File:Tetradrachm of Mithridates II of Parthia, minted at Seleucia between 120 and 109 BC.jpg|thumb|Drachma of [[Mithridates II of Parthia|Mithridates II]] (''r''.&nbsp;c.&nbsp;124–91&nbsp;BC). Reverse side: seated archer carrying a bow; inscription reading "of the [[King of Kings]] Arsaces the Renowned/Manifest Philhellene."]]
While the Parthians regained the territories lost in the west, another threat arose in the east. In 177–176&nbsp;BC the nomadic confederation of the [[Xiongnu]] dislodged the nomadic [[Yuezhi]] from their homelands in what is now [[Gansu]] province in [[Northwest China]];{{sfnp|Torday|1998|pp=80–1}} the Yuezhi then migrated west into Bactria and displaced the [[Saka]] (Scythian) tribes. The Saka were forced to move further west, where they invaded the Parthian Empire's northeastern borders.<ref>{{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=[https://archive.org/details/persians0000gart/page/76/mode/1up 76]}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=36–37}}.</ref> {{sfnp|Brosius|2006|pp=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/91/mode/1up 89, 91]}} Mithridates I was thus forced to retire to Hyrcania after his conquest of Mesopotamia.{{r|Brosius2006_89}}

Some of the Saka were enlisted in Phraates' forces against Antiochus. However, they arrived too late to engage in the conflict. When Phraates refused to pay their wages, the Saka revolted, which he tried to put down with the aid of former Seleucid soldiers, yet they too abandoned Phraates and joined sides with the Saka.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=38}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=[https://archive.org/details/persians0000gart/page/77/mode/1up 77]}}.</ref> Phraates II marched against this combined force, but he was killed in battle.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=38–9}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=[https://archive.org/details/persians0000gart/page/77/mode/1up 77]}}; {{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|p=11}}; {{harvp|Katouzian|2009|p=[https://archive.org/details/the-persians-ancient-mediaeval-and-modern-iran/page/42/mode/1up 42]}}.</ref> The Roman historian [[Justin (historian)|Justin]] reports that his harvp [[Artabanus I of Parthia|Artabanus I]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;128–124&nbsp;BC) shared a similar fate fighting nomads in the east. He claims Artabanus was killed by the Tokhari (identified as the Yuezhi), although Bivar believes Justin conflated them with the Saka.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=38–9}} [[Mithridates II of Parthia|Mithridates II]] (r. c.&nbsp;124–91&nbsp;BC) later recovered the lands lost to the Saka in [[Sakastan]].<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=40–41}}; {{harvp|Katouzian|2009|p=[https://archive.org/details/the-persians-ancient-mediaeval-and-modern-iran/page/42/mode/1up 42]}}.</ref>

[[File:Silk from Mawangdui 2.jpg|thumb|left|[[Han dynasty]] Chinese [[silk]] from [[Mawangdui]], 2nd century BC. Silk from [[History of China|China]] was perhaps the most lucrative luxury item the Parthians traded at the western end of the [[Silk Road]].{{sfnp|Garthwaite|2005|p=[https://archive.org/details/persians0000gart/page/78/mode/1up 78]}}]]

Following the Seleucid withdrawal from Mesopotamia, the Parthian governor of Babylonia, Himerus, was ordered by the Arsacid court to conquer [[Characene]], then ruled by [[Hyspaosines]] from [[Charax Spasinu]]. When this failed, Hyspaosines invaded Babylonia in 127&nbsp;BC and occupied Seleucia. Yet by 122&nbsp;BC, Mithridates II forced Hyspaosines out of Babylonia and made the kings of Characene [[vassal]]s under Parthian [[suzerainty]].<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=40}}; {{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|pp=11–2}}.</ref>{{r|Brosius2006_90}} After Mithridates II extended Parthian control further west, occupying [[Dura-Europos]] in 113&nbsp;BC, he became embroiled in a conflict with the [[Kingdom of Armenia (antiquity)|Kingdom of Armenia]].{{sfnp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|pp=11–2}} His forces defeated and deposed [[Artavasdes I of Armenia]] in 97&nbsp;BC, taking his son Tigranes hostage, who would later become [[Tigranes the Great|Tigranes II "the Great" of Armenia]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;95–55&nbsp;BC).{{r|n=Brosius2006_912|r={{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/91/mode/1up 91–2]}}.}} {{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=40–1}}

The [[Indo-Parthian Kingdom]], located in modern-day Afghanistan and Pakistan made an alliance with the Parthian Empire in the 1st century BC.{{sfnp|Bivar|2007|p=26}} Bivar claims that these two states considered each other political equals.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=41}} After the Greek philosopher [[Apollonius of Tyana]] visited the court of [[Vardanes I]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;40–47&nbsp;AD) in 42&nbsp;AD, Vardanes provided him with the protection of a caravan as he traveled to Indo-Parthia. When Apollonius reached Indo-Parthia's capital [[Taxila]], his caravan leader read Vardanes' official letter, perhaps written in Parthian, to an Indian official who treated Apollonius with great hospitality.{{sfnp|Bivar|2007|p=26}}

Following the [[Foreign relations of Imperial China|diplomatic venture]] of [[Zhang Qian]] into Central Asia during the reign of [[Emperor Wu of Han]] (''r''.&nbsp;141–87&nbsp;BC), the [[Han dynasty|Han Empire]] of China sent a delegation to Mithridates II's court in 121&nbsp;BC. The Han embassy [[Economy of the Han dynasty#Foreign trade and tributary exchange|opened official trade relations]] with Parthia via the [[Silk Road]] yet did not achieve a desired military alliance against the confederation of the Xiongnu.<ref>{{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/90/mode/1up 90–1]}}; {{harvp|Watson|1983|pp=540–2}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|pp=77–8}}.</ref> The Parthian Empire was enriched by taxing the Eurasian caravan trade in [[History of silk|silk]], the most highly priced luxury good [[Roman commerce|imported by the Romans]].<ref>{{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=78}}; {{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=122–3}}.</ref> Pearls were also a highly valued import from China, while the Chinese purchased Parthian spices, perfumes, and fruits.{{sfnp|Brosius|2006|pp=123–5}} Exotic animals were also given as gifts from the Arsacid to Han courts; in 87 AD [[Pacorus II of Parthia]] sent lions and Persian gazelles to [[Emperor Zhang of Han]] (''r''.&nbsp;75–88&nbsp;AD).{{sfnp|Wang|2007|pp=100–1}} Besides silk, Parthian goods purchased by Roman merchants included [[History of metallurgy in the Indian subcontinent|iron from India]], [[Spice trade|spices]], and fine leather.{{sfnp|Kurz|1983|p=560}} Caravans traveling through the Parthian Empire brought West Asian and sometimes [[Roman glass|Roman luxury glasswares]] to China.{{sfnp|Ebrey|1999|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=sHGdq4rLSTEC&pg=PA70 70]}}{{efn|For an archaeological survey of Roman glasswares in ancient Chinese burials, see {{harvp|An|2002|pp=79–84}}.}} The merchants of [[Sogdia]], speaking an [[Sogdian language|Eastern Iranian language]], served as the primary middlemen of this vital silk trade between [[China–Iran relations#Han-Parthian era|Parthia and Han China]].{{sfnp|Howard|2012|p=[https://archive.org/details/transnationalism0000howa/page/133/mode/1up 133]}}

===Rome and Armenia===
{{Main|Roman–Persian relations|Roman–Parthian Wars|Parthian invasion of 40 BC}}

[[File:Parthian prince, from Sham-Izeh, Malamir, Iran, c.50 BC-AD 150 (cast bronze), Parthian School (250 BC-226 AD) National Museum of Iran, Tehran, Iran.jpg|thumb|{{center|[[Statue, National Museum of Iran 2401|Bronze statue of a Parthian nobleman]] from the sanctuary at Shami in [[Elymais]] (modern-day [[Khūzestān Province]], [[Iran]], along the Persian Gulf), now located at the [[National Museum of Iran]]. Dated 50 BC – 150 AD, Parthian School.}}]]
The Yuezhi [[Kushan Empire]] in northern India largely guaranteed the security of Parthia's eastern border.{{sfnp|Brosius|2006|p=92}} Thus, from the mid-1st century BC onwards, the Arsacid court focused on securing the western border, primarily against Rome.{{sfnp|Brosius|2006|p=92}} A year following Mithridates II's subjugation of Armenia, [[Lucius Cornelius Sulla]], the Roman [[proconsul]] of [[Cilicia]], convened with the Parthian diplomat [[Orobazus]] at the [[Euphrates]] river. The two agreed that the river would serve as the border between Parthia and Rome, although several historians have argued that Sulla only had authority to communicate these terms back to Rome.<ref>{{harvp|Kennedy|1996|pp=73–8}}; {{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/91/mode/1up 91]}}; {{harvp|Sheldon|2010|pp=12–6}}.</ref>

Despite this agreement, in 93 or 92&nbsp;BC Parthia fought a war in Syria against the tribal leader [[Laodice of the Sameans|Laodice]] and her Seleucid ally [[Antiochus X Eusebes]] (''r''.&nbsp;95–92?&nbsp;BC), killing the latter.{{r|n=kennedy1996_778|r={{harvp|Kennedy|1996|pp=77–8}}.}} When one of the last Seleucid monarchs, [[Demetrius III Eucaerus]], attempted to besiege Beroea (modern [[Aleppo]]), Parthia sent military aid to the inhabitants and Demetrius was defeated.{{r|kennedy1996_778}}

Following the rule of Mithridates II, his son [[Gotarzes I]] succeeded him.<ref>{{harvp|Assar|2006|p=62}}; {{harvp|Shayegan|2011|p=225}}; {{harvp|Rezakhani|2013|p=[https://archive.org/details/oxfordhandbookof0000unse_s1j3/page/770/mode/1up 770]}}.</ref> He reigned during a period coined in scholarship as the "[[Parthian Dark Age]]", due to the lack of clear information on the events of this period in the empire, except a series of, apparently overlapping, reigns.{{sfnp|Shayegan|2011|pp=188–9}}{{sfnp|Sellwood|1976|p=2}} It is only with the beginning of the reign of [[Orodes II]] in {{circa|57 BC}}, that the line of Parthian rulers can again be reliably traced.{{sfnp|Sellwood|1976|p=2}} This system of split monarchy weakened Parthia, allowing Tigranes II of Armenia to annex Parthian territory in western Mesopotamia. This land would not be restored to Parthia until the reign of [[Sinatruces of Parthia|Sinatruces]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;78–69&nbsp;BC).{{r|Brosius2006_912}}

Following the outbreak of the [[Third Mithridatic War]], [[Mithridates VI of Pontus]] (''r''.&nbsp;119–63&nbsp;BC), an ally of Tigranes II of Armenia, requested aid from Parthia against Rome, but Sinatruces refused help.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=44–5}} When the Roman commander [[Lucullus]] marched against the Armenian capital [[Tigranocerta]] in 69&nbsp;BC, Mithridates VI and Tigranes II requested the aid of [[Phraates III]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;71–58). Phraates did not send aid to either, and after the [[Battle of Tigranocerta|fall of Tigranocerta]] he reaffirmed with Lucullus the Euphrates as the boundary between Parthia and Rome.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=45–6}}; {{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=94}}.</ref>

[[Tigranes the Younger]], son of Tigranes II of Armenia, failed to usurp the Armenian throne from his father. He fled to Phraates III and convinced him to march against Armenia's new capital at [[Artaxata]]. When this siege failed, Tigranes the Younger once again fled, this time to the Roman commander [[Pompey]]. He promised Pompey that he would act as a guide through Armenia, but, when Tigranes II submitted to Rome as a [[Client state|client king]], Tigranes the Younger was brought to Rome as a hostage.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=46–7}} Phraates demanded Pompey return Tigranes the Younger to him, but Pompey refused. In retaliation, Phraates launched an invasion into [[Corduene]] (southeastern Turkey) where, according to two conflicting Roman accounts, the Roman consul [[Lucius Afranius (consul)|Lucius Afranius]] forced the Parthians out by either military or diplomatic means.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=47}}{{efn|[[Cassius Dio]] writes that Lucius Afranius reoccupied the region without confronting the Parthian army, whereas [[Plutarch]] asserts that Afranius drove him out by military means.}}

Phraates III was assassinated by his sons [[Orodes II of Parthia]] and [[Mithridates IV of Parthia]], after which Orodes turned on Mithridates, forcing him to flee from Media to [[Syria (Roman province)|Roman Syria]].<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=48–9}}; see also {{harvp|Katouzian|2009|pp=[https://archive.org/details/the-persians-ancient-mediaeval-and-modern-iran/page/42/mode/1up 42–3]}}.</ref> [[Aulus Gabinius]], the Roman proconsul of Syria, marched in support of Mithridates to the Euphrates, but had to turn back to aid [[Ptolemy XII Auletes]] (''r''.&nbsp;80–58; 55–51&nbsp;BC) against a rebellion in Egypt.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=48–9}}; also, {{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=94–5}} mentions this in passing.</ref> Despite losing his Roman support, Mithridates managed to conquer Babylonia, and minted coins at Seleucia until 54&nbsp;BC. In that year, Orodes' general, known only as [[Surena]] after his noble family's clan name, recaptured Seleucia, and Mithridates was executed.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=49}}

[[File:Head of Marcus Licinius Crassus, middle of 1st century BC, from Italy, Moi, Auguste, Empereur de Rome exhibition, Grand Palais, Paris - 14649017884.jpg|thumb|left|upright|A Roman marble head of the triumvir [[Marcus Licinius Crassus]], who was [[Battle of Carrhae|defeated at Carrhae]] by [[Surena]]]]

[[Marcus Licinius Crassus]], one of the [[First Triumvirate|triumvirs]], who was now proconsul of Syria, invaded Parthia in 53&nbsp;BC in belated support of Mithridates.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=49–50}}; {{harvp|Katouzian|2009|pp=[https://archive.org/details/the-persians-ancient-mediaeval-and-modern-iran/page/42/mode/1up 42–3]}}.</ref> As his army [[Battle of Carrhae|marched to Carrhae]] (modern [[Harran]], southeastern Turkey), Orodes II invaded Armenia, cutting off support from Rome's ally [[Artavasdes II of Armenia]] (''r''.&nbsp;53–34&nbsp;BC). Orodes persuaded Artavasdes to a marriage alliance between the crown prince [[Pacorus I of Parthia]] (d.&nbsp;38&nbsp;BC) and Artavasdes' sister.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=55–6}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=79}}; see also {{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=94–5}} and {{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|pp=12–3}}.</ref>

Surena, with an army entirely on horseback, rode to meet Crassus.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=52–5}} Surena's 1,000 [[cataphract]]s (armed with lances) and 9,000 [[horse archer]]s were outnumbered roughly four to one by Crassus' army, comprising seven [[Roman legion]]s and auxiliaries including mounted [[Gaul]]s and light infantry.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=52}} Using a baggage train of about 1,000 camels, the Parthian army provided the horse archers with a constant supply of arrows.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=52}} The horse archers employed the "[[Parthian shot]]" tactic: feigning retreat to draw enemy out, then turning and shooting at them when exposed. This tactic, executed with heavy [[composite bow]]s on the flat plain, devastated Crassus' infantry.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=52–5}}; {{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=94–5}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|pp=78–9}}.</ref>

With some 20,000 Romans dead, approximately 10,000 captured, and roughly another 10,000 escaping west, Crassus fled into the Armenian countryside.<ref>{{harvp|Katouzian|2009|pp=[https://archive.org/details/the-persians-ancient-mediaeval-and-modern-iran/page/42/mode/1up 42–3]}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=79}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=52–5}}.</ref>{{r|n=Brosius2006_96|r={{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=96}}.}} At the head of his army, Surena approached Crassus, offering a [[parley]], which Crassus accepted. However, he was killed when one of his junior officers, suspecting a trap, attempted to stop him from riding into Surena's camp.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=52–5}}{{r|Brosius2006_96}} Crassus' defeat at Carrhae was one of the worst military defeats of Roman history.{{r|n=kennedy1996_78|r={{harvp|Kennedy|1996|p=78}}.}} Parthia's victory cemented its reputation as a formidable if not equal power with Rome.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=55–6}}{{r|Brosius2006_96}} With his camp followers, war captives, and precious Roman booty, Surena traveled some 700&nbsp;km (430&nbsp;mi) back to Seleucia where his victory was celebrated. However, fearing his ambitions even for the Arsacid throne, Orodes had Surena executed shortly thereafter.{{r|kennedy1996_78}}

[[Image:Antony with Octavian aureus.jpg|thumb|Roman [[aureus|aurei]] bearing the portraits of [[Mark Antony]] (left) and [[Octavian]] (right), issued in 41&nbsp;BC to celebrate the establishment of the [[Second Triumvirate]] by Octavian, Antony and [[Marcus Aemilius Lepidus (triumvir)|Marcus Lepidus]] in 43&nbsp;BC]]
Emboldened by the victory over Crassus, the Parthians attempted to capture Roman-held territories in [[West Asia]].{{efn|Kennedy asserts that permanent occupation was the obvious goal of the Parthians, especially after the cities of Roman Syria and even the Roman garrisons submitted to the Parthians and joined their cause.{{sfnp|Kennedy|1996|p=80}}}} [[Crown prince]] Pacorus I and his commander Osaces raided Syria as far as Antioch in 51 BC, but were repulsed by [[Gaius Cassius Longinus]], who ambushed and killed Osaces.<ref>{{harvp|Kennedy|1996|pp=78–9}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=56}}.</ref> The Arsacids sided with Pompey in [[Caesar's Civil War|the civil war against Julius Caesar]] and even sent troops to support the anti-Caesarian forces at the [[Battle of Philippi]] in 42&nbsp;BC.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=56–7}}; {{harvp|Strugnell|2006|p=243}}.</ref>

[[Quintus Labienus]], a general loyal to Cassius and [[Marcus Junius Brutus the Younger|Brutus]], sided with Parthia against the [[Second Triumvirate]] in 40 BC; the following year he [[Parthian invasion of 40 BC|invaded Syria alongside Pacorus I]].{{r|n=Biv1983_57str2006_244_ken1996_80|r={{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=57}}; {{harvp|Strugnell|2006|p=244}}; {{harvp|Kennedy|1996|p=80}}.}} The triumvir [[Mark Antony]] was unable to lead the Roman defense against Parthia due to his departure to Italy, where he amassed his forces to confront his rival [[Octavian]] and eventually [[Treaty of Brundisium|conducted negotiations with him]] at [[Brundisium]].{{sfnp|Syme|2002|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=F5ebGZNzSUIC&pg=PA214 214–7]}}

After Syria was occupied by Pacorus' army, Labienus split from the main Parthian force to invade [[Anatolia]] while Pacorus and his commander [[Barzapharnes]] invaded the Roman [[Levant]].{{r|Biv1983_57str2006_244_ken1996_80}} They subdued all settlements along the Mediterranean coast as far south as Ptolemais (modern [[Acre, Israel]]), with the lone exception of [[Tyre, Lebanon|Tyre]].{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=57}} In [[Judea]], the pro-Roman Jewish forces of high priest [[Hyrcanus II]], [[Phasael]], and [[Herod the Great|Herod]] were defeated by the Parthians and their Jewish ally [[Antigonus II Mattathias]] (r.&nbsp;40–37&nbsp;BC); the latter was made king of Judea while Herod fled to his fort at [[Masada]].{{r|Biv1983_57str2006_244_ken1996_80}}

Despite these successes, the Parthians were soon driven out of the Levant by a Roman counteroffensive. [[Publius Ventidius Bassus]], an officer under Mark Antony, defeated and then executed Labienus at the [[Battle of the Cilician Gates]] (in modern [[Mersin Province]], Turkey) in 39 BC.{{r|n=Biv1983_578_str2006_239_245_ken1996_80|r={{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=57–8}}; {{harvp|Strugnell|2006|pp=239, 245}}; {{harvp|Kennedy|1996|p=80}}.}}{{r|Brosius2006_96}} Shortly afterward, a Parthian force in Syria led by general Pharnapates was defeated by Ventidius at the [[Battle of Amanus Pass]].{{r|Biv1983_578_str2006_239_245_ken1996_80}}{{r|Brosius2006_96}}

As a result, Pacorus I temporarily withdrew from Syria. When he returned in the spring of 38&nbsp;BC, he faced Ventidius at the [[Battle of Mount Gindarus]], northeast of Antioch. Pacorus was killed during the battle, and his forces retreated across the Euphrates. His death spurred a succession crisis in which Orodes II chose [[Phraates IV]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;38–2&nbsp;BC) as his new heir.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=58}}; {{harvp|Kennedy|1996|pp=80–1}}; see also {{harvp|Strugnell|2006|pp=239, 245–6}}.</ref>{{r|Brosius2006_96}}
[[File:Tetradrachm coin of Phraates IV with Tyche on Reverse.jpg|thumb|Drachma of [[Phraates IV]] (''r''.&nbsp;c.&nbsp;38–2&nbsp;BC). Inscription reading ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΝ ΑΡΣΑΚΟΥ ΕΥΕΡΓΕΤΟΥ ΕΠΙΦΑΝΟΥΣ ΦΙΛΕΛΛΗΝΟΣ "of the [[King of Kings]] Arsaces the Renowned/Manifest Benefactor Philhellene"]]
Upon assuming the throne, Phraates IV eliminated rival claimants by killing and exiling his own brothers.{{sfnp|Garthwaite|2005|p=[https://archive.org/details/persians0000gart/page/79/mode/1up 79]}} One of them, [[Monaeses (nobleman)|Monaeses]], fled to Antony and persuaded him to [[Antony's Parthian War|invade Parthia]].<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=58–9}}; {{harvp|Kennedy|1996|p=81}}.</ref> Antony defeated Parthia's Judaean ally Antigonus in 37&nbsp;BC, installing Herod as a client king in his place.

The following year, when Antony marched to [[Erzurum|Theodosiopolis]], Artavasdes II of Armenia once again switched alliances by sending Antony additional troops. Antony invaded Media [[Atropatene]] (modern [[Iranian Azerbaijan]]), then ruled by Parthia's ally [[Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene]], with the intention of seizing the capital Praaspa, the location of which is now unknown. However, Phraates IV ambushed Antony's rear detachment, destroying a giant [[battering ram]] meant for the siege of Praaspa; after this, Artavasdes II abandoned Antony's forces.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=58–9}}

The Parthians pursued and harassed Antony's army as it fled to Armenia. Eventually, the greatly weakened force reached Syria.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=60–3}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=80}}; {{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|p=13}}.</ref> {{efn|Starting with Antony, Rome shifted its attention away from Syria to the Upper Euphrates.<ref>{{harvp|Kennedy|1996|p=81}}.</ref>}} Antony lured Artavasdes II into a trap with the promise of a marriage alliance. He was taken captive in 34 BC, paraded in Antony's mock [[Roman triumph]] in [[Alexandria]], Egypt,{{sfnp|Roller|2010|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=EZo6DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA99 99]}} and eventually executed by [[Cleopatra VII]] of the [[Ptolemaic Kingdom]].{{sfnp|Burstein|2004|p=[https://archive.org/details/ReignOfCleopatra/page/31/mode/1up 31]}}{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=64–5}}

Antony attempted to strike an alliance with Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene, whose relations with Phraates IV had recently soured. This was abandoned when Antony and his forces withdrew from Armenia in 33&nbsp;BC; they escaped a Parthian invasion while Antony's rival Octavian attacked his forces to the west.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=64–5}} After the defeat and suicides of Antony and Cleopatra in 30 BC,{{sfnp|Roller|2010|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=EZo6DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA145 145–51]}} Parthian ally [[Artaxias II]] reassumed the throne of Armenia.

===Peace with Rome, court intrigue, and contact with Chinese generals===
{{Further|Pax Romana}}

Following the defeat and deaths of Antony and [[Reign of Cleopatra VII|Cleopatra]] of [[Ptolemaic Egypt]] after the [[Battle of Actium]] in 31&nbsp;BC, Octavian consolidated his political power and in 27&nbsp;BC was named [[Augustus]] by the [[Roman Senate]], becoming the first [[Roman emperor]].<ref>{{harvp|Roller|2010|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=EZo6DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA138 138–51]}}; {{harvp|Bringmann|2007|pp=[https://archive.org/details/historyofromanre0000klau/page/304/mode/1up 304–7]}}.</ref> Around this time, [[Tiridates II of Parthia]] briefly overthrew Phraates IV, who was able to quickly reestablish his rule with the aid of Scythian nomads.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=65–6}} Tiridates fled to the Romans, taking one of Phraates' sons with him. In negotiations conducted in 20&nbsp;BC, Phraates arranged for the release of his kidnapped son. In return, the Romans received the lost [[Aquila (Roman)|legionary standards]] taken at Carrhae in 53&nbsp;BC, as well as any surviving prisoners of war.<ref>{{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=[https://archive.org/details/persians0000gart/page/80/mode/1up 80]}}; see also {{harvp|Strugnell|2006|pp=251–2}}.</ref> The Parthians viewed this exchange as a small price to pay to regain the prince.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=66–7}} Augustus hailed the return of the standards as a political victory over Parthia; this propaganda was celebrated in the minting of new coins, the [[Forum of Augustus|building of a new temple]] to house the standards, and even in fine art such as the [[breastplate]] scene on his statue [[Augustus of Prima Porta]].<ref>{{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=96–7, 136–7}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=66–7}}; {{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|pp=12–3}}.</ref>

[[File:Augustus Prima Porta (detail).PNG|thumb|left|A close-up view of the [[breastplate]] on the statue of [[Augustus of Prima Porta]], showing a Parthian man returning to [[Augustus]] the [[Aquila (Roman)|legionary standards]] lost by [[Marcus Licinius Crassus]] at [[Battle of Carrhae|Carrhae]]]]

Along with the prince, Augustus also gave Phraates IV an Italian slave-girl, who later became Queen [[Musa of Parthia]]. To ensure that her child Phraataces would inherit the throne without incident, Musa convinced Phraates IV to give his other sons to Augustus as hostages. Again, Augustus used this as propaganda depicting the submission of Parthia to Rome, listing it as a great accomplishment in his ''[[Res Gestae Divi Augusti]]''.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=67}}; {{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=96–9}}.</ref> When Phraataces took the throne as [[Phraates V]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;2&nbsp;BC – 4&nbsp;AD), Musa ruled alongside him, and according to [[Josephus]], married him. The Parthian nobility, disapproving of the notion of a king with non-Arsacid blood, forced the pair into exile in Roman territory.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=68}}; {{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=97–9}}; see also {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=80}}.</ref> Phraates' successor [[Orodes III of Parthia]] lasted just two years on the throne, and was followed by [[Vonones I]], who had adopted many Roman mannerisms during time in Rome. The Parthian nobility, angered by Vonones' sympathies for the Romans, backed a rival claimant, [[Artabanus II of Parthia]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;10–38&nbsp;AD), who eventually defeated Vonones and drove him into exile in Roman Syria.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=68–9}}; {{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=97–9}}.</ref>

During the reign of Artabanus II, two Jewish commoners and brothers, [[Anilai and Asinai]] from [[Nehardea]] (near modern [[Fallujah]], Iraq),{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=69–71}} led a revolt against the Parthian governor of Babylonia. After defeating the latter, the two were granted the right to govern the region by Artabanus II, who feared further rebellion elsewhere.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=71}} Anilai's Parthian wife poisoned Asinai out of fear he would attack Anilai over his marriage to a [[gentile]]. Following this, Anilai became embroiled in an armed conflict with a son-in-law of Artabanus, who eventually defeated him.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=71–2}} With the Jewish regime removed, the native Babylonians began to harass the [[Iraqi Jews|local Jewish community]], forcing them to emigrate to Seleucia. When that city rebelled against Parthian rule in 35–36&nbsp;AD, the Jews were expelled again, this time by the local [[Greeks]] and [[Aramaeans]]. The exiled Jews fled to Ctesiphon, Nehardea, and [[Nisibis]].{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=72–3}}

[[File:Augustus Denarius 19 BC 2230399.jpg|thumb|right|A [[denarius]] struck in 19&nbsp;BC during the reign of [[Augustus]], with the goddess [[Feronia (mythology)|Feronia]] depicted on the obverse, and on the reverse a Parthian man kneeling in submission while offering the Roman [[Aquila (Roman)|military standards]] taken at the [[Battle of Carrhae]]{{efn|For more information on Roman coins depicting Parthians returning the lost military standards to Rome, see {{harvnb|Brosius|2006|pp=137–8}}.}}]]

Although at peace with Parthia, Rome still interfered in its affairs. The Roman emperor [[Tiberius]] (r.&nbsp;14–37&nbsp;AD) became involved in a plot by [[Pharasmanes I of Iberia]] to place his brother [[Mithridates of Armenia|Mithridates]] on the throne of Armenia by assassinating the Parthian ally King Arsaces of Armenia.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=73}} Artabanus II tried and failed to restore Parthian control of Armenia, prompting an aristocratic revolt that forced him to flee to [[Scythia]]. The Romans released a hostage prince, [[Tiridates III of Parthia]], to rule the region as an ally of Rome. Shortly before his death, Artabanus managed to force Tiridates from the throne using troops from Hyrcania.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=73–4}} After Artabanus' death in 38&nbsp;AD, a long civil war ensued between the rightful successor [[Vardanes I]] and his brother [[Gotarzes II of Parthia|Gotarzes II]].{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=75–6}} After Vardanes was assassinated during a hunting expedition, the Parthian nobility appealed to Roman emperor [[Claudius]] (''r''. 41–54&nbsp;AD) in 49&nbsp;AD to release the hostage prince [[Meherdates]] to challenge Gotarzes. This backfired when Meherdates was betrayed by the governor of [[Edessa, Mesopotamia|Edessa]] and [[Izates bar Monobaz]] of [[Adiabene]]; he was captured and sent to Gotarzes, where he was allowed to live after having his ears mutilated, an act that disqualified him from inheriting the throne.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=76–8}}

In 97&nbsp;AD, the Chinese general [[Ban Chao]], the [[Protectorate of the Western Regions|Protector-General of the Western Regions]], sent his emissary [[Gan Ying]] on a diplomatic mission to reach the Roman Empire. Gan visited the court of [[Pacorus II]] at Hecatompylos before departing towards Rome.{{sfnp|Watson|1983|pp=543–4}} He traveled as far west as the [[Persian Gulf]], where Parthian authorities convinced him that an arduous sea voyage around the [[Arabian Peninsula]] was the only means to reach Rome.<ref>{{harvp|Watson|1983|pp=543–4}}; {{harvp|Yu|1986|pp=460–1}}; {{harvp|de Crespigny|2007|pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=49OvCQAAQBAJ&pg=PA239 239–40]}}; see also {{harvp|Wang|2007|p=101}}.</ref> Discouraged by this, Gan Ying returned to the Han court and provided [[Emperor He of Han]] (''r''.&nbsp;88–105&nbsp;AD) with a detailed report on the Roman Empire based on oral accounts of his Parthian hosts.<ref>{{harvp|Wood|2002|pp=[https://archive.org/details/silkroadtwothous0000wood/page/46/mode/1up?q=procurator 46–7]}}; {{harvp|Morton|Lewis|2005|p=59}}.</ref> William Watson speculates that the Parthians would have been relieved at the failed efforts by the Han Empire to open diplomatic relations with Rome, especially after Ban Chao's [[Han–Xiongnu War|military victories]] against the [[Xiongnu]] in [[Tarim Basin|eastern Central Asia]].{{sfnp|Watson|1983|pp=543–4}} However, Chinese records maintain that a [[Daqin|Roman embassy]], perhaps only a group of [[Roman commerce|Roman merchants]], arrived at the Han capital [[Luoyang]] by way of [[Jiaozhi]] (northern [[Vietnam]]) in 166&nbsp;AD, during the reigns of [[Marcus Aurelius]] (''r''. 161–180&nbsp;AD) and [[Emperor Huan of Han]] (''r''. 146–168&nbsp;AD).<ref>{{harvp|Yu|1986|pp=460–1}}; {{harvp|de Crespigny|2007|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=49OvCQAAQBAJ&pg=PA600 600]}}.</ref> Although it could be coincidental, [[Antonine]] Roman golden [[medal]]lions dated to the reigns of Marcus Aurelius and his predecessor [[Antoninus Pius]] have been discovered at [[Oc Eo]], Vietnam (among other Roman artefacts in the [[Mekong Delta]]), a site that is one of the suggested locations for the port city of "[[Cattigara]]" along the ''[[Magnus Sinus]]'' (i.e. [[Gulf of Thailand]] and [[South China Sea]]) in [[Ptolemy]]'s ''[[Geography (Ptolemy)|Geography]]''.<ref>{{harvp|Young|2001|p=29}}; {{harvp|Mawer|2013|p=38}}; {{harvp|Ball|2000|p=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=8Q2XxXx5ZdsC&pg=PA135 135]}}.</ref>

===Continuation of Roman hostilities and Parthian decline===
{{Main|Roman–Parthian War of 58–63|Trajan's Parthian campaign|Roman–Parthian War of 161–166|Parthian war of Caracalla}}

{{Further|Roman Armenia}}
[[File:Roman-Parthian War 58-60.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|Map of the troop movements during the first two years of the [[Roman–Parthian War of 58–63]] AD over the [[Kingdom of Armenia (antiquity)|Kingdom of Armenia]], detailing the Roman offensive into [[Armenia]] and capture of the country by [[Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo]]]]
[[File:King cornucopia Louvre Sb7302.jpg|thumb|Parthian king making an offering to the god [[Herakles]]-[[Verethragna]]. [[Masdjid-e Suleiman]], [[Iran]]. 2nd–3rd century AD. Louvre Museum Sb 7302.]]

After the [[Kingdom of Iberia (antiquity)|Iberian king]] Pharasmanes I had his son [[Rhadamistus]] (''r''.&nbsp;51–55&nbsp;AD) invade Armenia to depose the Roman client king Mithridates, [[Vologases I of Parthia]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;51–77&nbsp;AD) planned to invade and place his brother, the later [[Tiridates I of Armenia]], on the throne.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=79}} Rhadamistus was eventually driven from power, and, beginning with the reign of Tiridates, Parthia would retain firm control over Armenia—with brief interruptions—through the [[Arsacid dynasty of Armenia]].<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=79–81}}; {{harvp|Kennedy|1996|p=81}}.</ref> Even after the fall of the Parthian Empire, the Arsacid line lived on through the Armenian kings.<ref>{{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=82}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=79–81}}.</ref> However, not only did the Arsacid line continue through the Armenians, it also continued through the [[Georgia (country)|Georgian]] kings with the [[Arsacid dynasty of Iberia]], and for many centuries afterwards in [[Caucasian Albania]] through the [[Arsacid dynasty of Caucasian Albania]].{{r|n=Bausani1971_41|r={{harvp|Bausani|1971|p=[https://archive.org/details/persiansfromearl0000baus/page/41/mode/1up?q=Albania 41]}}.}}

When [[Vardanes II of Parthia]] rebelled against his father Vologases I in 55&nbsp;AD, Vologases withdrew his forces from Armenia. Rome quickly attempted to fill the political vacuum left behind.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=81}} In the [[Roman–Parthian War of 58–63]]&nbsp;AD, the commander [[Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo]] achieved some military successes against the Parthians while installing [[Tigranes VI of Armenia]] as a Roman client.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=81–5}} However, Corbulo's successor [[Lucius Caesennius Paetus]] was soundly defeated by Parthian forces and fled Armenia.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=83–5}} Following a peace treaty, Tiridates I traveled to [[Naples]] and Rome in 63 AD. At both sites the Roman emperor [[Nero]] (''r''.&nbsp;54–68&nbsp;AD) ceremoniously crowned him king of Armenia by placing the royal [[diadem]] on his head.<ref>{{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=99–100}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=85}}.</ref>

A long period of peace between Parthia and Rome ensued, with only the invasion of [[Alans]] into Parthia's eastern territories around 72&nbsp;AD mentioned by Roman historians.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=86}} Whereas Augustus and Nero had chosen a cautious military policy when confronting Parthia, later Roman emperors invaded and attempted to conquer the eastern [[Fertile Crescent]], the heart of the Parthian Empire along the [[Tigris River|Tigris]] and [[Euphrates]]. The heightened aggression can be explained in part by Rome's military reforms.{{sfnp|Kennedy|1996|pp=67, 87–8}} To match Parthia's strength in missile troops and mounted warriors, the Romans at first used foreign allies (especially [[Nabataeans]]), but later established a permanent ''[[auxilia]]'' force to complement their heavy legionary infantry.{{sfnp|Kennedy|1996|p=87}} The Romans eventually maintained regiments of horse archers (''[[sagittarii]]'') and even mail-armored [[cataphract]]s in their eastern provinces.<ref>{{harvp|Kennedy|1996|pp=87–8}}; see also {{harvp|Kurz|1983|pp=561–2}}.</ref> Yet the Romans had no discernible [[grand strategy]] in dealing with Parthia and gained very little territory from these invasions.{{sfnp|Sheldon|2010|pp=231–2}} The primary motivations for war were the advancement of the personal glory and political position of the emperor, as well as defending Roman honor against perceived slights such as Parthian interference in the affairs of Rome's client states.{{sfnp|Sheldon|2010|pp=9–10, 231–5}}

[[File:Parthian King Vologases at Behistun.jpg|thumb|upright|left|[[Vologases's relief|Rock relief]] of Parthian king at [[Mount Behistun|Behistun]], most likely [[Vologases III of Parthia|Vologases III]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;110–147&nbsp;AD){{sfnp|Olbrycht|2016|p=96}}]]

Hostilities between Rome and Parthia were renewed when [[Osroes I of Parthia]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;109–128&nbsp;AD) deposed the Armenian king [[Sanatruk]] and replaced him with [[Axidares of Armenia|Axidares]], son of Pacorus II, without consulting Rome.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=86–7}} The Roman emperor [[Trajan]] (''r''.&nbsp;98–117&nbsp;AD) had the next Parthian nominee for the throne, [[Parthamasiris of Armenia|Parthamasiris]], killed in 114&nbsp;AD, instead making Armenia a Roman province.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=88}}; {{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|p=13}}; {{harvp|Lightfoot|1990|p=117}}.</ref> His forces, led by [[Lusius Quietus]], also captured Nisibis; its occupation was essential to securing all the major routes across the northern Mesopotamian plain.<ref>{{harvp|Lightfoot|1990|pp=117–8}}; see also {{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=90–1}}.</ref> The following year, Trajan invaded Mesopotamia and met little resistance from only [[Meharaspes]] of Adiabene, since Osroes was engaged in a civil war to the east with [[Vologases III of Parthia]].{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=88–9}} Trajan spent the winter of 115–116 at Antioch, but resumed his campaign in the spring. Marching down the Euphrates, he captured Dura-Europos, the capital Ctesiphon<ref>{{cite book |last=Ralby |first=Aaron |date=2013 |chapter=Emperor Trajan, 98–117: Greatest Extent of Rome |title=Atlas of Military History |publisher=[[Parragon]] |isbn=9781472309631 |p=[https://archive.org/details/atlasofworldmili0000ralb_j5i6/page/239/mode/1up?q=nabataea 239]}}</ref> and Seleucia, and even subjugated Characene, where he watched ships depart to India from the [[Persian Gulf]].<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=88–90}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=81}}; {{harvp|Lightfoot|1990|p=120}}; see also {{harvp|Katouzian|2009|p=[https://archive.org/details/the-persians-ancient-mediaeval-and-modern-iran/page/44/mode/1up 44]}}.</ref>

In the last months of 116&nbsp;AD, Trajan captured the Persian city of Susa. When [[Sanatruces II of Parthia]] gathered forces in eastern Parthia to challenge the Romans, his cousin [[Parthamaspates of Parthia]] betrayed and killed him: Trajan crowned him the new king of Parthia.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=90–1}} Never again would the Roman Empire advance so far to the east. On Trajan's return north, the Babylonian settlements revolted against the Roman garrisons.<ref>{{harvp|Lightfoot|1990|p=120}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=90–1}}.</ref> Trajan was forced to retreat from Mesopotamia in 117&nbsp;AD, overseeing a failed siege of [[Hatra]] during his withdrawal.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=91}}; {{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|p=13}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=81}}.</ref> His retreat was—in his intentions—temporary, because he wanted to renew the attack on Parthia in 118 AD and "make the subjection of the Parthians a reality,"{{sfnp|Mommsen|2004|loc=p. 69 (p. [https://books.google.ca/books?id=uWEKAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA74 74] 1887 ed.)}} but Trajan died suddenly in August 117&nbsp;AD. During his campaign, Trajan was granted the title ''Parthicus'' by the Senate and coins were minted proclaiming the conquest of Parthia.<ref>{{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=90–1}}; see also {{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=137}} and {{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|p=13}}.</ref> However, only the 4th-century AD historians [[Eutropius (historian)|Eutropius]] and [[Festus (historian)|Festus]] allege that he attempted to establish a [[Mesopotamia (Roman province)|Roman province]] in lower Mesopotamia.{{sfnp|Lightfoot|1990|pp=120–4}}

[[File:ParthianInChains.jpg|thumb|A Parthian (right) wearing a [[Phrygian cap]], depicted as a prisoner of war in chains held by a Roman (left); [[Arch of Septimius Severus]], Rome, 203&nbsp;AD]]

Trajan's successor [[Hadrian]] (''r''.&nbsp;117–138&nbsp;AD) reaffirmed the [[Roman-Parthian Wars|Roman-Parthian]] border at the Euphrates, choosing not to invade Mesopotamia due to Rome's now limited military resources.<ref>{{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=100}}; see also {{harvp|Lightfoot|1990|p=115}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=81}}; and {{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=91}}.</ref> Parthamaspates fled after the Parthians revolted against him, yet the Romans made him king of [[Osroene]]. Osroes I died during his conflict with Vologases III, the latter succeeded by [[Vologases IV of Parthia]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;147–191&nbsp;AD) who ushered in a period of peace and stability.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=92–3}} However, the [[Roman–Parthian War of 161–166]]&nbsp;AD began when Vologases invaded Armenia and Syria, retaking Edessa. Roman emperor [[Marcus Aurelius]] (''r''.&nbsp;161–180&nbsp;AD) had co-ruler [[Lucius Verus]] (''r''.&nbsp;161–169&nbsp;AD) guard Syria while [[Marcus Statius Priscus]] invaded Armenia in 163&nbsp;AD, followed by the invasion of Mesopotamia by [[Avidius Cassius]] in 164&nbsp;AD.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|p=93}} The Romans captured and burnt Seleucia and Ctesiphon to the ground, yet they were forced to retreat once the Roman soldiers contracted a [[Antonine Plague|deadly disease]] (possibly [[smallpox]]) that soon ravaged the Roman world.<ref>{{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=100}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=93–4}}.</ref> Although they withdrew, from this point forward the city of Dura-Europos remained in Roman hands.<ref>{{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|p=13}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=93–4}}.</ref> When Roman emperor [[Septimius Severus]] (''r''.&nbsp;193–211&nbsp;AD) invaded Mesopotamia in 197&nbsp;AD during the reign of [[Vologases V of Parthia]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;191–208&nbsp;AD), the Romans once again marched down the Euphrates and captured Seleucia and Ctesiphon. After assuming the title ''Parthicus Maximus'', he retreated in late 198&nbsp;AD, failing as Trajan once did to capture Hatra during a siege.<ref>{{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=100}}; {{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|p=13}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=94}}; {{harvp|Katouzian|2009|p=[https://archive.org/details/the-persians-ancient-mediaeval-and-modern-iran/page/44/mode/1up 44]}}.</ref>

Around 212&nbsp;AD, soon after [[Vologases VI of Parthia]] (''r''. c.&nbsp;208–222&nbsp;AD) took the throne, his brother [[Artabanus IV of Parthia]] (d.&nbsp;224&nbsp;AD) rebelled against him and gained control over a greater part of the empire.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=94–5}} Meanwhile, the Roman emperor [[Caracalla]] (''r''.&nbsp;211–217&nbsp;AD) deposed the kings of Osroene and Armenia to make them Roman provinces once more. He marched into Mesopotamia under the pretext of marrying one of Artabanus' daughters, but the marriage was not allowed. Consequently, Caracalla made war on Parthia, conquering [[Arbil]]{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=94–5}} and sacking the Parthian tombs there.{{sfnp|Chegini|1996|p=40}} Caracalla was assassinated the next year on the road to Carrhae by his soldiers.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=94–5}} At the [[Battle of Nisibis (217)|Battle of Nisibis]], the Parthians were able to defeat the Romans, but both sides suffered heavy losses.<ref>{{cite book |last=Herodian of Antioch |author-link=Herodian |date=1961 |title=History of the Roman Empire, from the Death of Marcus Aurelius to the Accession of Gordian III |translator=Edward C. Echols |publisher=[[University of California Press]] |at=Book 4 15.5 |via=Livius.org |url=https://www.livius.org/sources/content/herodian-s-roman-history/herodian-4.15/}}</ref> After this debacle, the Parthians made a settlement with [[Macrinus]] (''r''.&nbsp;217–218) where the Romans paid Parthia over two-hundred million ''[[Denarius|denarii]]'' with additional gifts.<ref>{{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=100–1}}; see also {{harvp|Katouzian|2009|p=[https://archive.org/details/the-persians-ancient-mediaeval-and-modern-iran/page/44/mode/1up 44]}}.</ref>

The Parthian Empire, weakened by internal strife and wars with Rome, was soon to be followed by the [[Sasanian Empire]]. Indeed, shortly afterward, [[Ardashir I]], the local Iranian ruler of Persis (modern [[Fars province]], Iran) from [[Istakhr]] began subjugating the surrounding territories in defiance of Arsacid rule.{{r|n=Bros2006_101_Biv1983_956_Sar2007_14_Kat2009_44|r={{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=101}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=95–6}}; {{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|p=14}}; see also {{harvp|Katouzian|2009|p=[https://archive.org/details/the-persians-ancient-mediaeval-and-modern-iran/page/44/mode/1up 44]}}.}} He confronted Artabanus IV at the [[Battle of Hormozdgān]] on 28 April 224&nbsp;AD, perhaps at a site near [[Isfahan]], defeating him and establishing the Sasanian Empire.{{r|Bros2006_101_Biv1983_956_Sar2007_14_Kat2009_44}} There is evidence, however, that suggests Vologases VI continued to mint coins at Seleucia as late as 228&nbsp;AD.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=95–6}}

The Sassanians would not only assume Parthia's legacy as Rome's Persian nemesis, but they would also attempt to restore the boundaries of the Achaemenid Empire by [[Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628|briefly conquering]] the Levant, Anatolia, and Egypt from the [[Eastern Roman Empire]] during the reign of [[Khosrau II]] (''r''.&nbsp;590–628&nbsp;AD).{{sfnp|Frye|1983|pp=173–4}} However, they would lose these territories to [[Heraclius]]—the last Roman emperor before the [[Early Muslim conquests|Arab conquests]]. Nevertheless, for a period of more than 400 years, they succeeded the Parthian realm as Rome's principal rival.<ref>{{cite book |last=Stillman |first=Norman A. |date=1979 |title=The Jews of Arab Lands. A History and Source Book |publisher=[[Jewish Publication Society|Jewish Publication Society of America]] |pp=[https://books.google.ca/books?id=bFN2ismyhEYC&pg=PA22 22]  |isbn=0827601980 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |editor-last1=Jeffreys |editor-first1=Elizabeth |editor-last2=Gilliland |editor-first2=Judith |date=2006 |title=Proceedings of the 21st International Congress of Byzantine Studies, London, 21–26 August 2006 |volume=1 |publisher=[[Ashgate Publishing|Ashgate]] |pp=29 |isbn=075465740X }}</ref>

===Native and external sources===
{{multiple image| align = right | direction = horizontal | header = | header_align = left/right/center | footer = Parthian gold jewelry items found at a burial site in [[Nineveh]] (near modern [[Mosul]], Iraq) in the [[British Museum]]| footer_align = left | image1 = Parthian gold funerary objects by Nickmard Khoey.jpg | width1 = 126 | caption1 = | image2 = Parthian jewelry from Nineveh by Nickmard Khoey.jpg | width2 = 174 | caption2 = }}

Local and foreign written accounts, as well as non-textual artifacts, have been used to reconstruct Parthian history.{{sfnp|Widengren|1983|pp=1261–2}} Although the Parthian court maintained records, the Parthians had no formal study of [[history]]; the earliest [[Universal history (genre)|universal history]] of Iran, the ''[[Khwaday-Namag]]'', was not compiled until the reign of the last Sasanian ruler [[Yazdegerd III]] (r. 632–651&nbsp;AD).{{sfnp|Yarshater|1983|p=359}} Indigenous [[Primary source|sources]] on Parthian history remain scarce, with fewer of them available than for any other period of Iranian history.{{sfnp|Widengren|1983|p=1261}} Most contemporary written records on Parthia contain Greek as well as Parthian and Aramaic inscriptions.{{sfnp|Garthwaite|2005|pp=[https://archive.org/details/persians0000gart/page/75/mode/1up 75–6]}} The Parthian language was written in a distinct script derived from the [[Aramaic alphabet#Achaemenid Empire (The First Persian Empire)|Imperial Aramaic chancellery script]] of the Achaemenids, and later developed into the [[Pahlavi scripts|Pahlavi writing system]].{{sfnp|Boyce|1983|pp=1151–2}}

[[File:Samartian-Persian necklace and amulet.png|thumb|A Sarmatian-Parthian gold necklace and amulet, 2nd century AD. Located in Tamoikin Art Fund]]

The most valuable indigenous sources for reconstructing an accurate chronology of Arsacid rulers are the metal [[Ancient drachma|drachma]] coins issued by each ruler.<ref>{{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=67}}; {{harvp|Widengren|1983|p=1262}}; {{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/79/mode/1up 79–80]}}.</ref> These represent a "transition from non-textual to textual remains," according to historian [[Geo Widengren]].{{sfnp|Widengren|1983|p=1262}} Other Parthian sources used for reconstructing chronology include [[cuneiform]] astronomical tablets and colophons discovered in Babylonia.{{sfnp|Widengren|1983|p=1265}} Indigenous textual sources also include stone [[inscription]]s, [[parchment]] and [[papyri]] documents, and pottery [[ostraca]].{{sfnp|Widengren|1983|p=1262}} For example, at the early Parthian capital of Mithradatkert/Nisa in Turkmenistan, large caches of pottery ostraca have been found yielding information on the sale and storage of items like wine.<ref>{{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|pp=75–6}}; {{harvp|Widengren|1983|p=1263}}; {{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=118–9}}.</ref> Along with parchment documents found at sites like Dura-Europos, these also provide valuable information on Parthian governmental administration, covering issues such as taxation, military titles, and provincial organization.<ref>{{harvp|Widengren|1983|p=1263}}; {{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=118–9}}.</ref>

[[File:Golden Necklace - Parthian Empire 2nd AD.JPG|thumb|left|Parthian golden necklace, 2nd century AD, Iran, [[Reza Abbasi Museum]]]]
[[File:Iran-bastan-32.jpg|thumb|left|A Parthian ceramic [[oil lamp]], [[Khuzestan province|Khuzestan Province]], Iran, [[National Museum of Iran]]]]

The [[Greek historiography|Greek]] and [[Roman historiography|Latin histories]], which represent the majority of materials covering Parthian history, are not considered entirely reliable since they were written from the perspective of rivals and wartime enemies.<ref>{{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|pp=67, 75}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|p=22}}.</ref> These external sources generally concern major military and political events, and often ignore social and cultural aspects of Parthian history.<ref>{{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=75}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=80–1}}.</ref> The Romans usually depicted the Parthians as fierce warriors but also as a culturally refined people; recipes for Parthian dishes in the cookbook ''[[Apicius]]'' exemplifies their admiration for Parthian cuisine.{{sfnp|Kurz|1983|p=564}}{{efn|"Curiously, at the same time as the Parthian was depicted as uncivilised, he was also 'orientalised' in traditional fashion, being described as luxury-loving, leading an effeminate lifestyle, and demonstrating excessive sexuality."{{sfnp|Brosius|2006|p=138}}}} [[Apollodorus of Artemita]] and [[Arrian]] wrote histories focusing on Parthia, which are now lost and survive only as quoted extracts in other histories.{{sfnp|Widengren|1983|pp=1261, 1264}} [[Isidore of Charax]], who lived during the reign of Augustus, provides an account of Parthian territories, perhaps from a Parthian government survey.{{sfnp|Widengren|1983|p=1264}} To a lesser extent, people and events of Parthian history were also included in the histories of [[Justin (historian)|Justin]], [[Strabo]], [[Diodorus Siculus]], [[Plutarch]], [[Cassius Dio]], [[Appian]], [[Josephus]], [[Pliny the Elder]], and [[Herodian]].{{sfnp|Widengren|1983|pp=1265–6}}

Parthian history can also be reconstructed via the [[Twenty-Four Histories|Chinese historical records]] of events.{{sfnp|Widengren|1983|pp=1265, 1267}} In contrast to Greek and Roman histories, the early Chinese histories maintained a more neutral view when describing Parthia,<ref>{{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/80/mode/1up 80]}}; {{harvp|Posch|1998|p=363}}.</ref> although the habit of Chinese chroniclers to copy material for their accounts from older works (of undetermined origin) makes it difficult to establish a chronological order of events.{{sfnp|Posch|1998|p=358}} The Chinese called Parthia ''{{ill|Ānxī|zh|安息|vertical-align=sup}}'', perhaps after the Greek name for the Parthian city [[Merv|Antiochia in Margiana]] (Greek: Ἀντιόχεια ἡ ἐν τῇ Μαργιανῇ).{{sfnp|Watson|1983|pp=541–2}} However, this could also have been a transliteration of "Arsaces", after the dynasty's eponymous founder.{{sfnp|Wang|2007|p=90}} The works and historical authors include the ''[[Records of the Grand Historian|Shiji]]'' (also known as the ''Records of the Grand Historian'') by [[Sima Qian]], the ''[[Book of Han|Han shu]]'' (Book of Han) by [[Ban Biao]], [[Ban Gu]], and [[Ban Zhao]], and the ''[[Book of Later Han|Hou Han shu]]'' (Book of Later Han) by [[Fan Ye (historian)|Fan Ye]].{{sfnp|Wang|2007|p=88}} They provide information on the nomadic migrations leading up to the early [[Saka]] invasion of Parthia and valuable political and geographical information.{{sfnp|Widengren|1983|pp=1265, 1267}} For example, the ''Shiji'' (ch. 123) describes diplomatic exchanges, exotic gifts given by Mithridates II to the [[Han dynasty|Han court]], types of agricultural crops grown in Parthia, production of wine using grapes, itinerant merchants, and the size and location of Parthian territory.<ref>{{harvp|Wang|2007|pp=89–90}}; {{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/90/mode/1up 90–1], 122}}.</ref> The ''Shiji'' also mentions that the Parthians kept records by "writing horizontally on strips of leather," that is, parchment.<ref>{{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=118}}; see also {{harvp|Wang|2007|p=90}} for a similar translation.</ref>

In Islamic sources, the Parthian dynasty is mentioned with three dynastic branch names: Aškāniān (اشکانیان), Ašġāniān (اشغانیان), and Afquršāhān (افقورشاهان). The obvious differences between the names of Parthian dynastic branches in Islamic sources has been forgotten by modern Persian-speaking historians. Intentionally or unintentionally, because the translators and correctors of Arabic to Persian sources changed the letter "ġ" (غ) to "k" (ک) in all historical texts and also changed the word of "Persia" to "Iran", the true intention of the Islamic historical sources have been forgotten. As the consequence, these different dynastic branches have become a single dynasty in the form of the name Aškāniān (اشکانیان) in the new editions of Islamic sources.<ref>{{cite book |last=Kalani |first=Reza |date=2022 |title=Indo-Parthians and the Rise of Sasanians |location=[[Tehran]] |publisher=Tahouri Publishers |pp=95-111}}</ref> It is known, however, that the Arsacid royal family line survived within three ruling dynasties belonging to [[History of Armenia|Armenia]], [[Caucasian Iberia]], and [[Aghbania]] in the Caucasus.{{r|Bausani1971_41}}

==Government and administration==
===Central authority and semi-autonomous kings===
{{Main|List of Parthian kings}}

[[File:Coin of the Elymais king Kamnaskires III with his queen Anzaze.jpg|thumb|Coin of [[Kamnaskires III]], king of [[Elymais]] (modern [[Khūzestān Province]]), and his wife Queen [[Anzaze]], 1st century BC]]
Compared with the earlier Achaemenid Empire, the Parthian government was notably [[Decentralization|decentralized]].{{sfnp|Garthwaite|2005|pp=[https://archive.org/details/persians0000gart/page/67/mode/1up 67–8]}} An indigenous historical source reveals that territories overseen by the central government were organized in a similar manner to the Seleucid Empire. They both had a threefold division for their provincial hierarchies: the Parthian [[marzbān]], xšatrap, and dizpat, similar to the Seleucid [[satrapy]], [[eparchy]], and hyparchy.{{sfnp|Widengren|1983|p=1263}} The Parthian Empire also contained several subordinate semi-autonomous kingdoms, including the states of [[Kingdom of Iberia (antiquity)|Caucasian Iberia]], [[Kingdom of Armenia (antiquity)|Armenia]], [[Atropatene]], [[Gordyene]], [[Adiabene]], [[Edessa, Mesopotamia|Edessa]], [[Kingdom of Hatra|Hatra]], [[Mesene]], [[Elymais]], and [[Kings of Persis|Persis]].{{sfnp|Lukonin|1983|p=701}} The state rulers governed their own territories and minted their own coinage distinct from the royal coinage produced at the imperial mints.<ref>{{harvp|Lukonin|1983|p=701}}; {{harvp|Sarkhosh Curtis|2007|pp=19–21}}.</ref> This was not unlike the earlier Achaemenid Empire, which also had some city-states, and even distant satrapies who were semi-independent but "recognised the supremacy of the king, paid tribute and provided military support", according to Brosius.{{sfnp|Brosius|2006|pp=113–4}} However, the satraps of Parthian times governed smaller territories, and perhaps had less prestige and influence than their Achaemenid predecessors.{{sfnp|Brosius|2006|pp=115–6}} During the Seleucid period, the trend of local ruling dynasties with semi-autonomous rule, and sometimes outright rebellious rule, became commonplace, a fact reflected in the later Parthian style of governance.{{sfnp|Brosius|2006|pp=114–5}}

===Nobility===
{{Further|Seven Great Houses of Iran|List of rulers of Parthian sub-kingdoms}}
[[File:YoungManWithParthianCostume.jpg|thumb|upright|A statue of a young Palmyran in fine Parthian trousers, from a funerary [[stele]] at [[Palmyra]], early 3rd century AD]]

The King of Kings headed the Parthian government. He maintained [[polygamous]] relations, and was usually succeeded by his first-born son.{{r|n=Brosius2006_1034|r={{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=[https://archive.org/details/persiansintroduc0000bros/page/103/mode/1up 103–4]}}.}} Like the Ptolemies of Egypt, there is also record of Arsacid kings marrying their nieces and perhaps even half-sisters; [[Musa of Parthia|Queen Musa]] is said by [[Josephus]] to have married her own son, though this would be an extreme and isolated case.{{r|Brosius2006_1034}} Brosius provides an extract from a letter written in Greek by King Artabanus II in 21&nbsp;AD, which addresses the governor (titled "[[archon]]") and citizens of the city of [[Susa]]. Specific government offices of Preferred Friend, Bodyguard and Treasurer are mentioned and the document also proves that "while there were local jurisdictions and proceedings to appointment to high office, the king could intervene on behalf of an individual, review a case and amend the local ruling if he considered it appropriate."{{sfnp|Brosius|2006|p=119}}

The hereditary titles of the hierarchic nobility recorded during the reign of the first Sasanian monarch Ardashir I most likely reflect the titles already in use during the Parthian era.{{sfnp|Lukonin|1983|pp=699–700}} There were three distinct tiers of nobility, the highest being the regional kings directly below the King of Kings, the second being those related to the King of Kings only through marriage, and the lowest order being heads of local clans and small territories.{{sfnp|Lukonin|1983|pp=700–4}}

By the 1st century AD, the Parthian nobility had assumed great power and influence in the succession and deposition of Arsacid kings.{{sfnp|Brosius|2006|pp=99–100, 104}} Some of the nobility functioned as court advisers to the king, as well as holy priests.{{sfnp|Brosius|2006|pp=104–5, 117–8}} [[Strabo]], in his ''[[Geographica]]'', preserved a claim by the Greek philosopher and historian [[Poseidonius]] that the Council of Parthia consisted of noble kinsmen and [[magi]], the two groups from which "the kings were appointed."<ref>{{Cite book |date=1961 |orig-date=1928 |translator=Horace Leonard Jones |title=The Geography of Strabo |series=(in 8 volumes) |volume=V |lang=el, en |publisher=[[Harvard University Press]] |at=Book 11 Ch. 9.3 (pp. [https://archive.org/details/Strabo08Geography17AndIndex/Strabo%2005%20Geography%2010-12/page/275/mode/1up 275-7]) }} See also online text at [https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Strabo/11I*.html penelope.uchicago.edu].</ref> Of the great noble Parthian families listed at the beginning of the Sassanian period, only two are explicitly mentioned in earlier Parthian documents: the [[House of Suren]] and the [[House of Karen]].{{sfnp|Lukonin|1983|pp=704–5}} The historian [[Plutarch]] noted that members of the Suren family, the first among the nobility, were given the privilege of crowning each new Arsacid King of Kings during their coronations.<ref>{{harvp|Lukonin|1983|p=704}}; {{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=104}}.</ref>

===Military===
{{Further|Parthian army}}

The Parthian Empire had no [[standing army]], yet were able to quickly recruit troops in the event of local crises.<ref>{{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=116, 122}}; {{harvp|Sheldon|2010|pp=231–2}}.</ref> There was a permanent armed guard attached to the person of the king, comprising nobles, [[serf]]s and [[mercenaries]], but this royal retinue was small.{{sfnp|Kennedy|1996|p=84}} Garrisons were also permanently maintained at border forts; Parthian inscriptions reveal some of the military titles granted to the commanders of these locations.{{sfnp|Kennedy|1996|p=84}} Military forces could also be used in diplomatic gestures. For example, when Chinese envoys visited Parthia in the late 2nd century BC, the ''[[Shiji]]'' maintains that 20,000 horsemen were sent to the eastern borders to serve as escorts for the embassy, although this figure is perhaps an exaggeration.{{sfnp|Wang|2007|pp=99–100}} 
{{multiple image
| image1            = ParthianHorseman.jpg
| caption1          = Parthian [[horse archer]], now on display at the [[Palazzo Madama, Turin]]
| image2            = ParthianCataphract.JPG
| caption2          = Parthian [[cataphract]] fighting a lion
| image3            = Zahhak castle stucco 2.JPG
| caption3          = Relief of an infantryman, from [[Zahhak Castle]], Iran
| total_width       = 500
| footer            = The combination of horse archers and cataphracts formed an effective backbone for the Parthian military
}}

The main striking force of the Parthian army was its [[cataphract]]s, heavy cavalry with man and horse decked in [[Mail (armour)|mailed armor]].{{r|n=Bro2006_120_Gar2005_78|r={{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=120}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=78}}.}} The cataphracts were equipped with a [[Kontos (weapon)|''kontos'' lance]] for charging into enemy lines,<ref>{{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=120}}; {{harvp|Kennedy|1996|p=84}}; {{harvp|Bivar|1983|pp=31–3}}.</ref> but were not equipped with bows and arrows which were restricted to horse archers.<ref>{{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=120}}; {{harvp|Kennedy|1996|p=84}}.</ref> These units proved particularly decisive in open field battles and later influenced heavy cavalry traditions in Roman and Sasanian armies.{{sfnp|Bivar|1983|pp=31–3}} Due to the cost of their equipment and armor, cataphracts were recruited from among the aristocratic class who, in return for their services, demanded a measure of autonomy at the local level from the Arsacid kings.<ref>{{harvp|Brosius|2006|pp=116–8}}; see also {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=78}} and {{harvp|Kennedy|1996|p=84}}.</ref> The light cavalry was recruited from among the commoner class and acted as [[horse archer]]s; they wore a simple tunic and trousers into battle.{{r|Bro2006_120_Gar2005_78}} They used [[composite bow]]s and were able to shoot at enemies while riding and facing away from them; this technique, known as the [[Parthian shot]], was a highly effective tactic.<ref>{{harvp|Brosius|2006|p=120}}; {{harvp|Garthwaite|2005|p=78}}; {{harvp|Kurz|1983|p=561}}.</ref> It appears that most of the Parthian army was cavalry, for tactical and strategic reasons. The light cavalry is thought to have carried a sword into battle as well, while cataphracts likely were also armed with short swords or knives.{{sfnp|Shahbazi|2019|}} The Parthians also made use of the [[camel]] in armed combat.{{sfnp|Shahbazi|2019|}} The heavy and light cavalry of Parthia proved to be a decisive factor in the [[Battle of Carrhae]] where a Parthian force defeated a much larger Roman army under Crassus. Light infantry units, composed of [[Conscription|levied commoners]] and mercenaries, were used to disperse enemy troops after cavalry charges.{{sfnp|Brosius|2006|p=122}}

The Parthians do not appear to have ever used [[Chariot|war chariots]] in battle.
