Westernization drove the idea that all sexual behavior not resulting in reproduction was aberrant.<ref name="SullivanJackson2001" />{{rp|pp=30–31}}

From 1865 onward, the liberty of being employed in silk factories allowed some women to live in communes with other women, styling themselves ''tzu-shu nii'' (never to marry) or ''sou-hei'' (self-combers, for adopting hairstyles of married women). These communes ended as a result of the Great Depression and were subsequently discouraged by the communist government as a relic of feudal China.<ref name="Norton1997" />{{rp|p=195}}

"Golden Orchid Associations," which existed in Southern China into the 20th century, promoted formal marriages between women, who were then allowed to adopt children.<ref name="Norton1997" />{{rp|p=187}} In contemporary Chinese society, ''tongzhi'' (same goal or spirit) is the term used to refer to homosexuals; most Chinese people are reluctant to divide this classification further to identify lesbians.<ref name="SullivanJackson2001" />{{rp|p=28}}

===India===
The ''[[Arthashastra]]'', an ancient Indian treatise on statecraft likely edited and compiled between the second and third centuries CE,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kauṭalya |title=The Arthaśāstra : selections from the classic Indian work on statecraft |publisher=Hackett Pub. Co |others=Translated by Mark McClish and Patrick Olivelle |year=2012 |isbn=978-1-60384-849-7 |location=Indianapolis, Ind. |pages=xiv |language=en |oclc=789148479}}</ref> describes the fines individuals must pay for engaging in ''[[ayoni]]'', non-vaginal sex. This category includes both heterosexual and homosexual sex, and the fine for two women is lower than the fine for heterosexual sex. Overall, lesbian sex is "unsanctioned" in the ''Arthashastra'', but is also "treated as a minor offense."{{sfn|Vanita|Kidwai|2000|p=25}}

The ''[[Manusmriti]]'', a first century legal text, places a very small fine upon sex between nonvirgin women; however, one who "manually [[deflower]]s a virgin" is sentenced to the loss of two fingers.{{sfn|Vanita|Kidwai|2000|p=25}} If two virgins are caught, the 'doer' "has to pay double the girl's [[dowry]] and is given ten whiplashes."{{sfn|Vanita|Kidwai|2000|p=26}} The ''Manusmriti'' fails to provide a punishment for ''mutual'' [[Cunnilingus|oral]] or non-penetrative sex.{{sfn|Vanita|Kidwai|2000|p=26}}

Sanskrit medical texts mention "sexual act[s] in which both the parties are female."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bhishagratna |first=Kaviraj Kunja Lal |url=https://archive.org/details/englishtranslati00susruoft/page/132/mode/2up?view=theater |title=An English Translation of the Sushruta Samhita in Three Volumes |publisher=Self-published |year=1911 |volume=II |location=Calcutta |page=132 |language=en}}</ref> The [[Sushruta Samhita]] and [[Charaka Samhita]] both classify lesbianism as a disease resulting from an atypical conception.{{sfn|Sweet|Zwilling|1993|p=597}} The latter describes it as incurable, and states that a lesbian is "a woman who has an aversion for man and who has no breasts."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Shree Gulabkunverba Ayurvedic Society |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.325783/page/n583/mode/2up?view=theater |title=The Caraka Saṃhitā |publisher=The Ayurveda Mudranalaya |year=1949 |volume=IV |location=Jamnagar |page=584 |language=sa, hi, gu, en}}</ref> The term used for a lesbian in these texts is {{Lang|sa|nārīṣaṇḍha}}.{{sfn|Sweet|Zwilling|1993|p=593}}

The [[Kama Sutra]] mentions phallus-shaped bulbs, roots, and fruits used as [[dildo]]s in lesbian sex, and also records [[cunnilingus]] between women.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Doniger |first1=Wendy |title=Vatsyayana Kamasutra |last2=Kakar |first2=Sudhir |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-19-953916-1 |edition=Reissued paperback |location=Oxford |pages=68, 125 |language=en}}</ref>

Conversations around the visibility and acceptance of lesbianism in India were prompted by Deepa Mehta's 1996 film ''[[Fire (1996 film)|Fire]]'', the release of which caused some theaters in India to be attacked by religious extremists.<ref>{{Cite web |date=1998-12-20 |title=Film breaks silence of India's lesbians |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/film-breaks-silence-of-india-s-lesbians-1193533.html |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=The Independent |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-03-20 |title=The Portrayal of Female Desire and Lesbianism in Deepa Mehta's Fire |url=https://retrospectjournal.com/2022/03/20/the-portrayal-of-female-desire-and-lesbianism-in-deepa-mehtas-fire/ |access-date=2026-04-02 |website=Retrospect Journal |language=en}}</ref>

Terms used to label homosexuals are often rejected by Indian activists for being the result of imperialist influence, but most discourse on homosexuality centers men. Women's rights groups in India continue to debate the legitimacy of including lesbian issues in their platforms, as lesbians and material focusing on female homosexuality are frequently suppressed.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vanita |first1=Ruth |title=Lesbian Studies and Activism in India |journal=[[Journal of Lesbian Studies]] |date=2007 |volume=11 |issue=3–4 |pages=244–253 |doi=10.1300/J155v11n03_07 |pmid=17954460 |s2cid=8782756}}</ref>

=== Japan ===
Relationships between women are described in The Princess in Search of Herself,<ref name=":Pflugfelder">{{Cite journal |last=Pflugfelder |first=Gregory M. |date=1992 |title=Strange Fates. Sex, Gender, and Sexuality in Torikaebaya Monogatari |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2385103 |journal=Monumenta Nipponica |volume=47 |issue=3 |page=367 |doi=10.2307/2385103 |jstor=2385103 |issn=0027-0741|url-access=subscription }}</ref> a piece of literature from either the [[Heian period|Heian]]{{sfn|Mostow|1996|pp=7, 450}} or [[Kamakura period|Kamakura]] period.{{sfn|Keene|1989|p=16}} Chūjō is a [[lady-in-waiting]] for the High Priestess at Ise, and the two are romantically involved. Chūjō becomes angry and jealous when the high priestess abandons her to pursue a relationship with Kozaishō, another lady-in-waiting.<ref name=":Pflugfelder" />{{sfn|Keene|1989|p=19}} The text describes physical intimacy between women clearly.<ref name=":Pflugfelder" />

[[File:Two Japanese women make love.jpg|thumb|upright=0.8|A historic [[Shunga (art)|shunga]] woodblock printing (c. 1500) from Japan depicting two women having sex|alt=]]

It has been suggested that the famous Heian period writer [[Murasaki Shikibu]] loved women,<ref name=":Lunsing">{{Cite book |last=Lunsing |first=Wim |title=Beyond Common Sense: Sexuality and Gender in Contemporary Japan |publisher=Routledge |year=2016 |isbn=978-0-710-30593-0 |location=London and New York |pages=28–29 |language=en}}</ref> based on potentially homoerotic poems exchanged with other women.{{sfn|Mostow|1996|p=5}} One section of her diary reads:{{sfn|Bowring|1996|p=81}}
{{blockquote|<poem>
In particular I missed Lady Dainagon{{nbsp}}...I sent her the following:
:How I long for those waters on which we lay,
:A longing keener than the frost on a duck's wing.
To which she replied:
:Awakening to find no friend to brush away the frost,
:The mandarin duck longs for her mate at night.
</poem>}}Bowring notes that the [[mandarin duck]] was a firmly established metaphor for lovers at the time, but states that the relationship was only platonic.{{sfn|Bowring|1996|p=176}} Some have criticized the hesitance to acknowledge lesbian readings of poems like these as "an explaining away of the simplest interpretation of a text in favor of a more complicated, but heterosexually normative, reading."{{sfn|Mostow|1996|p=6}}

Edward Kamens notes the erotically charged nature of poetic exchanges between Senshi and Kodaifu, and Ukon and Taifu, both in the Heian period. He argues that they "would readily be read as explicit tropes of sexual desire" if they had not been exchanged between two women.{{sfn|Mostow|1996|pp=6–7}}

Other references to same-sex practices between women before the [[Edo period]] are more ambiguous. In the [[Kojiki]] the sun goddess [[Amaterasu]] is lured out of a cave by [[Ame-no-Uzume|Ame no Uzume]] dancing and removing her clothes.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wieringa |first=Saskia E. |title=Women's Sexualities and Masculinities in a Globalizing Asia |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan |year=2007 |isbn=9781403977687 |editor-last=Wieringa |editor-first=Saskia E. |location=USA |page=28 |language=en |chapter=Silence, Sin, and the System: Women's Same-Sex Practices in Japan |editor-last2=Blackwood |editor-first2=Evelyn |editor-last3=Bhaiya |editor-first3=Abha|editor-link3=Abha Bhaiya}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dumont |first1=Éric |last2=Manigot |first2=Vincent |date=2014 |title=Une histoire du striptease japonais |url=https://journals.openedition.org/cipango/2230 |journal=Cipango |issue=21 |doi=10.4000/cipango.2230 |issn=1164-5857 |doi-access=free |archive-date=21 June 2023 |access-date=20 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230621053549/https://journals.openedition.org/cipango/2230 |url-status=live }}</ref> Dildos dating from as early as the [[Nara period]] may have been used for masturbation rather than lesbian sex.<ref name=":Lunsing" />

The term {{lang|ja-latn|rezubian}}, a Japanese pronunciation of "lesbian," was used during the 1920s. Westernization brought more independence for women and allowed some Japanese women to wear pants.<ref name="Aldrich2006"/>{{rp|p=246}}

=== Malaysia ===
The term ''pondan'' is used in [[Malaysia]] to refer to gay men, but since there is no historical context to reference lesbians, the term is used for female homosexuals as well.<ref name="SullivanJackson2001" />{{rp|p=145}} As in many Asian countries, open homosexuality is discouraged in many social levels, so many Malaysian lesbians lead double lives.<ref name="SullivanJackson2001" />{{rp|pp=148–150}}

=== South Korea ===
[[Deposed Crown Princess Bong|Crown Princess Sun]] was banished from her home in [[Joseon]] in 1454, after it was discovered that she had an intimate relationship with one of her maids.<ref>Sejong Sillok, vol.75</ref>

Women in South Korea are taught to prioritize motherhood, chastity, and virginity. Very few women are free to express themselves through sexuality, although there is a growing organization for lesbians named {{lang|ko-latn|Kkirikkiri}}.<ref name="SullivanJackson2001" />{{rp|p=75}}

===Thailand===
Sources on female [[LGBT history in Thailand|homosexuality in Thai history]] primarily discuss royal harems, using the label {{Lang|th|เล่นเพื่อน}} {{Transliteration|th|len-phuean}}, which literally means "to play [with] friends."{{sfn|Singhakowinta|2010|p=157}} One of the earliest references is a law from King [[Borommatrailokkanat]] (who reigned 1448–1488), which penalizes lesbian relationships between palace women with whipping and which survives as part of the [[Three Seals Law]].{{sfn|Singhakowinta|2010|p=158}}{{sfn|Sinnott|2004|p=49}}<ref name=":Numun">{{Cite journal |last=Numun |first=Wanna |date=2012 |title=Significance of Homosexuality in Thai Society |journal=Journal of Humanities and Social Sciences |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=160}}</ref> There is no evidence of this punishment ever being used, and an American ambassador in the 19th century wrote that homosexuality was very common, and that only monks had been punished for it.{{sfn|Singhakowinta|2010|p=159}}

Another source of evidence for female same-sex relationships is poetry and fiction based partly on real royal harems.{{sfn|Singhakowinta|2010|pp=160–161}} The earliest such literature, from the [[Rattanakosin Kingdom (1782–1932)|Rattanakosin Kingdom]], is unusual in focusing more on female homosexuality than male homosexuality.<ref name=":Numun" /> However, many of the literary sources are critical, and describe lesbianism as something to be avoided.{{sfn|Singhakowinta|2010|p=162}}{{sfn|Sinnott|2004|p=50}}<ref name=":Numun" /> A mural at [[Wat Klang Bang Kaeo|Wat Khongkharam]] depicts women surreptitiously touching each other's breasts, but also depicts women being punished for lesbianism.{{sfn|Sinnott|2004|p=53}}

=== The Philippines ===
[[Leona Florentino]] was born in the [[Philippines]] during the Spanish colonial regime in 1849. She is the mother of Philippine women's literature and the pioneer in Philippine lesbian literature, known for kickstarting her homeland's feminist movement, which also led her to be honored as the mother of feminist literature in the country.<ref>Jolo, J. B. & Manansala, A. M. B. (2020). "Courting the Gaze, Romancing the Margins: Queer Re-Orientation in Emiliana Kampilan's Komix". ''Review of Women's Studies''. University of the Philippines.</ref><ref>Blanton, S. (2016). A Threshold of Flowers: Public and Private Eroticism in the Poems of Leona Florentino. University of North Carolina.</ref><ref>Mabanglo, R. E. (2020). Leona Florentino: Mother of Filipina poetry. Philippine Graphic.</ref> The term [[tomboy]] is used in the [[Philippines]], particularly in [[Manila]], to denote women who are more masculine.<ref name="SullivanJackson2001" />{{rp|p=122}}

== Greece ==

===Ancient Greece===

====Sappho====
The lives of ancient Greek women are in general little-documented.<ref name="Rabinowitz2002" /> In a notable exception, [[Sappho]] of Lesbos ({{Circa|630|570 BC}}) wrote extensive poetry regarding her love for other women, fragments of which survive.<ref>{{cite web |last=Dunn |first=Daisy |date=30 July 2024 |title=The First Lesbian: How Sappho's Poetry Paved the Way for Modern Queer Literature |url=https://lithub.com/the-first-lesbian-how-sapphos-poetry-paved-the-way-for-modern-queer-literature/ |website=LitHub |access-date=5 July 2025}}</ref>

Sappho is the most cited example of an ancient Greek woman who may have actually engaged in sexual relationships with women. The earliest evidence of Sappho's reputation for homosexual desire comes from the [[Hellenistic period]], with a fragment of a biography found in the [[Oxyrhynchus Papyri]] criticizing Sappho for being "gynaikerastria."<ref>I.e. a woman who loves other women.</ref>{{sfn|Dover|1978|p=174}}

In her [[Ode to Aphrodite]], the poet asks [[Aphrodite]] for aid in wooing another woman.{{sfn|Dover|1978|p=177}} One fragment, [[Sappho 94]], contains a clear mention of lesbian sexual acts:<ref>{{cite journal|last=McEvilly|first=Thomas|title=Sappho, Fragment 94|journal=Phoenix|volume=25|issue=1|year=1971|pages=2–3}}</ref>

[[File:Amanda Brewster Sewell, Sappho, 1891.jpg|alt=Painting of a woman dressed in Greek robes holding a lyre, with three partially nude women sitting in front of her on a long marble bench.|left|thumb|273x273px|''Sappho'' by [[Amanda Brewster Sewell]], 1891. [[Sappho]] of [[Lesbos]] gave the term ''lesbian'' the connotation of erotic desire between women.]]

<blockquote>'''Sappho Fragment 94'''<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gillianspraggs.com/translations/sappho94.html |title=Fragment 94}}</ref>

I'm not pretending; I wish I were dead."
She was leaving me in tears,

and over and over she said to me: 
"Sappho, it hurts; what's happened to us is just so grim;
it isn't my choice, I swear it, to leave like this.."

These were the words that I answered her:
"Go and be happy; remember me, 
for you know how we have paid court to you:

and if not, then I want to remind you ... and the good things we have enjoyed:

for at my side, many the crowns of violets and roses ... you have put on yourself,

and many the garlands woven from flowers you have cast round your delicate neck,

and with quantities of ... flowery perfume ... fit for a queen even, you anointed yourself all over,

and on soft beds ... delicate ... you have satisfied desire ...</blockquote>

Sappho's sexuality has been debated by historians. Some, such as [[Denys Page]], argue that Sappho was attracted to women. Others, such as Eva Stigers, argue that the descriptions of love between women in Sappho's writings are not necessarily evidence of her own sexuality.{{sfn|Downing|1994|p=192}} Still further historians claim that Sappho's circle were involved in female homosexuality as a kind of initiation ritual.{{sfn|Downing|1994|p=193}}

At least two other woman poets wrote in the style of Sappho, [[Erinna]] of Teos or Telos ({{Circa|late 400s BC}}) and [[Nossis]] of Locri ({{Circa|300 BC}}).<ref>{{Cite book |title=Women in the classical world : image and text |date=1994 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |first1=Elaine |last1=Fantham |author1-link=Elaine Fantham |first2=Helene P. |last2=Foley |author2-link=Helene P. Foley |first3=Natalie |last3=Kampen |author3-link=Natalie Kampen |first4=Sarah B. |last4=Pomeroy |author4-link=Sarah B. Pomeroy |first5=H. Alan |last5=Shapiro |isbn=0-19-506727-4 |location=New York |pages=164–165 |oclc=27265657}}</ref>

====Other Ancient Greek works====
Among the Athenians, the discussion and depiction of female homosexual activity seems to have been taboo.{{sfn|Dover|1978|p=182}} [[Kenneth Dover]] suggests that, due to the role played by the phallus in ancient Greek men's conceptions of sexuality, female homosexual love was not explicitly defined as a sexuality by the authors of surviving sources.{{sfn|Downing|1994|p=171}}

Some male-written works reference lesbianism. One example, from the 300s BC, is the tale of the four-legged humans told by [[Aristophanes]] in [[Plato]]'s ''[[Symposium (Plato)|Symposium]]''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Plato |title=The Symposium |url=https://www.gutenberg.org/files/1600/1600-h/1600-h.htm |location=Project Gutenberg |publisher=Project Gutenberg |page= |isbn= |access-date=}}</ref>{{refn|group=note|"[H]e begins by treating of the origin of human nature. The sexes were originally three, men, women, and the union of the two; and they were made round—having four hands, four feet, two faces on a round neck, and the rest to correspond. Terrible was their strength and swiftness; and they were essaying to scale heaven and attack the gods. Doubt reigned in the celestial councils; the gods were divided between the desire of quelling the pride of man and the fear of losing the sacrifices. At last Zeus hit upon an expedient. Let us cut them in two, he said; then they will only have half their strength, and we shall have twice as many sacrifices. He spake, and split them as you might split an egg with an hair; and when this was done, he told Apollo to give their faces a twist and re-arrange their persons, taking out the wrinkles and tying the skin in a knot about the navel. The two halves went about looking for one another, and were ready to die of hunger in one another's arms. Then Zeus invented an adjustment of the sexes, which enabled them to marry and go their way to the business of life. Now the characters of men differ accordingly as they are derived from the original man or the original woman, or the original man-woman. Those who come from the man-woman are lascivious and adulterous; those who come from the woman form female attachments; those who are a section of the male follow the male and embrace him, and in him all their desires centre."}} Another example, from the 100s CE, is the [[List of works by Lucian|Dialogues of the Courtesans]], where a female character talks about being seduced by two lesbian characters.<ref>{{cite web |last= |first= |date= |title=LUCIAN:Dialogues of the Courtesans Section 5: LEAENA AND CLONARIUM |url=https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/pwh/lucian-court.asp |website=Internet History Sourcebooks Project |location= |publisher=Fordham University |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241003133203/https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/pwh/lucian-court.asp |archive-date=October 3, 2024 |access-date=May 21, 2025}}</ref>

Later references to female homosexuality in Greek literature include an epigram by [[Asclepiades of Samos|Asclepiades]], which describes two women who reject Aphrodite's "rules" but instead do "other things which are not seemly."<ref>Asklepiades, ''The Greek Anthology'' 5.207</ref> Dover comments on the "striking" hostility shown in the epigram to female homosexuality, contrasting it with Asclepiades' willingness to discuss his own homosexual desire in other works, suggesting that this apparent male anxiety about female homosexuality in ancient Greece is the reason for the paucity of sources discussing it.{{sfn|Dover|1978|pp=172–173}}

The poet [[Alcman]] ([[Floruit|fl]]. 7th century BC) wrote hymns known as ''partheneia'',<ref>"Maiden-songs", so-called because they were apparently composed for choruses of young girls to sing as part of religious celebrations.</ref> which discuss attraction between young women. Though these hymns are ambiguous, historians have posited that they are erotic or sexual.{{sfn|Dover|1978|p=179}}<ref>{{Cite web|date=2007-11-10|title=Why were the ancient Greeks so confused about homosexuality, asks James Davidson|url=http://www.theguardian.com/books/2007/nov/10/history.society|access-date=2021-10-21|website=the Guardian|language=en|archive-date=2021-10-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211021220426/https://www.theguardian.com/books/2007/nov/10/history.society|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:Apollodoros (attr.), kylix attica con due etere alla toeletta, 490-480 ac.jpg|thumb|A red-figure kylix depicting two women in an intimate setting. Attributed to the painter Apollodorus, c. 490–480 BCE. (Tarquinia National Museum)|218x218px]]

Some find evidence in [[Plutarch]] that [[Women in ancient Sparta|Spartan women]] engaged in homosexual activities, although Plutarch wrote many centuries after classical Greece. In Plutarch's biography of [[Lycurgus of Sparta]], part of his ''[[Parallel Lives]]'', the author claims that older [[Sparta]]n women formed relationships with girls that were similar to the [[Pederasty in ancient Greece|''erastes''/''eromenos'' relationships]] that existed between some older and younger male Greeks.{{sfn|Dover|1978|p=173}} Historian [[Sarah B. Pomeroy]] believes that Plutarch's depiction of homosexual relationships between Spartan women is plausible. Pomeroy argues that homosexual relationships between girls would have "flourished" in the girls' choirs that performed the ''partheneia'' of Alcman.<ref>{{cite book |last=Pomeroy |first=Sarah B. |title=Goddesses, Whores, Wives, & Slaves |publisher=Pimlico |year=1995 |location=London |page=55}}</ref>

In Greek mythology, the story of [[Callisto (mythology)|Callisto]] has been interpreted as implying that [[Artemis]] and Callisto were lovers.{{sfn|Downing|1994|p=180}} The myth of the [[Amazons]] has also been interpreted as referring to female homosexual activities.{{sfn|Downing|1994|p=176}}

In visual culture, some ancient Greek [[Pottery of ancient Greece|red vase]] images portray women in affectionate or erotic scenes.<ref name="Bremmer1989">{{cite book |editor-last=Bremmer |editor-first=Jan |date=1989 |title=From Sappho to de Sade: Moments in the History of Sexuality |publisher=[[Routledge]] |isbn=0-415-02089-1}}</ref>{{rp|pp=27–28}}<ref name="Rabinowitz2002" /> For example, a plate from [[Archaic Greece|Archaic]] [[Santorini|Thera]] appears to show two women courting.{{sfn|Dover|1978|p=173}} An [[Attica|Attic]] [[Red-figure pottery|red figure vase]] in the collection of the [[Tarquinia National Museum]] in Italy shows a kneeling woman [[Fingering (sexual act)|fingering]] the genitals of another woman in a rare explicit portrayal of sexual activity between women in Greek art,{{sfn|Dover|1978|p=173}} although it has also been interpreted as depicting one prostitute shaving or otherwise grooming the other in a non-sexual fashion.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.finestresullarte.info/en/works-and-artists/the-erotic-ceramics-of-the-national-archaeological-museum-in-tarquinia|title=The erotic ceramics of the National Archaeological Museum in Tarquinia.|website=Finestre sull' Arte|author=Federico Giannini, Ilaria Baratta}}</ref>

== Middle East ==

===Ancient Mesopotamia===
Women's sexuality in [[ancient Mesopotamia]] is not well documented. Stephanie Lynn Budin, writing on love magic, argues that "there remains no evidence for lesbianism in this regard (or any other from Mesopotamia)."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Budin |first=Stephanie Lynn |title=Women in Antiquity: Real women across the Ancient World |publisher=[[Routledge]] |year=2016 |isbn=978-1-138-80836-2 |location=New York |page=11 |language=en |chapter=Female sexuality in Mesopotamia}}</ref> However, there are at least two pieces of textual evidence for Mesopotamian lesbianism.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bahrani |first=Zainab |date=1993 |title=The Iconography of the Nude in Mesopotamia |journal=Source: Notes in the History of Art |language=en |volume=12 |issue=2 |page=13 |doi=10.1086/sou.12.2.23202931 |s2cid=193110588 |issn=0737-4453}}</ref> One is a divinatory text which mentions female same-sex activity,<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bottéro |first1=J. |title=Reallexikon der Assyriologie und Vorderasiatischen Archäologie |last2=Petschow |first2=H. |publisher=[[Walter de Gruyter]] |year=1975 |isbn=3-11-006772-2 |editor-last=Edzard |editor-first=Dietz Otto |volume=IV: Ḫa-a-a - Hystaspes |location=Berlin |page=468 |language=fr, de |chapter=Homosexualität}}</ref> while another, more explicit text remains unpublished.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bottéro |first=Jean |title=Le couple interdit, entretiens sur le racisme |publisher=Mouton |year=1980 |isbn=2-7193-0469-7 |editor-last=Poliakov |editor-first=Léon |location=Paris |page=33 |language=fr |chapter=L'"amour libre" à Babylone et ses "servitudes"}}</ref>

In addition, an [[Old Assyrian period|Old Assyrian]] text writes of two women, Ewanika and Adi-matum, who had a betrothal contract for their "daughter." It is possible that the father died, leaving the two women as widows.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stol |first1=Marten |title=Women in the Ancient Near East |publisher=[[Walter de Gruyter]] |year=2016 |isbn=978-1-61451-323-0 |page=76 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Medieval ===
In the 7th and 8th centuries, some women dressed in male attire when gender roles were less strict. The [[Caliphate|Caliphal]] court in [[Baghdad]] featured women who dressed as men, including false facial hair, but they competed with other women for the attentions of men.<ref name="Murray1997" />{{sfn|Amer|2009}}

[[Arabic]]-language historical records have used various terms to describe sexual practices between women.{{sfn|Amer|2009}} A common one is ''sahq'', which refers to rubbing.

In the medieval Arab world, lesbianism<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Allouche |first1=Sabiha |title=The Reluctant Queer |journal=[[Kohl: A Journal for Body and Gender Research]] |date=Spring 2019 |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=11–22 |doi=10.36583/kohl/5-1-3 |doi-access=free}}</ref> was considered to be caused by heat generated in a woman's [[labia]], which could be alleviated by [[tribadism|friction against another woman's genitalia]].{{sfn|Amer|2009|p=217}} [[Al-Kindi]] wrote:{{sfn|Amer|2009|pp=216–217}}

{{blockquote|Lesbianism is due to a vapor which, condensed, generates in the labia heat and an itch which only dissolve and become cold through friction and orgasm. When friction and orgasm take place, the heat turns into coldness because the liquid that a woman ejaculates in lesbian intercourse is cold whereas the same liquid that results from sexual union with men is hot. Heat, however, cannot be extinguished by heat; rather, it will increase since it needs to be treated by its opposite. As coldness is repelled by heat, so heat is also repelled by coldness.}}

Medical texts considered lesbianism to be congenital. For instance, [[Masawaiyh]] reported:{{sfn|Amer|2009|p=217}}

{{blockquote|Lesbianism results when a nursing woman eats [[celery]], [[Rocket (plant)|rocket]], [[melilot]] leaves and the flowers of a [[bitter orange]] tree. When she eats these plants and suckles her child, they will affect the labia of her suckling and generate an itch which the suckling will carry through her future life.}}

Ali ibn Nasr al-Katib's [[Encyclopedia of Pleasure]] contains a story about what is said to be the first lesbian couple in Arab history: the seventh-century [[Al-Hurqah|Hind bint al-Nuʿmān]], a Christian poet, and the legendary Arabic poet [[Hind bint al-Khuss]]. When Hind Bint al-Khuss died, her faithful lover "cropped her hair, wore black clothes, rejected worldly pleasures, vowed to God that she would lead an ascetic life until she passed away," and even built a monastery to commemorate her love.{{sfn|Amer|2009|p=218}} The 10th-century work [[al-Fihrist]] gives the titles of books about twelve other lesbian couples, but nothing other than the women's names has survived.{{sfn|Amer|2009|p=219}} According to the 12th-century writings of Sharif al-Idrisi, highly intelligent women were more likely to be lesbians; their intellectual prowess put them on a more even par with men.<ref name="Murray1997">{{cite book |last1=Murray |first1=Stephen O. |last2=Roscoe |first2=Will |date=1997 |title=Islamic Homosexualities: Culture, History and Literature |publisher=[[New York University Press]] |isbn=0-8147-7468-7 |pages=98–104, 283–284}}</ref>

[[Wallada bint al-Mustakfi]], sometimes called the Arab Sappho, was an Andalusian poet whose love poetry to her student [[Muhja bint al-Tayyani]] has been [[Lesbian erasure|lost]] since later authors refused to cite its sexually explicit content.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Murray |first=Stephen O. |title=Islamic Homosexualities: Culture, History, and Literature |publisher=[[New York University Press]] |year=1997 |isbn=0-8147-7467-9 |editor-last=Murray |editor-first=Stephen O. |location=New York |pages=99 |language=en |chapter=Woman-Woman Love in Islamic Societies |editor-last2=Roscoe |editor-first2=Will}}</ref> Elsewhere, lesbian poetry has survived. [[Al-Jahiz]] cites the couplet "I drank wine for love of flirting/and I shifted towards lesbianism for fear of pregnancy." In ''[[A Promenade of the Hearts]]'', [[Ahmad al-Tifashi]] cites several poems by lesbians where massage is used as a pretext for lesbian sex,<ref>{{Cite book |last=al-Tîfâchî |first=Ahmad |title=Les délices des cœurs |publisher=Phébus |year=1981 |isbn=2-266-02779-4 |location=Paris |pages=273–274 |language=fr |translator-last=Khawam |translator-first=René R. |trans-title=A Promenade of Hearts}}</ref><ref name="El-Feki2013">{{cite book |first=Shereen |last=El-Feki |title=Sex and the Citadel: Intimate Life in a Changing Arab World |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p4QRDdZn-AAC&pg=PA223 |year=2013 |publisher=Chatto & Windus |isbn=978-0-7011-8316-5 |pages=223–225}}</ref> as well as the same-sex philosophy of Rose, the head of one such lesbian massage group.{{sfn|Amer|2009|p=220}}

[[Leo Africanus]] describes with disgust the practices of female diviners in [[Fez, Morocco|Fez]] who cure illnesses, saying that they are in fact ''sahacat'', his rendition of the Arabic word for lesbians ({{langx|ar|سحاقيات|translit=siḥāqiyyāt}}).{{sfn|Amer|2009|p=220}}<ref name="Africanus">{{Cite book |last=Africanus |first=Leo |title=A geographical historie of Africa |publisher=George Bishop |year=1600 |location=London |pages=148–149 |language=en |translator-last=Pory |translator-first=John}}</ref> He describes how lesbians pretend to be sick so that the diviners will come to them. They then claim that the woman is possessed and that the only cure is to join the diviners, enabling her to leave her husband and become part of a lesbian community.<ref name="Africanus" />

Some fictional women from Arabic folk epics can be viewed as lesbian, like Alûf from [[Delhemma]], who says "I do neither long for marriage nor for men, but my heart has an inclination for the ladies."{{sfn|Amer|2009|p=228}} Rumors of harem lesbianism in the Arab world, like those reported by [[Allen Edwardes]], tend to come from male [[Orientalism|Orientalist]] writers and have not been verified.{{sfn|Amer|2009|loc=p. 220, footnote 11}}

===Contemporary Arab World===
While male-written accounts of lesbianism in the Middle East exist, a 1978 treatise about repression in [[Iran]] asserted that women were completely silenced: "In the whole of Iranian history, [no woman] has been allowed to speak out for such tendencies ... To attest to lesbian desires would be an unforgivable crime."<ref name="Murray1997" />

In 1991, a lesbian anthropologist visited [[Yemen]] and reported that women in the town she visited were unable to comprehend her romantic relationship to another woman. Women in Pakistan are expected to marry men; those who do not are ostracized. Women may have intimate relations with other women so long as their wifely duties are met, their private matters are kept quiet, and the woman with whom they are involved is somehow related by family or logical interest to her lover.<ref name="Murray1997" />

The common term used to describe lesbianism in Arabic today is essentially the same term used to describe men, and thus the distinction between male and female homosexuality is to a certain extent linguistically obscured in contemporary queer discourse.{{sfn|Amer|2009}} Overall, the study of contemporary lesbian experience in the region is complicated by power dynamics in the postcolonial context, shaped even by what some scholars refer to as "[[homonationalism]]", the use of politicized understanding of sexual categories to advance specific national interests on the domestic and international stage.

Individuals identifying with or otherwise engaging in lesbian practices in the region can face family violence and societal persecution, including "[[honor killing]]s". The justifications provided by murderers relate to a person's perceived sexual immorality and loss of virginity (outside of acceptable frames of marriage).<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Fisk |first1=Robert |title=Robert Fisk: The crimewave that shames the world |work=[[The Independent]] |date=7 September 2010 |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/opinion/commentators/fisk/the-crimewave-that-shames-the-world-2072201.html |access-date=8 September 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121025122521/https://www.independent.co.uk/voices/commentators/fisk/robert-fisk-the-crimewave-that-shames-the-world-2072201.html |archive-date=October 25, 2012 |url-status=live}}</ref> Lesbians also face government persecution in the Middle East. In [[Yemen]], homosexuality is criminalized, and women can face lashings, up to three years in prison or the death penalty for consensual lesbian sex.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gaylawnet.com/laws/ye.htm|title=GayLawNet - Laws - Yemen|website=Gaylawnet.com|access-date=21 May 2025|archive-date=7 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211107002433/https://www.gaylawnet.com/laws/ye.htm|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Gerber |first=Paula |url=https://antigaylaws.org/regional/middle-east/ |title=Countries that still criminalise homosexuality |website=AntiGayLaws |date=17 March 2014 |access-date=21 May 2025}}</ref>

== Continental Europe ==

=== Medieval and Renaissance ===
A 13th-century [[trobairitz]], [[Bieiris de Romans]], wrote a [[Canso (song)|canso]] to another woman, Maria:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bogin |first=Meg |title=The Women Troubadours |publisher=Paddington Press Ltd |year=1976 |isbn=0-8467-0113-8 |pages=133}}</ref>

{{blockquote|<poem>
Thus I pray you, if it please you that true love
And celebration and sweet humility
should bring me such relief with you,
if it please you, lovely woman, then give me
that which most hope and joy promises
for in you lie my desire and my heart.
</poem>}}

The canso is the genre in which love poems were written, but some have argued that it is possible that Maria was not a lover but a "female acquaintance, friend, confidante, or close relative."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rieger |first=Angelica |title=The Voice of the Trobairitz: Perspectives on the Women Troubadours |publisher=[[University of Pennsylvania Press]] |year=1989 |isbn=0-8122-8167-5 |editor-last=Paden |editor-first=William D. |pages=73, 82 |chapter=Was Bieiris de Romans Lesbian? Women's Relations with Each Other in the World of the Troubadours}}</ref> Clearer evidence for lesbian relationships is found in a 12th-century manuscript from [[Tegernsee Abbey|Tegernsee]]. It contains lesbian love poems which were likely composed at a local monastery for women.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Matter |first=E. Ann |date=1986 |title=My Sister, My Spouse: Woman-Identified Women in Medieval Christianity |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25002043 |journal=Journal of Feminist Studies in Religion |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages= 81–93 [82]|jstor=25002043 |issn=8755-4178}}</ref> The quote below, which "seems to presuppose a passionate physical relationship",<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dronke |first=Peter |title=Medieval Latin and the Rise of the European Love-Lyric |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |year=1966 |volume=II: Medieval Latin Love-Poetry |pages=482}}</ref> is from A's poem to G:{{sfn|Boswell|1981|p=220}}
{{blockquote|<poem>
When I recall the kisses you gave me,
And how with tender words you caressed my little breasts,
I want to die
Because I cannot see you.
</poem>}}

The earliest law against female homosexuality appeared in France, in the legal treatise {{Lang|fro|[[Li livres de jostice et de plet]]}} ({{Circa|1260}}), which prescribed [[dismemberment]] for the first two offences and [[death by burning]] for the third.<ref name="Norton1997" />{{rp|page=191}} This penalty was a near exact copy of the penalty for a man, although what "dismemberment" could mean for a medieval woman is unknown.{{sfn|Boswell|1981|pp=289–290}}{{sfn|Crompton|1981|p=13}}

There exist records of about a dozen women in the medieval period who were involved in lesbian sex, as defined by historian [[Judith Bennett]] as same-sex genital contact. All of these women are known through their involvement with the courts, and were imprisoned or executed.{{sfn|Bennett|2000|p=3}}{{sfn|Crompton|1981|p=17}}

In the Holy Roman Empire under [[Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor|Charles V]], a law on sexual offences specifically prohibits sex acts between women.{{sfn|Crompton|1981|p=18}} In Spain, Italy, and the Holy Roman Empire, sodomy between women was included in acts considered unnatural and punishable by burning to death, although few instances are recorded of this taking place.<ref name="Aldrich2006" />{{rp|page=130}} The earliest such execution occurred in [[Speyer|Speier, Germany]], in 1477.<ref name="Norton1997" />{{rp|p=190}}

[[Catharina Margaretha Linck]] was a [[Prussia]]n woman who for most of her adult life presented herself as a man. She married a woman and, based on their sexual activity together, was convicted of [[sodomy]] and executed by order of King [[Frederick William I of Prussia|Frederick William I]] in 1721. Linck's execution was the last for lesbian sexual activity in Europe and an anomaly for its time.<ref name="crompton">{{cite book |last=Crompton |first=Louis |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TfBYd9xVaXcC&pg=PA473 |title=Homosexuality & Civilization |publisher=[[Harvard University Press]] |year=2006 |isbn=0-674-02233-5 |pages=473–475 |access-date=1 August 2014 |archive-date=12 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230412032906/https://books.google.com/books?id=TfBYd9xVaXcC&pg=PA473 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Matter |first1=E. Ann |date=1986 |title=My Sister, My Spouse: Woman-Identified Women in Medieval Christianity |journal=Journal of Feminist Studies in Religion |volume=2 |issue=2 |page=91 |jstor=25002043}}</ref> Linck and other women who were accused of using dildos, such as two nuns in 16th century Spain executed for using "material instruments," were punished more severely than those who did not.<ref name="Norton1997" />{{rp|p=191}}<ref name="Faderman1991" />{{rp|pp=51–54}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=Velasco |first=Sherry |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ouHqtw239HwC&q=material+instruments |title=Lesbians in Early Modern Spain |date=2011 |publisher=[[Vanderbilt University Press]] |isbn=978-0-8265-1752-4 |language=en |access-date=2022-04-14 |archive-date=2023-04-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230412032848/https://books.google.com/books?id=ouHqtw239HwC&q=material+instruments |url-status=live}}</ref>

Not all women were so harshly punished, though. In the early fifteenth century, a Frenchwoman, Laurence, wife of Colin Poitevin, was imprisoned for her affair with another woman, Jehanne. She pleaded for clemency on the grounds that Jehanne had been the instigator and she regretted her sins, and was freed to return home after six months imprisonment.

Forty days' [[penance]] was demanded of nuns who "rode" each other or were discovered to have touched each other's breasts. In [[Pescia]], Italy, an abbess, Sister [[Benedetta Carlini]], was documented in inquests between 1619 and 1623 as having committed grave offences including a passionately erotic love affair with another nun. She claimed to have been possessed by a divine male spirit named "Splenditello." She was declared the victim of a "diabolical obsession" and placed in the convent's prison for the last 35 years of her life.<ref>{{cite news |last=Randall |first=Frederika |date=19 January 1986 |title=Divine Visions, Diabolical Obsessions |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1986/01/19/books/divine-visions-diabolical-obsessions.html |newspaper=The New York Times |location=New York |access-date=5 February 2014 |archive-date=19 May 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090519040616/https://www.nytimes.com/1986/01/19/books/divine-visions-diabolical-obsessions.html |url-status=live}}</ref>{{sfn|Bennett|2000|pp=18–19}}

An Italian surgeon, William of Bologna, attributed lesbianism to a "growth emanating from the mouth of the womb and appearing outside the vagina as a pseudopenis."{{sfn|Greenberg|2008|p=278}}

The Christian Church took a strict view on same-sex relations between women. [[Penitentials]], developed by Celtic monks in Ireland, were unofficial guidebooks which became popular, especially in the [[British Isles]]. These books listed crimes and the [[penance]]s that must be done for them. For example, "...he who commits the male crime of the [[Sodom and Gomorrah|Sodomites]] shall do penance for four years." The several versions of the ''[[Paenitentiale Theodori]]'', attributed to [[Theodore of Tarsus]], who became [[archbishop]] of [[Canterbury]] in the 7th century, make special references to lesbianism. The ''Paenitentiale'' states, "If a woman practices vice with a woman she shall do penance for three years."<ref>''Paenitentiale Umbrense'', 2.12</ref> Penitentials soon spread from the British Isles to mainland [[Europe]]. Most medieval penitentials either did not explicitly discuss lesbian activities at all, or treated them as a less serious sin than male homosexuality.{{sfn|Bennett|2000|p=5}}

During the Renaissance, some women put on male personae and went undetected for years or decades. These women have been described as [[transvestite]] lesbians.<ref name="Dekker">{{Cite book |last1=Dekker |first1=Rudolf M. |title=The Tradition of Female Transvestism in Early Modern Europe |last2=van de Pol |first2=Lotte C. |date=1989 |publisher=[[Palgrave Macmillan]] |isbn=978-0333412527 |location=London, United Kingdom}}</ref><ref name="Lucas1988">{{Cite journal |last=Lucas |first=R. Valerie |date=1988 |title="Hic Mulier": The Female Transvestite in Early Modern England |journal=[[Renaissance and Reformation]] |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=65–84 |issn=0034-429X |jstor=43445585}}</ref> Some historians view cases of cross-dressing women to be manifestations of women seizing social power, or their way of making sense out of their desire for women.<ref name="Faderman1991" />{{rp|pp=51–54}}

Female homoeroticism later became so common in literature and theater that historians suggest it was fashionable for a period during the [[Renaissance]].<ref name="Jennings2007">{{cite book |last=Jennings |first=Rebecca |date=2007 |title=A Lesbian History of Britain |publisher=[[Greenwood World Publishing]] |isbn=978-1-84645-007-5}}</ref>{{rp|p=1}}

=== Eastern Bloc ===
In the [[Eastern Bloc]], although there were no standard laws regarding discrimination against gays and lesbians, self-expression was discouraged as it encouraged people toward actions that were outside the accepted norms of a harmonious socialist society. As such, state police often used blackmail and kept dossiers on homosexual people as a way for them to be manipulated by the state.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Torra |first1=Michael Jose |title=Gay Rights after the Iron Curtain |journal=[[The Fletcher Forum of World Affairs]] |date=Summer 1998 |volume=22 |issue=2 |pages=73–88 [75]|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/45289040 |access-date=14 June 2022 |publisher=[[The Fletcher School at Tufts University]] |location=Medford, Massachusetts |jstor=45289040 |issn=1046-1868 |oclc=8897849563 |archive-date=13 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220113135406/https://www.jstor.org/stable/45289040 |url-status=live }}</ref> Activists in Eastern Europe were aware of events in the West, but forming associations for any type of special interest group was forbidden until the 1980s.<ref name="CEU">{{cite web |title=Tracing the Hungarian LGBT Movement |url=https://www.ceu.edu/article/2014-01-28/tracing-hungarian-lgbt-movement |website=[[Central European University]] |access-date=14 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200820002044/https://www.ceu.edu/article/2014-01-28/tracing-hungarian-lgbt-movement |archive-date=20 August 2020 |location=Budapest, Hungary |date=28 January 2014 |url-status=live}}</ref>{{sfn|McLellan|2012|pp=113–114, 118–119}} Because state sanction was not given, many support systems for lesbians operated clandestinely. For example, in 1986 in [[East Germany]], [[Ursula Sillge]] formed the [[Sonntags-Club|Sunday Club]] to offer a means for lesbians both to gather outside state-sanctioned churches and for them to provide educational materials about homosexuality to each other and press authorities to acknowledge the discrimination faced by lesbians and gays.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Dobler |first1=Jens |last2=Schmidt |first2=Kristine |last3=Nellißen |first3=Kay |title=Sonntags im Club |url=http://lernen-aus-der-geschichte.de/Lernen-und-Lehren/content/11666 |website=lernen-aus-der-geschichte |publisher=Agentur für Bildung – Geschichte, Politik und Medien e.V |access-date=9 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200927231406/http://lernen-aus-der-geschichte.de/Lernen-und-Lehren/content/11666 |archive-date=27 September 2020 |location=Berlin, Germany |language=German |trans-title=Sundays at the Club |date=20 January 2015 |url-status=live}}</ref>{{sfn|McLellan|2012|p=124}} The Sunday Club would not gain official sanction and the ability to register as an organization until 1990.<ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Tammer |first1=Teresa |title=Schwul bis über die Mauer: Die Westkontakte der Ost-Berliner Schwulenbewegung in den 1970er und 1980er Jahren |date=2013 |access-date=9 June 2022 |type=Masterarbeit |publisher=Institut für Geschichtswissenschaften, [[Humboldt University of Berlin]] |url=https://archive.org/details/Teresa-Tammer_Schwul-bis-ueber-die-Mauer/page/30/mode/1up |language=German |page=48 |location=Berlin, Germany |trans-title=Gay over the Wall: The East Berlin Gay Movement's Contacts with the West in the 1970s and 1980s |id=No. 541240}}</ref> In Hungary, the first legally recognized organization to represent the LGBT community was {{ill|Homéros Association|lt=Homéros|hu|Homérosz Egyesület}}.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Renkin |first1=Hadley Z. |editor1-last=Kuhar |editor1-first=Roman |editor2-last=Takács |editor2-first=Judit |title=Beyond the Pink Curtain: Everyday Life of LGBT People in Eastern Europe |url=http://www.policy.hu/takacs/books/isbn9616455459/ |date=2007 |publisher=Mirovni inštitut |location=Ljubljana, Slovenia |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180215220549/http://www.policy.hu/takacs/books/isbn9616455459/ |archive-date=15 February 2018 |chapter=Predecessors and Pilgrims: Lesbian History-making and Belonging in Post-socialist Hungary |pages=269–286 |chapter-url=http://www.bs.ceu.hu/sites/default/files/publications/renkin-2007-predecessors-and-pilgrims.pdf |isbn=978-961-6455-45-9 |url-status=live}}</ref> It was organized in 1988 at the [[Ipoly Cinema]], where [[Ildikó Juhász]] operated an after-hours safe space for lesbians to come together to create social networks.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Kuruc |first1=Andrej |title=Ildi Juhász: Pre lesby za socializmu v Maďarsku nebol priestor |magazine=Magazin QYS |date=Summer 2021 |pages=50–54 |url=https://issuu.com/nomantinels/docs/qys_magaz_n_leto2021 |access-date=13 June 2022 |trans-title=Ildi Juhász: There Was No Room for Lesbians under Socialism in Hungary |publisher=Nomantinels |location=Bratislava, Slovakia |language=Slovak |issn=2453-9023 |archive-date=12 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220612215051/https://issuu.com/nomantinels/docs/qys_magaz_n_leto2021 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |url=https://labrisz.hu/content/_common/attachments/file19.pdf |title=Secret Years: Sixteen Lesbian Life Stories |date=2016 |publisher=[[Labrisz Lesbian Association|Labrisz Books]] |editor1-last=Borgos |editor1-first=Anna |edition=English language |location=Budapest, Hungary |pages=82, 98, 251 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220121093757/https://labrisz.hu/content/_common/attachments/file19.pdf |archive-date=21 January 2022 |url-status=live}} (Hungarian version {{isbn|978-963-08-0856-9}} was published in 2011.)</ref>

=== France ===
[[File:Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec 036.jpg|thumb|left|upright|In Paris in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century, lesbians became more visible in art and in the public sphere. A painting by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec of entertainer [[Cha-U-Kao]] at the Moulin Rouge.]] 

Anne Grandjean, disguised as male, married and relocated with her wife to Lyons, but was exposed by a woman with whom she had had a previous affair and sentenced to time in the stocks and prison.<ref name="Faderman1991" />{{rp|pp=51–54}}<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://hal.science/hal-02455104v1/document |title=‘An individual of ill-defined type’ (‘Un individu d’un genre mal de fini) Hermaphroditism in Marriage Annulment Proceedings in Nineteenth-Century France |last=Houbre |first=Gabrielle |journal=Gender & History |volume=27 |issue=1 |date=April 2015 |access-date=26 June 2026 |ISSN=0953-5233 |pages=112-130}}</ref>

[[Marie Antoinette]] was the subject of lesbian speculation between 1795 and 1796.<ref name="Jennings2007" />{{rp|pp=17–18}}

Before the late nineteenth century, only among the less respectable members of society does it seem that there was any sort of a lesbian subculture. Academics believe that there was such a subculture amongst dancers and prostitutes in 18th- and early-19th-century Paris (as well as in 18th-century Amsterdam).<ref name="Clarke96-26">{{cite journal|last=Clarke|first=Anna|title=Anne Lister's Construction of Lesbian Identity|journal=Journal of the History of Sexuality|year=1996|volume=7|issue=1|page=26}}</ref>

The late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries saw an increase in lesbian visibility in [[France]], both in the public sphere and in art and literature. [[Fin de siècle]] society in [[Paris]] included bars, restaurants, and cafés frequented and owned by lesbians, such as [[Le Hanneton (lesbian bar)|Le Hanneton]], [[Palmyre (bar owner)|La Souris]], and Le Rat Mort. Descriptions of these venues were included in tourist guides and journalism of the era. These guides and articles also mentioned houses of prostitution that were uniquely for lesbians. [[Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec]] created paintings of many of the lesbians he met, some of whom frequented or worked at the famed [[Moulin Rouge]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.univers-l.com/portrait_montmartre_repaire_de_lesbiennes.html |title=Stéphanie Bee, Montmartre fin de siècle un repaire de lesbiennes, L'Univers, 1 November, 2010 |date=November 2010 |access-date=2016-10-25 |archive-date=2016-10-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161026002449/http://www.univers-l.com/portrait_montmartre_repaire_de_lesbiennes.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>Nicole G Albert, "De la topographie invisible à l'espace public et littéraire :les lieux de plaisir lesbien dans le Paris de la Belle Époque" ''Revue d'histoire moderne et contemporaine'' 2006 /4 (no 53–54)</ref>

Private salons, like the one hosted by the American expatriate [[Nathalie Barney]], drew many lesbian and bisexual artists and writers, including [[Julie d'Aubigny]], [[Romaine Brooks]], [[Renee Vivien]], [[Colette]], [[Djuna Barnes]], [[Gertrude Stein]], and [[Radclyffe Hall]]. One of Barney's lovers, the courtesan [[Liane de Pougy]], published a best-selling novel based on their romance called ''l'Idylle Saphique'' (1901).

Many publicly acknowledged lesbians and bisexual women were entertainers and actresses. Some, like the writer Colette and her lover [[Mathilde de Morny]], performed lesbian theatrical scenes in cabarets; these drew outrage and censorship.

=== Germany ===
[[File:Die Freundin April 30 1930.jpg|thumb|upright=0.8|Berlin's thriving lesbian community in the 1920s published ''[[Die Freundin]]'' magazine between 1924 and 1933.|alt=Reproduction of a German magazine cover with the title "Die Freundin" showing a nude woman sitting on a horse, looking behind her.]]Although it was sometimes tolerated, homosexuality was illegal in Germany and law enforcement used permitted gatherings as an opportunity to register the names of homosexuals for future reference.<ref name="Tamagne2004">{{cite book |last=Tamagne |first=Florence |date=2004 |title=A History of Homosexuality in Europe Berlin, London, Paris, 1919–1939 |volume=1 |publisher=Algora |isbn=0-585-49198-4 |pages=53–57}}</ref> However, there was no specific law against lesbianism.

Magnus Hirschfeld's [[Scientific-Humanitarian Committee]], which promoted tolerance for homosexuals in [[Germany]], welcomed lesbian participation, and drove a surge of lesbian-themed writing and political activism in the German feminist movement.<ref name="Edsall2003">{{cite book |last=Edsall |first=Nicholas |date=2003 |title=Toward Stonewall: Homosexuality and Society in the Modern Western World |publisher=[[University of Virginia Press]] |isbn=0-8139-2211-9}}</ref>{{rp|pp=230–231}}

[[Berlin]] had a vibrant homosexual culture in the 1920s. {{lang|de|[[Die Freundin]]}} magazines like ''The Girlfriend'' and ''[[Garçonne (magazine)|Garçonne]]'' (AKA {{lang|de|Frauenliebe}}'', or Woman Love'') were aimed at lesbians and [[transvestites]].<ref name="Aldrich2006" />{{rp|pp=241–244}} These publications were owned, published, and written by men. Around 1926, [[Selli Engler]] founded ''[[Die BIF – Blätter Idealer Frauenfreundschaften]]'' (''The BIF – Papers on Ideal Women Friendships''), the first lesbian publication owned, published, and written by women.

Around 50 clubs, varying from large tourist attractions to small neighborhood cafés, catered to lesbians. In 1928, the lesbian bar and nightclub guide ''Berlins lesbische Frauen'' (''The Lesbians of Berlin'') by [[Ruth Margarete Roellig|Ruth Margarite Röllig]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Brendan |date=January 10, 2012 |title=Berlin's Lesbische Frauen |url=http://www.cabaret-berlin.com/?p=546 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200528125430/http://www.cabaret-berlin.com/?p=546 |archive-date=28 May 2020 |access-date=13 June 2020 |website=Cabaret Berlin}} (originally published by ''Slow Travel Berlin'')</ref> popularized the German capital as a center of lesbian activity. The cabaret song {{lang|de|"[[Das lila Lied]]"}} ("The Lavender Song") became an anthem to the lesbians of Berlin.

Homosexual subculture disappeared in Germany with the rise of the Nazis in 1933.<ref name="Aldrich2006" />{{rp|pp=191–193}} During the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]], lesbians who were Jewish, Roma, or politically dissident were persecuted primarily for these other characteristics.<ref name="Lesbians-USHMM">{{Cite web |date=March 31, 2021 |title=Lesbians Under the Nazi Regime |url=https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/lesbians-under-the-nazi-regime |access-date=12 June 2021 |website=[[Holocaust Encyclopedia]] |publisher=[[United States Holocaust Memorial Museum]] |archive-date=25 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220325155611/https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/lesbians-under-the-nazi-regime |url-status=live }}</ref> Prior to 1939, lesbians were imprisoned as "asocials," which was "a broad category applied to all people who evaded Nazi rule."<ref name="Elman">{{Cite journal |last=Elman |first=Amy |date=Winter 1996–97 |title=Triangles and Tribulations: The Gay Appropriation of Nazi Symbols |url=http://www.troubleandstrife.org/issues/Issue34_FullScan.pdf |journal=[[Trouble & Strife]] |issue=34 |pages=64 |access-date=12 June 2021 |quote=An earlier version of this article appeared in ''[[Journal of Homosexuality]]'', Vol. 30, issue 3, 1996. |archive-date=10 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210610150809/http://www.troubleandstrife.org/issues/Issue34_FullScan.pdf |url-status=live }} ({{doi|10.1300/J082v30n03_01}}. {{PMID|8743114}}. {{ISSN|0091-8369}}.)</ref> Asocials were [[Nazi concentration camp badge#Table of camp inmate markings|identified]] with an [[Black triangle (badge)|inverted black triangle]].<ref name="Lesbians-USHMM" /> In the United States during the 1990s, some lesbians used the black triangle symbol as an identifier; the pink triangle was also used for the combined lesbian-gay movement.<ref name="Elman" /> [[File:Black triangle.svg|thumb|upright=0.7|People who did not conform to Nazi ideals were considered asocial, imprisoned, and identified with a [[Black triangle (badge)|black triangle]]. Lesbians were deemed asocial.|alt=An upside down black triangle.]]
[[File:Pink triangle.svg|thumb|upright=0.7|Many lesbians reclaimed the symbolism of the [[pink triangle]], though the Nazis only applied it to [[gay men]].|alt=An upside down pink triangle.]]

=== Italy ===
[[Laudomia Forteguerri]] was an accomplished Italian poet and a member of one of the most powerful families in the sixteenth-century [[Republic of Siena]]. She has been called Italy's earliest lesbian writer, and she was famous for her beauty, wit, and intelligence.<ref>{{cite book |last= Eisenbichler |first=Konrad |title="Laudomia Forteguerri: Constructions of a Woman." The Sword and the Pen: Women, Politics, and Poetry in Sixteenth-century Siena. |publisher=[[University of Notre Dame Press]] |year=2012}}</ref>

=== Spain ===
[[Eleno de Céspedes]], was a Spanish [[surgeon]] born into slavery who married a man and later a woman, and was tried by the [[Spanish Inquisition]]. Céspedes may have been an [[intersex]] person, as different doctors' accounts portray her as having either female anatomy or both sets of genitals. If a woman, Céspedes may have been a [[lesbian]] and/or the first female surgeon known in Spain and perhaps in Europe.<ref>{{cite book |first=Sherry |last=Velasco |article=Interracial Lesbian Erotics in Early Modern Spain |title=Tortilleras: Hispanic and U.S. Latina Lesbian Expression |year=2003 |isbn=1592130070 |editor1-last=Torres |editor1-first=Lourdes |editor2-last=Perpetusa-Seva |editor2-first=Inmaculada |page=214 |publisher=[[Temple University Press]]}}</ref>

[[Princess Isabella of Parma]] found more fulfillment in her relationship with her [[Sibling-in-law|sister-in-law]], Archduchess [[Maria Christina, Duchess of Teschen|Maria Christina]], than with her husband.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Falvai |first=Róbert |title=A Hofburg dámái |publisher=Duna International |year=2012 |isbn=978-6155129568 |editor-last=Gottesmann |editor-first=Péter |language=hu |trans-title=Ladies of the Hofburg |chapter=Izabella, Izabella! Aki igazán a sógornőjét szerette |trans-chapter=Isabella, Isabella! She Who Really Loved Her Sister-In-Law |pages=15, 28 |oclc=909849482}}</ref>

=== Sweden ===
Queen [[Christina of Sweden]] (b. 1626) frequently dressed as a man, abdicated the throne in 1654 to avoid marriage, and was known to pursue romantic relationships with women.<ref name="Faderman1981">{{Cite book |last=Faderman |first=Lillian |author-link=Lillian Faderman |date=1981 |title=Surpassing the Love of Men: Romantic Friendship and Love Between Women from the Renaissance to the Present |publisher=Quill |isbn=0-688-00396-6}}</ref>{{rp|pp=54–55}} Her relationships were noted during her lifetime. She never married. Christina seems to have written passionate letters to and slept in the same bed as [[Ebba Sparre]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://lithub.com/queen-christina-lesbian-icon-on-swedens-delightfully-nonconformist-monarch/ |title=Queen Christina, Lesbian Icon? On Sweden's Delightfully Nonconformist Monarch |date=7 June 2024 |last=Medhurst |first=Eleanor}}</ref> According to [[Veronica Buckley]], Christina was a "dabbler" who was "painted a lesbian, a prostitute, a hermaphrodite, and an atheist" by her contemporaries, though "in that tumultuous age, it is hard to determine which was the most damning label."{{Citation needed|date=May 2023}}

== British Isles ==

=== England ===
[[File:Hermaphrodite engraving circa 1690.jpg|thumb|upright=0.7|Lesbianism and hermaphroditism, depicted here in an engraving {{circa|1690}}, were very similar concepts during the Renaissance.|alt=A front and back illustration of a Renaissance-era hermaphrodite showing a person with female facial features, breasts, and what appears to be a small penis or large clitoris. She wears a small hood and open robe tied multiple times around the legs. Where it opens in the front, the apparent rear appearance shows it to be perhaps a shell of some kind, as one with her body. Two squares are missing from her the back of her head and torso. She has no buttocks.]]

Ideas about women's sexuality were linked to contemporary understanding of female physiology. The [[vagina]] was considered an inward version of the penis; in lesbians, nature was thought to be trying to right itself by prolapsing the vagina to form a penis.<ref name="Jennings2007" />{{rp|p=12}}Consequently, [[Hermaphrodite|hermaphroditism]] was understood as synonymous with lesbianism. A longer, engorged clitoris was thought to be used in lesbian sex. Penetration was the focus of concern in all sexual acts, and a woman who was thought to have uncontrollable desires because of her engorged clitoris was called a ''tribade'' (literally, one who rubs).<ref name="Jennings2007" />{{rp|pp=14–16}} For a while, masturbation and lesbian sex carried the same meaning.<ref name="Aldrich2006" />{{rp|p=129}}

Tribades were simultaneously considered members of the lower class trying to ruin virtuous women, and representatives of an aristocracy corrupt with debauchery. Satirical writers began to suggest that political rivals (or more often, their wives) engaged in tribadism in order to harm their reputations. [[Anne, Queen of Great Britain|Queen Anne]] was rumored to have had passionate relationships with her courtier [[Abigail Masham, Baroness Masham]], and her close advisor [[Sarah Churchill, Duchess of Marlborough|Sarah Churchill]], Duchess of Marlborough.<ref>Gregg, pp. 275–276; Somerset, pp. 360–361; Waller, pp. 324–325</ref> When Churchill was ousted as the queen's favorite, she purportedly spread allegations of the queen having affairs with her bedchamberwomen.<ref name="Aldrich2006" />{{rp|p=137}}

Some historians, such as Valerie Traub, have argued that a period of acceptance led to increasing cultural sanctions against lesbian behaviors.{{sfn|Craft-Fairchild|2006|p=409}} For instance, in 1709, [[Delariviere Manley]] published ''The New Atlantis'', attacking lesbian activities.{{sfn|Craft-Fairchild|2006|p=413}} However, others, such as Friedli and [[Lillian Faderman]] have played down the cultural opposition to female homosexuality, pointing out that it was better tolerated than male homosexual activities.{{sfn|Craft-Fairchild|2006|p=408}}

Despite social stigma, English courts did not prosecute homosexual activities between women, and lesbianism was largely ignored by the law in England.{{sfn|Craft-Fairchild|2006|p=408}} Although, according to Henry Fielding, [[Mary Hamilton (transvestite)|Charles Hamilton (female husband)]] was whipped for fraud, the courts and the press of the time do not seem to have believed she committed any crimes.{{sfn|Craft-Fairchild|2006|p=418}} [[Terry Castle]] contends that English law in the eighteenth century ignored female homosexual activity not out of indifference, but out of male fears about acknowledging and reifying lesbianism.{{sfn|Craft-Fairchild|2006|p=409}}

[[Lady Catherine Jones]]' decision not to marry, and her close relationships and cohabitation with women throughout her life and into her death, merit speculation that she was a lesbian. The minimal surviving documentation of her life makes this difficult to assert with confidence, but readers can read her 'close unions' with Kendall and Astell as not entirely platonic.<ref>{{cite web |title=Richard Jones, Earl of Ranelagh |url=http://www.westminster-abbey.org/our-history/people/richard-jones,-earl-of-ranelagh |access-date=1 January 2018 |website=[[Westminster Abbey]] |archive-date=1 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180101194818/http://www.westminster-abbey.org/our-history/people/richard-jones,-earl-of-ranelagh |url-status=live}}</ref> Englishwoman [[Mary Frith]] has also been described as lesbian.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Chess |first1=Simone |title=Male-to-Female Crossdressing in Early Modern English Literature: Gender, Performance, and Queer Relations |date=2016 |page=16 |publisher=[[Routledge]] |location=New York |isbn=978-1138951211 |quote=(and Frith, by extension) has been described in scholarship as a roaring girl, a transvestite, a lesbian, and, more recently, as both (proto-) butch and transgender. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Z2z7CwAAQBAJ&pg=PA16}}</ref> In 1680, Arabella Hunt married a "James Howard." Their marriage was annulled two years later upon the discovery that "James Howard" was actually a woman, Amy Poulter.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mendelson |first=Sara H |date=3 January 2008 |title=Hunt, Arabella (1662–1705) |url=https://www.oxforddnb.com/display/10.1093/ref:odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-14190 |access-date=3 April 2026 |website=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography}}</ref>

Literature of the time attempted to rationalize some lesbian activities, commonly searching for visible indications of sapphic tendencies.{{sfn|Craft-Fairchild|2006|p=415}} In ''The New Atlantis'', the "real" lesbians are depicted as masculine.{{sfn|Craft-Fairchild|2006|p=415}} However, Catherine Craft-Fairchild argues in "Sexual and Textual Indeterminacy: Eighteenth-Century English Representations of Sapphism" (2006) that Delariviere Manley fails to establish a coherent narrative of lesbians as anatomically distinct from other women.{{sfn|Craft-Fairchild|2006|p=417}} In ''The Female Husband'', Fielding focuses on the corruption of Hamilton's mind.{{sfn|Craft-Fairchild|2006|p=420}} [[Jonathan Swift]], writing for ''[[The Tatler (1709 journal)|The Tatler]]'' in 1711, acknowledges the inherent difficulty in establishing such a narrative framework, by describing a woman having her virginity tested by a lion. Despite the onlookers' failure to detect anything amiss, the lion identified her as "no true Virgin."<ref>Jonathan Swift. ''Tatler'' no. 5, 1711</ref>{{sfn|Craft-Fairchild|2006|pp=420–421}}

During the same period, positive writings concerning female homosexuality drew on the languages of both female same-sex friendship and heterosexual romance.

==== 18th century ====
The term "lesbian" came into use in Britain during the 1730s.{{sfn|Bennett|2000}}

Two marriages between women were recorded in [[Cheshire]], England in 1707 (Hannah Wright and Anne Gaskill) and 1708 (Ane Norton and Alice Pickford), with no comment about both parties being female.<ref name="Jennings2007" />{{rp|p=30}}<ref name="Aldrich2006" />{{rp|p=136}}

In 1709, English aristocrat [[Lady Mary Wortley Montagu]] wrote to Anne Wortley: "Nobody was so entirely, so faithfully yours ... I put in your lovers, for I don't allow it possible for a man to be so sincere as I am."<ref name="Faderman1981" />{{rp|p=119}}

Poet [[Anna Seward]] had a devoted friendship with [[Honora Sneyd]]. Sneyd was the subject of many of Seward's poems. When Sneyd married despite Seward's protest, Seward's poems became angry, and she continued to write about Sneyd long after her death.<ref name="Faderman1981" />{{rp|pp=132–136}}

Writer and philosopher [[Mary Wollstonecraft]] was attached to a woman named [[Fanny Blood]]. Writing to another woman, Wollstonecraft declared, "The roses will bloom when there's peace in the breast, and the prospect of living with my Fanny gladdens my heart:—You know not how I love her."<ref name="Faderman1981" />{{rp|p=139}}{{refn|group=note|Wollstonecraft and Blood set up a girls' boarding school so they could live and work together, and Wollstonecraft named her first child after Blood. Wollstonecraft's first novel ''[[Mary: A Fiction]]'', in part, addressed her relationship with Fanny Blood.<ref name="Foster1956"/>{{rp|pp=55–60}}}}

[[File:Lister anne.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Anne Lister]]]]

==== 19th century ====
Diarist [[Anne Lister]] recorded her affairs with women between 1817 and 1840. Some of her diaries, detailing her sexual relationships with Marianna Belcombe and Maria Barlow, were written in code.<ref name="Castle2003">{{cite book |editor-last=Castle |editor-first=Terry |editor-link=Terry Castle |date=2003 |title=The Literature of Lesbianism: A Historical Anthology from Ariosto to Stonewall |publisher=[[Columbia University Press]] |isbn=0-231-12510-0}}</ref>{{rp|p=390}} She is sometimes considered the first modern lesbian.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=a6pmym6T5EkC&dq=anne+lister+first+modern+lesbian&pg=PA10 |isbn=9781452235288 |title=Finding Out: An Introduction to LGBT Studies |date=14 February 2013 |last1=Gibson |first1=Michelle A. |last2=Meem |first2=Deborah T. |last3=Alexander |first3=Jonathan |access-date=19 March 2023 |archive-date=12 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230412032859/https://books.google.com/books?id=a6pmym6T5EkC&dq=anne+lister+first+modern+lesbian&pg=PA10 |url-status=live}}</ref>

==== 20th century ====
[[Helen Boyle]], the first female GP in [[Brighton]], spent the last 17 years of her life with partner Marguerite du Pre Gore Lindsay.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Helen Boyle (1869-1957) |url=https://brightonmuseums.org.uk/discovery/history-stories/helen-boyle-1869-1957/ |access-date=2026-04-03 |website=Brighton & Hove Museums |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Louisa Martindale]], also a GP in Brighton, spent three decades with her female partner, Ismay FitzGerald, per her autobiography ''A Woman Surgeon''.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2011 |title=LGB&T Timeline |url=http://www.help.northwest.nhs.uk/lgbt_timeline/timeline.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110620181900/http://www.help.northwest.nhs.uk/lgbt_timeline/timeline.html |archive-date=20 June 2011 |access-date=3 April 2026 |website=NHS North West}}</ref>
[[File:Gwen Lally.jpg|thumb|[[Gwen Lally]]]]
Actress, pageant master, and theatre producer [[Gwen Lally]] was known for her masculine dress sense, and spent at least 40 years with partner Mabel Gibson.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Gwen Lally, Pageant Master |url=https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/1066-battle-of-hastings-abbey-and-battlefield/history-and-stories/gwen-lally/ |access-date=2026-04-03 |website=English Heritage}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Experiments in Gender: Women and Masculine Dress |url=https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/learn/histories/women-in-history/experiments-in-gender/ |access-date=2026-04-03 |website=English Heritage}}</ref>

A section to create an offence of "gross indecency" between females was added to a bill in the United Kingdom [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] and passed there in 1921, but was rejected in the [[House of Lords]], apparently because they were concerned any attention paid to sexual misconduct would also promote it.<ref name="Jennings2007" />{{rp|pp=109–114}}

Authors and lifelong friends [[Virginia Woolf]] and [[Vita Sackville-West]] were lovers between 1925 and 1935, exchanging extensive romantic correspondence.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=DeSalvo |first=Louise A. |date=1982 |title=Lighting the Cave: The Relationship between Vita Sackville-West and Virginia Woolf |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3173896 |journal=Signs |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=195–214 |issn=0097-9740}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Sackville-West |first=Vita |title=Love Letters: Vita and Virginia |last2=Woolf |first2=Virginia |publisher=Random House |isbn=9781473582408 |edition=1st |publication-date=4 February 2021}}</ref> In 1926, while vacationing in Milan, Sackville-West wrote the below letter to Woolf:<blockquote>I am reduced to a thing that wants Virginia. I composed a beautiful letter to you in the sleepless nightmare hours of the night, and it has all gone: I just miss you, in a quite simple desperate human way. You, with all your un-dumb letters, would never write so elementary phrase as that; perhaps you wouldn’t even feel it. And yet I believe you’ll be sensible of a little gap. But you’d clothe it in so exquisite a phrase that it would lose a little of its reality. Whereas with me it is quite stark: I miss you even more than I could have believed; and I was prepared to miss you a good deal. So this letter is just really a squeal of pain. It is incredible how essential to me you have become. I suppose you are accustomed to people saying these things. Damn you, spoilt creature; I shan’t make you love me any the more by giving myself away like this—But oh my dear, I ''can’t'' be clever and stand-offish with you: I love you too much for that. Too truly. You have no idea how stand-offish I can be with people I don’t love. I have brought it to a fine art. But you have broken down my defences. And I don’t really resent it …

Please forgive me for writing such a miserable letter.

V.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Woolf |first=Vita Sackville-West & Virginia |date=2016-03-09 |title=A Thing That Wants Virginia by Vita Sackville-West & Virginia Woolf |url=https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2016/03/09/a-thing-that-wants-virginia/ |access-date=2026-04-03 |website=The Paris Review |language=en}}</ref></blockquote>In a 1927 letter to Sackville-West, Woolf wrote, "Yes yes yes I do like you. I am afraid to write the stronger word."<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-02-01 |title=14 romantic quotes from the love letters of Virginia Woolf and Vita Sackville-West |url=https://www.penguin.co.uk/discover/articles/valentines-day-14-romantic-quotes-from-the-love-letters-of-virginia-woolf-and-vita-sackville-west/ |access-date=2026-04-03 |website=www.penguin.co.uk |language=en}}</ref>
[[File:George Charles Beresford - Virginia Woolf in 1902 - Restoration.jpg|thumb|[[Virginia Woolf]] in 1902]]
In the postwar period, a movement to eliminate homosexuals from public service positions began in the UK<ref name="Jennings2007" />{{rp|pp=109–114}} (as well as in Australia<ref name="Willett2000">{{cite book |last=Willett |first=Graham |date=2000 |title=Living Out Loud: A History of Gay and Lesbian Activism in Australia |publisher=[[Allen & Unwin]] |isbn=1-74115-113-9 |pages=10–11}}</ref> and Canada<ref name="Warner2002">{{cite book |last=Warner |first=Tom |date=2002 |title=Never Going Back: A History of Queer Activism in Canada |publisher=[[University of Toronto Press]] |isbn=0-8020-8460-5 |page=27}}</ref>).

British lesbians published the magazine ''[[Arena Three (magazine)|Arena Three]]'' beginning in 1964.<ref name="Jennings2007" />{{rp|pp=153–158}}

In 1974, [[Maureen Colquhoun]] came out as the first lesbian [[Member of Parliament|MP]] for the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] in the UK. When elected, she was in a heterosexual marriage.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.totalpolitics.com/print/1783/where-are-they-now-maureen-colquhoun.thtml |title=Where are they now: Maureen Colquhoun |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131214160313/http://www.totalpolitics.com/print/1783/where-are-they-now-maureen-colquhoun.thtml |archive-date=2013-12-14 }}</ref>

The pop singer [[Dusty Springfield]] dated women throughout her life, including American folk singer [[Norma Tanega]], photojournalist Faye Harris, musician [[Carole Pope]], and actress Teda Bracci.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Valentine |first=Penny |title=Dusty Springfield: The Authorized Biography |date=2001 |publisher=St. Martin's Press |others=Vicki Wickham |isbn=978-1-4668-7821-1 |edition=1st |location=New York}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Bartlett |first=Karen |title=Dusty: An Intimate Portrait of a Musical Legend |date=2014 |publisher=Biteback Publishing |isbn=978-1-84954-763-5 |location=New York}}</ref>

During the miners' strike from 1984 to 1985, lesbians organized in favor of Welsh miners as part of the activist group [[Lesbians and Gays Support the Miners]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-10-01 |title=Miners' strike: Valley community and gay activists' enduring friendships |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-wales-62998313 |access-date=2026-04-03 |language=en-GB}}</ref> A later group, [[Lesbians Against Pit Closures]], was formed after an ideological schism within Lesbians and Gays Support the Miners.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-01-31 |title=Lesbians and Gays Support the Miners in their protests for 'Coal not Dole' |url=https://unlockideas.wordpress.com/2014/01/31/lesbians-and-gays-support-the-miners-in-their-protests-for-coal-not-dole/ |access-date=2026-04-03 |website=Unlocking Ideas Worth Fighting For |language=en}}</ref> This story is dramatized in the 2014 film ''[[Pride (2014 film)|Pride]]''.[[File:Viola and the Countess - Frederick Richard Pickersgill.jpg|thumb|upright=0.8|Gender masquerade was a popular dramatic device in the 16th and 17th centuries, such as this scene of [[Viola (Twelfth Night)|Viola]] and [[Olivia (Twelfth Night)|Olivia]] from [[Shakespeare]]'s ''[[Twelfth Night]]'' painted by [[Frederick Pickersgill]] (1859).|alt=Painting of a Renaissance-era woman dressed as a man, standing and looking away, as a woman dressed as a woman holds the other's hand to her breast, looking imploringly at the other, set against a bucolic backdrop.]]

====In literature====
Homoerotic elements in early literature were pervasive, specifically the masquerade of one gender for another to seduce an unsuspecting woman. Such plot devices were used in ''[[Twelfth Night]]'' (1601), ''[[The Faerie Queene]]'' (1590), and ''[[The Bird in a Cage]]'' (1633).<ref name="Jennings2007" />{{rp|pp=1–11, 22–24}}

In 1928, Radclyffe Hall published the novel ''[[The Well of Loneliness]]''. The novel's plot centers around Stephen Gordon, an [[Sexual inversion (sexology)|invert]] woman. The novel was intended to be a call for tolerance for inverts by publicizing their disadvantages and lack of control over the condition.<ref name="Faderman1981" />{{rp|p=320}} The novel's trial for obscenity was described as "''the'' crystallizing moment in the construction of a visible modern English lesbian subculture" by professor Laura Doan.<ref name="Doan2001">{{cite book |last=Doan |first=Laura |date=2001 |title=Fashioning Sapphism: The Origins of a Modern English Lesbian Culture |publisher=[[Columbia University Press]] |isbn=0-231-11007-3 |pages=XIII, XV, 64–66}}</ref>
