Many women of the [[Gay liberation|Gay Liberation]] movement felt frustrated at the domination of the movement by men and formed separate organizations. Some who felt gender differences between men and women could not be resolved developed "[[lesbian separatism]]," influenced by writings such as [[Jill Johnston]]'s 1973 book ''[[Lesbian Nation]]''. Disagreements between different political philosophies, in particular over views on [[Feminist views on BDSM|sadomasochism]], [[Feminist views on prostitution|prostitution]] and [[Feminist views on transgender topics|transgenderism]], were, at times, extremely heated and became known as the [[lesbian sex wars]].<ref>[http://www.glbtq.com/social-sciences/lesbian_sex_wars.html Lesbian Sex Wars] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060321044928/http://www.glbtq.com/social-sciences/lesbian_sex_wars.html |date=2006-03-21 }}, article by Elise Chenier from GLBTQ encyclopedia.</ref> Pro-sex feminists argued against anti-pornography feminists, contending that a new way for female desire to be advertised and demonstrated was needed.<ref>Guy, Laura (2016). "Sex Wars Revisited". Aperture. 225: 54–59.</ref>

===Political lesbianism===
[[Political lesbianism]] originated in the late 1960s among second-wave [[radical feminists]] as a way to fight sexism and [[compulsory heterosexuality]], as detailed in [[Adrienne Rich]]'s essay "[[Compulsory Heterosexuality and Lesbian Existence]]." [[Sheila Jeffreys]], a lesbian, helped to develop the concept when she co-wrote "Love Your Enemy? The Debate Between Heterosexual Feminism and Political Lesbianism"<ref>{{cite web|last=Jeffreys|first=Sheila|title=Love Your Enemy? The Debate Between Heterosexual Feminism and Political Lesbianism|url=https://docs.google.com/file/d/0B3dD4VR6trTUMzYzZTExNmMtY2FlMC00MjlhLTg1ZjItYjFhNGMzMWNlMGIx/edit?authkey=CN6ixb8C&pli=1|access-date=2018-10-14|archive-date=2021-06-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210607073721/https://docs.google.com/file/d/0B3dD4VR6trTUMzYzZTExNmMtY2FlMC00MjlhLTg1ZjItYjFhNGMzMWNlMGIx/edit?authkey=CN6ixb8C&pli=1|url-status=live}}</ref> with the [[Leeds Revolutionary Feminist Group]]. They argued that women should abandon support of heterosexuality and stop sleeping with men, encouraging women to rid men "from your beds and your heads."<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2009/jan/30/women-gayrights |title=My sexual revolution |last=Bindel |first=Julie |newspaper=[[The Guardian]] |date=30 January 2009 |access-date=3 October 2012 |archive-date=7 August 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130807025250/http://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2009/jan/30/women-gayrights |url-status=live }}</ref> While the main idea of political lesbianism is to be separate from men, this does not necessarily mean that political lesbians ''have'' to sleep with women; some choose to be [[celibate]] or identify as [[asexuality|asexual]]. The Leeds Revolutionary Feminist Group definition of a political lesbian is "a woman identified woman who does not fuck men." They proclaimed men the enemy and women who were in relationships with them collaborators and complicit in their own oppression. Heterosexual behavior was seen as the basic unit of the [[patriarchy]]'s political structure, with lesbians who reject heterosexual behavior therefore disrupting the established political system.<ref>{{cite web|last=Bunch|first=Charlotte|title=Lesbians in Revolt|url=http://library.duke.edu/rubenstein/scriptorium/wlm/furies/|publisher=The Furies: Lesbian/Feminist Monthly|access-date=12 May 2014|archive-date=9 March 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130309191328/http://library.duke.edu/rubenstein/scriptorium/wlm/furies/|url-status=live}}</ref> Lesbian women who have identified themselves as "political lesbians" include [[Ti-Grace Atkinson]], [[Julie Bindel]], [[Charlotte Bunch]], [[Yvonne Rainer]], and Sheila Jeffreys.

===Lesbians of color===
[[File:NYC Pride Parade 2012 - 034 (7457177728).jpg|thumb|upright=0.7|Attendees at 2012 New York City [[Pride parade]]]]

"Lesbians of color" is an umbrella term for Black, Latina, Asian, Arab, Native American, and other non-white lesbians. Lesbians of color have often been a marginalized group,<ref name="Myers">{{cite book|last1=Myers |first1=JoAnne |title=Historical Dictionary of the Lesbian and Gay Liberation Movements |year=2013 |edition=1st |page=85 |chapter=Black Lesbians |publisher=[[Scarecrow Press]] |location=Lanham, Maryland |lccn=2019715841|isbn=978-0810872264}}</ref> and experience racism in addition to homophobia and misogyny.<ref name="Zimmerman2000">{{cite book |last=Zimmerman |first=Bonnie |author-link=Bonnie Zimmerman |title=Encyclopedia of Lesbian Histories and Cultures |date=2000 |edition=1st |publisher=[[Garland Publishing]] |location=New York |isbn=9780203825532 |url=https://archive.org/details/encyclopediaofle00bzim/page/747/mode/2up |url-access=registration}}</ref>{{page needed|date=January 2024}}

Some scholars have noted that past lesbian communities were primarily white and American, and that lesbians of color have had difficulties integrating into these communities at large. Many lesbians of color have stated that they have been systematically excluded from lesbian spaces based on the fact that they are women of color.<ref name="RuthR">{{Cite book |title=LGBT Psychology and Mental Health: Emerging Research and Advances |date=2017 |publisher=[[Praeger Publishing]] |isbn=978-1440843372 |editor1-last=Ruth |editor1-first=Richard |location=Santa Barbara, California |editor2-last=Santacruz |editor2-first=Erik}}</ref> The early lesbian feminist movement was criticized for excluding race and class issues from their spaces and for a lack of focus on issues that did not benefit white women.<ref name="Myers" />

Additionally, lesbians of color face unique sets of challenges within their respective racial communities, as communities of color often view homosexuality as a "white" lifestyle and see the acceptance of homosexuality as a setback in achieving equality.<ref name="Zimmerman2000" />{{page needed|date=January 2024}} Lesbians of color, especially those of immigrant populations, often hold the sentiment that their orientation adversely affects assimilation into the dominant culture.<ref name="Myers" /> Within racial communities, the decision to [[Coming out|come out]] can be costly, as the threat of loss of support from family, friends, and the community at large is probable. Lesbians of color are often exposed to a range of adverse consequences, including [[microaggression]]s, discrimination, and violence.<ref name="RuthR" />

[[Audre Lorde]], [[Barbara Smith]], and [[Cherrie Moraga]] are cited as major theorists within the various lesbians of color movements for their insistence on inclusion and equality among both communities of color and white lesbian communities.<ref name="Myers" />

Lesbians of color are more likely to experience mental illness and psychological distress due to their intersecting experiences of sexism, racism, and homophobia.<ref name="BridgesSK">{{Cite journal |last1=Bridges |first1=Sara K. |last2=Selvidge |first2=Mary M. D. |last3=Matthews |first3=Connie R. |date=April 2003 |title=Lesbian Women of Color: Therapeutic Issues and Challenges |journal=[[Journal of Multicultural Counseling and Development]] |volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=113–130 |doi=10.1002/j.2161-1912.2003.tb00537.x |issn=0883-8534}}</ref> Mental health providers often use [[Heteronormativity|heteronormative]] standards to gauge the health of lesbian relationships, and the relationships of lesbian women of color are often subjects of judgment because they are seen as the most deviant.<ref name="BridgesSK" />

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: History of water supply and sanitation
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=September 2026}}
[[Image:Qanat Kashan.jpg|thumb|[[Qanat]] in [[Kashan]] surfacing within the [[Fin (garden)|Fin Garden]]; it is thought to have served Iran's [[Sialk]] area for thousands of years.]]
Ever since the emergence of [[Sedentism|sedentary]] societies (often precipitated by the development of [[agriculture]]), [[human settlement]]s have had to contend with the closely-related [[Logistics|logistical]] challenges of [[sanitation]] and of reliably obtaining [[Water supply|clean water]]. Where water resources, infrastructure or sanitation systems were insufficient, diseases spread and people fell sick or died prematurely.
[[File:Showering on Skylab (9456594881).jpg|thumb|Astronaut Jack Lousma taking a shower in space, 1974]]
Major human settlements could initially develop only where fresh surface water was plentiful{{mdash}}for instance, in areas near rivers or [[Spring (hydrology)|natural springs]]. Over time, various societies devised a variety of systems which made it easier to obtain clean water or to dispose of (and, later, also treat) [[wastewater]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.academia.edu/22932774|title=The Art of Plumbing as Recorded through History|via=Academia.edu|access-date=10 March 2016}}{{dead link|date=April 2021|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

For much of this history, [[sewage treatment]] consisted in the conveyance of raw sewage to a natural body of water{{mdash}}such as a [[river]] or [[ocean]]{{mdash}}in which, after disposal, it would be diluted and eventually dissipate.

Over the course of millennia, technological advances have significantly increased the distances across which water can be practically transported. Similarly, treatment processes to purify [[drinking water]] and to treat wastewater have also improved.

{{TOC limit|3}}

==Prehistory==
[[File:Skara Brae house 1 5.jpg|thumb|right|[[Skara Brae]], a Neolithic village in [[Orkney]], Scotland, with what might have been [[Flush toilet|water-flushing toilets]], 3180–2500 BCE]]
 
During the [[Neolithic]] era, humans dug the first permanent [[water well]]s, from where vessels could be filled and carried by hand. Wells dug around 8500{{nbsp}}[[BCE]] have been found on Cyprus,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dawson |first=Helen |date=January 2015 |title=Deciphering the elements: Cultural meanings of water in an island setting |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311534774}}</ref> and 6500&nbsp;BCE in the [[Jezreel Valley]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Ashkenazi|first=Eli|title=Ancient well reveals secrets of first Jezreel Valley farmers|url=https://www.haaretz.com/news/national/ancient-well-reveals-secrets-of-first-jezreel-valley-farmers-1.476288|work=haaretz.com|publisher=Haaretz|access-date=26 March 2014|date=9 November 2012|archive-date=29 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140329061051/http://www.haaretz.com/news/national/ancient-well-reveals-secrets-of-first-jezreel-valley-farmers-1.476288|url-status=dead}}</ref> The size of human settlements was largely dependent on the amount of water available nearby.

A primitive indoor fresh- and wastewater system, consisting of two stone channels lined with tree bark, appears to have featured in the houses of [[Skara Brae]] and the [[Barnhouse Settlement]] in Orkney from around 3000 BCE Combined with a cell-like enclave in a number of houses at Skara Brae, it has been suggested that these may have functioned as an early indoor [[latrine]].<ref name="Pre">{{cite journal |last1=Childe |first1=V. |last2=Paterson |first2=J. |last3=Thomas |first3=Bryce |title=Provisional Report on the Excavations at Skara Brae, and on Finds from the 1927 and 1928 Campaigns. With a Report on Bones |journal=Proceedings of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland |date=30 November 1929 |volume=63 |pages=225–280 |doi=10.9750/PSAS.063.225.280 |s2cid=182466398 |url=http://journals.socantscot.org/index.php/psas/article/view/7758/7726 |access-date=6 May 2020 |archive-date=3 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201003105621/http://journals.socantscot.org/index.php/psas/article/view/7758/7726 |url-status=live |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Suddath |first1=Claire |title=A Brief History of Toilets |url=http://content.time.com/time/health/article/0,8599,1940525,00.html |access-date=6 May 2020 |agency=Time |publisher=Time |date=19 November 2009 |archive-date=19 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200219180926/http://content.time.com/time/health/article/0,8599,1940525,00.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Mark |first1=Joshua J. |title=Skara Brae |url=https://www.worldhistory.org/Skara_Brae/ |website=[[World History Encyclopedia]] |date=18 October 2012 |access-date=6 May 2020 |archive-date=28 September 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200928230454/https://www.ancient.eu/Skara_Brae/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Grant |first1=Walter G. |last2=Childe |first2=V. G. |title=A STONE-AGE SETTLEMENT AT THE BRAES OF RINYO, ROUSAY, ORKNEY. (FIRST REPORT.) |journal=Proceedings of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland |date=1938 |volume=72 |url=http://soas.is.ed.ac.uk/index.php/psas/article/download/8098/8066 |access-date=6 May 2020 |archive-date=3 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201003074231/http://soas.is.ed.ac.uk/index.php/psas/article/download/8098/8066 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Childe|first1=Vere Gordon|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XI4wAQAAIAAJ&q=drain|title=Skara Brae|last2=Clarke|first2=D. V.|publisher=H.M.S.O., previously: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner & Company, Limited|year=1931|location=UK|pages=12, 20, 28|isbn=9780114917555|language=en|access-date=25 May 2020|archive-date=19 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419172106/https://books.google.com/books?id=XI4wAQAAIAAJ&q=drain|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Wastewater reuse activities ===
Waste [[water reuse]] is an ancient practice connected to the development of sanitation provision.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www-wds.worldbank.org/external/default/WDSContentServer/WDSP/IB/1994/04/01/000009265_3961006165519/Rendered/PDF/multi_page.pdf|title=Reuse of wastewater in agriculture: A guide for planners|last2=Kalbermatten|first2=J. M.|last3=Bartone|first3=C. R.|last1=Khouri|first1=N|access-date=29 July 2016|archive-date=5 May 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200505225959/http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/435431468170669836/pdf/multi-page.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> Reuse of untreated [[municipal wastewater]] has been practiced for many centuries with the objective of diverting [[human waste]] outside of urban settlements. Likewise, land application of domestic wastewater is an old and common practice, which has gone through different stages of development.

Domestic wastewater was used for irrigation by ancient civilizations (e.g. [[Mesopotamia]]n, [[Indus Valley|Indus valley]], and [[Minoan civilization|Minoan]]) since the Bronze Age {{avoid wrap|({{circa|3200|1100}} BCE)}}.<ref>{{cite journal|last2=Snyder|first2=Shane A.|date=9 September 2015|title=Wastewater Treatment and Reuse: Past, Present, and Future|journal=Water|language=en|volume=7|issue=9|pages=4887–4895|doi=10.3390/w7094887|author1-link=Andreas N. Angelakis|last1=Angelakis|first1=Andreas N.|bibcode=2015Water...7.4887A |doi-access=free}}</ref> Thereafter, wastewater was used for [[Waste disposal|disposal]], [[irrigation]], and [[Fertilizer|fertilization]] by Hellenic civilizations and later by Romans in areas surrounding cities (e.g. Athens and Rome).<ref>{{cite journal|last2=Paranychianaki|first2=N. V.|last3=Angelakis|first3=A. N.|date=1 March 2007|title=Soil as a wastewater treatment system: historical development|journal=Water Science and Technology: Water Supply|language=en|volume=7|issue=1|pages=67–75|doi=10.2166/ws.2007.008|issn=1606-9749|last1=Tzanakakis|first1=V. E. |bibcode=2007WatSu...7...67T }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.oieau.fr/rome/france/expert/theme_3/shuval.htm|title=Wastewater recycling and reuse as a water source for Mediterranean countries: Hygienic and technological aspects|website=oieau.fr|last1=Shuval|first1=H|access-date=29 July 2016|archive-date=14 June 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150614021300/http://www.oieau.fr/rome/france/expert/theme_3/shuval.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Wastewater reuse und management in the Middle East and North Africa a case study of Jordan|date=2010|publisher=Univ.-Verl. der TU|isbn=978-3798322684|edition=[Online-Ausg.].|location=Berlin|last1=Ghneim|first1=Azmi}}</ref>

==Bronze and early Iron Ages==

=== Ancient Americas ===
In [[ancient Peru]], the [[Nazca culture|Nazca people]] employed a system of interconnected wells and an underground watercourse known as [[puquios]].{{citation needed|date=August 2024}}

The Mayans were the third earliest civilization to have employed a system of indoor plumbing using pressurized water.<ref name="Penn State"/>

===Ancient Near East===
{{See also|Qanats#Qanats by country}}

====Mesopotamia====
The Mesopotamians introduced clay sewer pipes around 4000 BCE, with the earliest examples found in the Temple of Bel at [[Nippur]] and at [[Eshnunna]],<ref name="FLUORIDATED WATER CONTROVERSY">{{cite book|last1=Burke|first1=Joseph|title=FLUORIDATED WATER CONTROVERSY|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fdIoDwAAQBAJ&q=The+Babylonians+introduced+the+world+to+clay+sewer+pipes,+c4000+BCE,+with+the+earliest+examples+found+in+the+Temple+of+Bel+at+Nippur+and+at+Eshnunna,+Babylonia.&pg=PA2|access-date=4 August 2017|isbn=9781365912870|date=24 April 2017|publisher=Lulu Press, Incorporated |archive-date=19 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419172047/https://books.google.com/books?id=fdIoDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA2&lpg=PA2&dq=The+Babylonians+introduced+the+world+to+clay+sewer+pipes%2C+c4000+BCE%2C+with+the+earliest+examples+found+in+the+Temple+of+Bel+at+Nippur+and+at+Eshnunna%2C+Babylonia.|url-status=live}}</ref> utilised to remove wastewater from sites, and capture rainwater, in wells. The city of [[Uruk]] also demonstrates the first examples of brick constructed [[latrine]]s, from 3200 BCE.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Mitchell|first=Piers D.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HU6rCwAAQBAJ&q=McMahon,+A.+in+Sanitation,+Latrines+and+Intestinal+Parasites+in+Past+Populations&pg=PA263|title=Sanitation, Latrines and Intestinal Parasites in Past Populations|date=3 March 2016|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-317-05953-0|pages=22|language=en|access-date=25 May 2020|archive-date=4 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201104021315/https://books.google.com/books?id=HU6rCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA263&lpg=PA263&dq=McMahon,+A.+in+Sanitation,+Latrines+and+Intestinal+Parasites+in+Past+Populations|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Wald|first=Chelsea|date=26 May 2016|title=The secret history of ancient toilets|url=http://www.nature.com/news/the-secret-history-of-ancient-toilets-1.19960|journal=Nature News|language=en|volume=533 |issue=7604 |pages=456–458 |doi=10.1038/533456a |pmid=27225101 |bibcode=2016Natur.533..456W |s2cid=4398699 |access-date=14 May 2020|archive-date=3 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200803093130/https://www.nature.com/news/the-secret-history-of-ancient-toilets-1.19960|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Clay pipes were later used in the [[Hittites|Hittite]] city of [[Hattusa]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Burney|first=Charles|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=azPl5Jzv930C&q=Hattusa+clay+pipes&pg=PA307|title=Historical Dictionary of the Hittites|date=19 April 2004|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-6564-8|language=en|access-date=25 May 2020|archive-date=7 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201107112919/https://books.google.com/books?id=azPl5Jzv930C&pg=PA307&lpg=PA307&dq=Hattusa+clay+pipes|url-status=live}}</ref> They had easily detachable and replaceable segments, and allowed for cleaning.

====Ancient Persia====
{{main|Traditional water sources of Persian antiquity}}
{{see also|Qanat|Ab anbar|Shushtar Historical Hydraulic System|Pillar of Gor}}

The first sanitation systems within [[prehistoric Iran]] were built near the city of [[Zabol]].<ref name="FLUORIDATED WATER CONTROVERSY" /> Persian [[qanat]]s and [[ab anbar]]s have been used for [[Traditional water sources of Persian antiquity|water supply and cooling]].

==== Ancient Egypt ====
The {{circa|2400 BCE}}, [[Pyramid of Sahure#Drainage system|Pyramid of Sahure]], and adjoining temple complex at [[Abusir]], was discovered to have a network of copper drainage pipes.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Bunson|first=Margaret|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-6EJ0G-4jyoC&q=Abusir+copper+pipe+ancient+egypt&pg=PA6|title=Encyclopedia of Ancient Egypt|date=14 May 2014|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-0997-8|pages=6|language=en|access-date=25 May 2020|archive-date=15 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200915065451/https://books.google.com/books?id=-6EJ0G-4jyoC&pg=PA6&lpg=PA6&dq=Abusir+copper+pipe+ancient+egypt|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Ancient East Asia===
====Ancient China ====
[[File:Model well, burial find, China, Han dynasty, 206 BC to 220 AD, earthenware - Östasiatiska museet, Stockholm - DSC09578.JPG|thumb|upright|A Chinese ceramic model of a well with a water [[pulley]] system, excavated from a tomb of the [[Han Dynasty]] (202 BCE – 220 CE) period]]

Some of the earliest evidence of water wells are located in China. The Neolithic Chinese discovered and made extensive use of deep drilled groundwater for drinking.{{citation needed|date=June 2019}} The Chinese text ''[[I Ching|The Book of Changes]]'', originally a divination text of the Western Zhou dynasty (1046–771 BCE), contains an entry describing how the ancient Chinese maintained their wells and protected their sources of water.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kuhn |first=Oliver |date=30 June 2004 |title=Ancient Chinese Drilling |url=https://csegrecorder.com/articles/view/ancient-chinese-drilling |journal=Canadian Society of Exploration Geophysicists |volume=29 |issue=6 |access-date=31 October 2017 |archive-date=9 April 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200409140550/https://csegrecorder.com/articles/view/ancient-chinese-drilling |url-status=live }}</ref> Archaeological evidence and old Chinese documents reveal that the prehistoric and ancient Chinese had the aptitude and skills for digging deep water wells for drinking water as early as 6000 to 7000 years ago.{{citation needed|date=June 2019}} A well excavated at the [[Hemudu culture|Hemedu]] excavation site was believed to have been built during the Neolithic era.<ref name="Chang 2012 31">{{Cite book |title=Forest Hydrology: An Introduction to Water and Forests |last= Chang  |first=Mingteh |publisher= CRC Press |year=2012 |isbn= 978-1439879948 |edition=3rd |publication-date=1 November 2012 |page=31}}</ref> The well was constructed with four rows of logs with a square frame attached to them at the top of the well. Sixty additional tile wells southwest of Beijing are also believed to have been built around 600{{nbsp}}BCE for drinking and irrigation.<ref name="Chang 2012 31" /><ref>{{Cite news |title=How the ancient Chinese looked after their drinking water |last=Koon |first=Wee Kek |date=25 July 2015 |url=https://www.scmp.com/magazines/post-magazine/article/1843012/how-ancient-chinese-looked-after-their-drinking-water |work=South China Morning Post |location=Hong Kong}}</ref> Plumbing is also known to have been used in [[East Asia]] since the [[Qin dynasty|Qin]] and [[Han Dynasty|Han]] Dynasties of China.<ref>{{cite web |last=Chavalas |first=Mark |title=Great Events from History: The Ancient World, Prehistory-476 C.E. |url=http://salempress.com/store/samples/great_events_from_history_ancient_world/great_events_from_history_ancient_world_qin.htm|access-date=4 May 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140504070918/http://salempress.com/store/samples/great_events_from_history_ancient_world/great_events_from_history_ancient_world_qin.htm |archive-date=4 May 2014 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== Indus Valley Civilization ===
{{Further|Sanitation of the Indus Valley Civilisation}}
[[File:WellAndBathingPlatforms-Harappa.jpg|right|thumb|A large well and bathing platforms at [[Harappa]], remains of the city's final phase of occupation from 2200 to 1900{{nbsp}}BCE]]
[[File:Lothal - bathroom structure.jpg|thumb|The bathroom-toilet structure of the ruler's house, on [[Lothal]]'s acropolis {{circa|2350 BCE}}]]
[[File:The drainage system at Lothal 2.JPG|thumb|Bathing platform and communal drain, [[Lothal]]'s acropolis, {{circa|2350 BCE|lk=no}}]]
[[File:Lothal - ancient well.jpg|thumb|Well, and drain, [[Lothal]]'s acropolis, {{circa|2350 BCE|lk=no}}]]
The [[Indus Valley civilization]] in Asia shows early evidence of public water supply and sanitation. The system the Indus developed and managed included a number of advanced features. An exceptional example is the Indus city of [[Lothal]] ({{circa|2350|1810 BCE}}).<ref>{{Cite web|title=Imagining Life in Lothal {{!}} Harappa|url=https://www.harappa.com/blog/imagining-life-lothal|access-date=20 February 2022|website=harappa.com}}</ref> In Lothal, the ruler's house had their own private bathing platform and latrine, which was connected to an open street drain that discharged into the town's dock. A number of the other houses of the acropolis had burnished brick bathing platforms, that drained into a covered brick sewer, held together with a gypsum-based mortar, that ran to a [[cesspit|soak pit]] outside the towns walls, while the lower town offered soak jars (large buried urns, with a hole in the bottom to permit liquids to drain), the latter of which were regularly emptied and cleaned.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Khan |first1=Saifullah |title=1 Chapter 2 Sanitation and wastewater technologies in Harappa/Indus valley civilization ({{circa|2600|1900|lk=no}} BCE )|url=https://www.academia.edu/5937322|access-date=9 April 2015 |via=Academia.edu |archive-date=9 April 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200409140548/https://www.academia.edu/5937322 |url-status=live}}</ref> Water was supplied from two wells in the town, one in the acropolis, and the other on the edge of the dock.

The urban areas of the Indus Valley civilization included public and private baths.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Brady |date=26 August 2022 |title=Who Invented Indoor Plumbing? |url=https://www.fountainplumbinginc.com/who-invented-indoor-plumbing/ |access-date=11 November 2022 |website=fountainplumbinginc.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Sewage was disposed through underground drains built with precisely laid bricks, and a sophisticated water management system with numerous reservoirs was established. In the drainage systems, drains from houses were connected to wider public drains. Many of the buildings at Mohenjo-daro had two or more stories. Water from the roof and upper story bathrooms was carried through enclosed terracotta pipes or open chutes that emptied out onto the street drains.<ref>Rodda, J. C. and Ubertini, Lucio (2004). The Basis of Civilization – Water Science? p. 161. International Association of Hydrological Sciences (International Association of Hydrological Sciences Press 2004).</ref>

The earliest evidence of urban sanitation was seen in [[Harappa]], [[Mohenjo-daro]], and the recently discovered [[Rakhigarhi]] of Indus Valley civilization. This urban plan included the world's first urban sanitation systems. Within the city, individual homes or groups of homes obtained water from [[Water well|wells]]. From a room that appears to have been set aside for bathing, waste water was directed to covered drains, which lined the major streets.{{citation needed|date=August 2024}}

Devices such as [[shadoof]]s were used to lift water to ground level. Ruins from the Indus Valley Civilization like [[Mohenjo-daro]] in Pakistan and [[Dholavira]] in [[Gujarat]] in India had settlements with some of the ancient world's most sophisticated sewage systems.{{citation needed|date=June 2019}} They included drainage channels, [[rainwater harvesting]], and street ducts.

[[Stepwell]]s have mainly been used in the Indian subcontinent.

===Southern Europe===
==== Ancient Greece ====
The [[Minoan civilization]] of [[Crete]] built underground clay pipes for sanitation and water supply.<ref name="Crete0">{{cite journal | last1=Yannopoulos | first1=Stavros | last2=Yapijakis | first2=Christos | last3=Kaiafa-Saropoulou | first3=Asimina | last4=Antoniou | first4=George | last5=Angelakis | first5=Andreas N. | title=History of sanitation and hygiene technologies in the Hellenic world | journal=Journal of Water, Sanitation and Hygiene for Development | publisher=IWA Publishing | volume=7 | issue=2 | date=14 February 2017 | issn=2043-9083 | doi=10.2166/washdev.2017.178 | pages=163–180| bibcode=2017JWSHD...7..163Y | doi-access=free }}</ref> Their capital, [[Knossos]], had a well-organized water system for bringing in clean water, taking out waste water and storm sewage canals for overflow when there was heavy rain. One site possibly had a 16th-century BCE [[flush toilet]].{{r|Crete0}} These Minoan sanitation facilities were connected to stone sewers that were regularly flushed by rain, flowing in through the collection system.{{r|Crete0}} In addition to sophisticated water and sewer systems they devised elaborate heating systems. The Ancient Greeks of [[Athens]] and [[Asia Minor]] also used an indoor plumbing system, used for pressurized showers.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ancient Inventions Showers |url=http://www.inventions.org/culture/ancient/showers.html |work=inventions.org |access-date=26 March 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080509052435/http://www.inventions.org/culture/ancient/showers.html |archive-date=9 May 2008 }}</ref> The Greek inventor [[Hero of Alexandria|Heron]] used pressurized piping for firefighting purposes in the City of [[Alexandria]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Jaffe|first=Eric|title=Old World, High Tech|url=http://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/old-world-high-tech-141284744/?no-ist=|work=smithsonianmag.com|publisher=Smithsonian Magazine|access-date=26 March 2014|archive-date=9 April 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200409140614/http://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/old-world-high-tech-141284744/?no-ist=|url-status=live}}</ref>

An inverted siphon system, along with glass-covered clay pipes, was used for the first time in the palaces of Crete, Greece. It is still in working condition after about 3000 years.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Minoan Innovation |url=https://www.tinyepicshistory.com/minoan-innovation#:~:text=In%20addition%20to%20sophisticated%20water%20and%20sewer%20systems,still%20in%20working%20condition,%20after%20about%203000%20years. |access-date=4 January 2025 |website=Tiny Epics History |language=en}}</ref>

==== Roman Empire ====
{{Further|Sanitation in ancient Rome}}
[[File:Pont du Gard BLS.jpg|thumb|left|[[Pont du Gard]], a [[Roman aqueduct]] in France]]
In ancient Rome, the [[Cloaca Maxima]], considered a marvel of engineering, discharged into the [[Tiber]]. Public [[latrine]]s were built over the Cloaca Maxima.<ref name="about">{{cite web|title=The History of Toilets|url=http://inventors.about.com/od/pstartinventions/a/Plumbing_3.htm|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130116044250/http://inventors.about.com/od/pstartinventions/a/Plumbing_3.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=16 January 2013|access-date=29 December 2010|publisher=Mary Bellis}}</ref>

Beginning in the [[Imperial Roman|Roman era]] a [[water wheel]] device known as a [[noria]] supplied water to [[Aqueduct (water supply)|aqueducts]] and other water distribution systems in major cities in Europe and the Middle East.

The [[Roman Empire]] had [[Sanitation in Ancient Rome|indoor plumbing]], meaning a system of aqueducts and pipes that terminated in homes and at public wells and fountains for people to use. Rome and other nations used [[lead]] pipes; while commonly thought to be the cause of lead poisoning in the Roman Empire, the combination of running water which did not stay in contact with the pipe for long and the deposition of [[Fouling|precipitation scale]] actually mitigated the risk from lead pipes.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://penelope.uchicago.edu/~grout/encyclopaedia_romana/wine/leadpoisoning.html |title=Lead Poisoning and Rome |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |access-date=4 June 2013 |archive-date=26 May 2012 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120526104339/http://penelope.uchicago.edu/~grout/encyclopaedia_romana/wine/leadpoisoning.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Hodge |first=A. Trevor |date=1992 |title=Roman Aqueducts & Water Supply |location=London |publisher=Duckworth |isbn=0-7156-2194-7 |page=308}}</ref>

Towns and garrisons in the [[Roman Britain]] (between 46 BCE and 410{{nbsp}}[[Common Era|CE]]) had complex water supply and sewer networks. Supply pipes were often lead but could also be wooden with iron-ring reinforcement at intervals, and some were hollowed logs, jointed together.<ref>{{cite book |title=Romano-British Buildings and Earthworks |last=Ward|first= John| publisher=Methuen & Co. |location=London |date=1911 |pages=280–281 |chapter=XI. Construction § Water Supply |url= https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Gazetteer/Places/Europe/Great_Britain/_Periods/Roman/_Texts/WARRBE/11*.html |via=LacusCurtius}}</ref> Stone-lined drains connected to sometimes massive sewer tunnels, such as at York.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Buckland |first1=Paul Christopher |title=The environmental evidence from the Church Street Roman sewer system |date=1976 |publisher=Council for British archaeology |isbn=978-0-900312-41-0 |url=https://www.collections.yorkarchaeologicaltrust.co.uk/files/original/74479/GB2837-PUB-AY-14-01_The-Environtmental-Evidence-from-the-Church-Street-Sewer_P-C-Buckland.pdf}}</ref> Latrines, such as those for the Hadrian's Wall garrison located at [[Housesteads Roman Fort|Housesteads]] were flushed with collected standing or rainwater.<ref>{{multiref2|1={{cite web|ref=none |title=7 Ingenious Ideas From Roman Britain |url=https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/inspire-me/ingenious/roman-ingenuity/ |website=English Heritage}}|2={{cite web |title=Housesteads. Latrines |url=https://www.odysseyadventures.ca/articles/hadrian-wall/article_hadrianswall-housesteads-lat.htm |website=Odyssey Adventures in Archaeology|ref=none}} }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Read |first1=Geoffrey F. |editor1=Geoffrey F. Read |others=With assistant editor Ian G. Vickridge |title=Sewers: Rehabilitation and New Construction |volume=1: ''Repair and Renovation'' |date=1995 |publisher=Arnold |location=London; New York |isbn=9780340544723 |pages=1–21 |language=en |chapter=The Development of Public Health Engineering}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Utilities: Scheduling Selection Guide |date=2018 |publisher=Historic England |location=Swindon, UK |pages=2–4, 13 |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/images-books/publications/dssg-utilities/heag255-utilities-ssg/ |chapter=Historical Summary: § Roman" "Considerations by Period: § Roman}}</ref>

==Medieval and early modern ages==
===Nepal===
[[File:In line for water in Kathmandu 3514396453.jpg|left|thumb|People waiting in line for water from Manga Hiti in the city of [[Patan, Nepal|Patan]], Nepal]]
{{main|Dhunge dhara}}
In Nepal the construction of water conduits like drinking fountains and wells is considered a pious act.<ref name="UNHABITAT2007">[http://un.info.np/Net/NeoDocs/View/6229 UN-HABITAT, 2007. Water Movement in Patan with reference to Traditional Stone Spouts] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210322165449/https://un.info.np/Net/NeoDocs/View/6229 |date=22 March 2021 }}, {{ISBN|9789937203913}}</ref><ref name="jvs-GWP">{{citation|mode=cs1|last=Shresthra|first=Vijaya|url=https://jvs-nwp.org.np/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/Water-Nepal-A-historical-Perspective.pdf |chapter=Drinking Water Harvesting and Management Tradition in Nepal|title=Water Nepal: A Historical Perspective |pages=15–20 |publisher=GWP Nepal; JVS |editor=((Jalsrot Vikas Sanstha (JVS)))|date=September 2018|archive-date=14 March 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240314160123/https://jvs-nwp.org.np/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/Water-Nepal-A-historical-Perspective.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

A drinking water supply system was developed starting at least as early as 550 AD.<ref name="Disaster2012">[http://www.r-dmuch.jp/en/project/dl_files/report/2012+03+KTM+Final+Report.pdf Disaster Risk Management for the Historic City of Patan, Nepal] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210111071619/http://www.r-dmuch.jp/en/project/dl_files/report/2012+03+KTM+Final+Report.pdf |date=11 January 2021 }} by Rits-DMUCH, Ritsumeikan University, Kyoto, Japan and Institute of Engineering, Tribhuvan University, Kathmandu, Nepal, 2012, retrieved 16 September 2019</ref> This ''[[dhunge dhara]]'' or ''hiti'' system consists of carved stone fountains through which water flows uninterrupted from underground sources. These are supported by numerous ponds and canals that form an elaborate network of water bodies, created as a water resource during the dry season and to help alleviate the water pressure caused by the monsoon rains. After the introduction of modern, piped water systems, starting in the late 19th century, this old system has fallen into disrepair and some parts of it are lost forever.{{r|UNHABITAT2007|jvs-GWP}} Nevertheless, many people of Nepal still rely on the old hitis on a daily basis.<ref name="ngoforum2010">[http://www.ngoforum.net/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=9800 Traditional stonespouts] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220706224213/http://www.ngoforum.net/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=9800 |date=6 July 2022 }}, Posted by Administrator of NGOforum.net, 28 September 2010. Retrieved 6 September 2019.</ref>

In 2008 the dhunge dharas of the Kathmandu Valley produced 2.95 million [[litre]]s of water per day.<ref name="Groundwater2012">[http://people.ucalgary.ca/~hayashi/kathmandu_2016/reading/Shrestha_etal_2012_KVGW.pdf Kathmandu Valley Groundwater Outlook] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210322165441/http://people.ucalgary.ca/~hayashi/kathmandu_2016/reading/Shrestha_etal_2012_KVGW.pdf |date=22 March 2021 }}. Shrestha S., Pradhananga D., Pandey V.P. (Eds.), 2012, Asian Institute of Technology (AIT), The Small Earth Nepal (SEN), Center of Research for Environment Energy and Water (CREEW), International Research Center for River Basin Environment-University of Yamanashi (ICRE-UY), Kathmandu, Nepal</ref>

Of the 389 stone spouts found in the Kathmandu Valley in 2010, 233 were still in use, serving about 10% of Kathmandu's population. 68 had gone dry, 45 were lost entirely and 43 were connected to the municipal water supply instead of their original source.{{r|ngoforum2010}}

===Islamic world===
[[File:Comares Bath (5921125878).jpg|thumb|The Comares Baths at the [[Alhambra]] in [[Granada]], Spain (14th century)]]
Islam stresses the importance of cleanliness and personal hygiene.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Majeed |first1=Azeem |title=How Islam changed medicine |journal=BMJ |date=22 December 2005 |volume=331 |issue=7531 |pages=1486–1487 |doi=10.1136/bmj.331.7531.1486 |pmid=16373721 |pmc=1322233 |language=en |issn=0959-8138}}</ref> [[Islamic hygienical jurisprudence]], which dates back to the 7th century, has a number of elaborate rules. Taharah (ritual purity) involves performing [[wudu]] (ablution) for the five daily [[salah]] (prayers), as well as regularly performing [[ghusl]] (bathing), which led to [[Turkish bath|bathhouses]] being built across the [[Islamic world]].<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/tahara-Islam | title=Ṭahāra &#124; Islam | encyclopedia=Encyclopædia Britannica | access-date=7 September 2019 | archive-date=16 March 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200316051842/https://www.britannica.com/topic/tahara-Islam | url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Ṭahāra |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/tahara-Islam |website=Encyclopædia Britannica |access-date=7 September 2019 |archive-date=16 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200316051842/https://www.britannica.com/topic/tahara-Islam |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Islamic toilet etiquette|Islamic toilet hygiene]] also requires [[Anal cleansing|washing with water]] after using the toilet, for purity and to minimize germs.<ref>{{citation |author=Israr Hasan |year=2006 |title=Muslims in America |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k5J493fDF38C&pg=PA144 |isbn=978-1-4259-4243-4 |page=144 |publisher=AuthorHouse |access-date=25 May 2020 |archive-date=7 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201107183740/https://books.google.com/books?id=k5J493fDF38C&pg=PA144 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In the [[Abbasid Caliphate]] (8th–13th centuries), its capital city of [[Baghdad]] (Iraq) had 65,000 baths, along with a sewer system.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Judith Kidd |author2=Rosemary Rees |author3=Ruth Tudor |year=2000 |title=Life in Medieval Times |publisher=Heinemann |isbn=0435325949 |page=165 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J5wtyi4-GsgC&pg=PA165 |access-date=7 September 2019 |archive-date=27 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200727121051/https://books.google.com/books?id=J5wtyi4-GsgC&pg=PA165 |url-status=live }}</ref> Cities of the [[medieval Islamic world]] had [[water supply system]]s powered by [[hydraulic]] technology that supplied [[drinking water]] along with much greater quantities of water for ritual washing, mainly in [[mosques]] and [[Turkish bath|hammams]] (baths). Bathing establishments in various cities were rated by Arabic writers in [[travel guide]]s. Medieval Islamic cities such as Baghdad, [[Córdoba, Spain|Córdoba]] ([[Islamic Spain]]), [[Fez, Morocco|Fez]] (Morocco) and [[Fustat]] (Egypt) also had sophisticated [[waste disposal]] and [[sewage system]]s.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Nizamoglu |first1=Cem |title=Pro-Environmental Practices in Muslim Civilization |magazine=Muslim Heritage |date=6 November 2021 |url=https://muslimheritage.com/pro-environmental/ |publisher=FSTC Ltd; Foundation for Science, Technology and Civilisation, UK }}</ref> The city of Fustat also had multi-storey [[tenement]] buildings (with up to six floors) with [[flush toilet]]s, which were connected to a water supply system, and [[flue]]s on each floor carrying waste to underground channels.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Colin Chant, David Goodman |title=Pre-Industrial Cities and Technology |date=2005 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=1134636202 |pages=136–138 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hK-EAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA136 |access-date=7 September 2019 |archive-date=27 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200727122533/https://books.google.com/books?id=hK-EAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA136 |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Al-Karaji]] ({{circa|953|1029|lk=no}}) wrote a book, ''The Extraction of Hidden Waters'', which presented ground-breaking ideas and descriptions of hydrological and hydrogeological perceptions such as components of the hydrological cycle, groundwater quality, and driving factors of groundwater flow. He also gave an early description of a [[water filtration]] process.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ataie-Ashtiani |first1=Behzad |last2=Simmons |first2=Craig T. |title=The millennium old hydrogeology textbook The Extraction of Hidden Waters by the Persian mathematician and engineer Abubakr Mohammad Karaji ({{circa|53|1029}}) |journal=Hydrology and Earth System Sciences Discussions |date=15 August 2019 |pages=1–19 |doi=10.5194/hess-2019-407 |language=en |issn=1027-5606|doi-access=free }}</ref>

As the [[Islamic Golden Age]] waned and in later times, both Arab and European scholars criticised the condition of canals, streets and waterways at certain urban locations in Egypt. The Egyptian physician [[Ali ibn Ridwan]] wrote in the 11th century "the people of al-Fustat are in the habit of throwing whatever dies in their homes{{nbsp}}... out into the streets and alleys where they decay, and their corruption mixes with the air.{{nbsp}}... The sewers from their latrines also empty into the Nile. When the flow of water is cut off, the people drink this corruption mingled with the water".<ref>{{cite book |translator-last=Dole |translator-first= Michael W. |others=Introduction by Michael Dole |title=Medieval Islamic Medicine: Ibn Ridwan's Treatise "On the Prevention of Bodily Ills in Egypt" |date= 1984 |editor-last= Gamal |editor-first= Adil S. |language=en |doi=10.1525/9780520350953 |isbn=978-0-520-35095-3  |publisher=University of California Press |pages=105–106 |url=https://archive.org/details/AdilS.GamalMichaelW.DolsMedievalIslamicMedicineIbnRidwansTreatiseOnThePrevention/page/n117/mode/2up }}</ref> The 18th-century French Consul in Egypt, De Pauw, blamed the abandonment of the embalming practices of the Ancient Egyptians and the unsuitability of modern burial practices for the Nile delta for the area becoming "a hotbed of the plague".<ref>{{Cite book |title=A History of Epidemics in Britain: From A.D. 664 to the Extinction of Plague|first=Charles |last=Creighton |publisher=Cambridge University Press |date=1891 |url=https://www.gutenberg.org/files/42686/42686-h/42686-h.htm#CHAPTER_III |access-date=20 April 2024 |via=Project Gutenberg |page=158}}</ref> Some colonial commentary of this kind seemed informed by attitudes underpinning the ruling powers. For instance, the British doctor J. W Simpson wrote in 1883 "the residents of Damietta [Egypt] have little respect for water, contaminating the Nile and its canals{{nbsp}}... Arabs do not know mud from clean water"; the historians Schultz, Hipwood and Lee, writing in 2023, conclude the tenor of Simspson's report "reinforces the British colonial view of Egyptians as inferior to European colonisers".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Schultz |first1=Alexandra |last2=Hipwood |first2=Tara |last3=Lee |first3=Seyeon |title=Preserving home: Resistance to cholera sanitation procedures in Egypt |journal= Architecture_MPS|date=March 2023 |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=4 |doi=10.14324/111.444.amps.2023v24i1.003 |issn=2050-9006 |quote= Less than a year after the British occupation of Egypt in 1882, cholera struck in late June 1883. The country experienced three subsequent epidemics in 1895–96, 1902 and 1947. Over the course of these four epidemics, the British colonial government and its agencies closed access to water resources, forcibly entered homes and removed sick people from their families, ostensibly to prevent the spread of the disease. Concerns for the public’s health served as a convenient pretext to practice emergency sanitary measures which were cheaper than comprehensive reform and reinforced the British colonial view of Egyptians as inferior to European colonisers. Public health measures also supported subsidiary goals to control water, control bodies and police the private spaces of the home. The British characterisation of Egyptian water practice and home sanitation as unclean, even dirty, underpinned these methods, even though proper sanitation had always been an important part of Egyptian and Ottoman culture.|doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Sub-Saharan Africa===
In post-classical [[Kilwa Kisiwani|Kilwa]], plumbing was prevalent in the stone homes of the natives.<ref>The Travels of Ibn Battuta</ref>{{r|Cartwright 2019}} The Husani Kubwa Palace, as well as other buildings for the ruling elite and wealthy, included the luxury of indoor plumbing.<ref name="Cartwright 2019">{{Cite encyclopedia|last=Cartwright|first=Mark|url=https://www.worldhistory.org/Kilwa/=false|encyclopedia=[[World History Encyclopedia]]|title=Kilwa|date=29 March 2019|access-date=13 September 2020|archive-date=19 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419172058/https://www.worldhistory.org/Kilwa/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In the [[Ashanti Empire]], toilets were housed in two story buildings that were flushed with gallons of boiling water.

===Medieval Europe===
[[File:Agkistro Byzantine bath.jpg|thumb|[[Agkistro]] Byzantine bath]]
[[File:Wismarer Wasserkunst.jpg|thumb|right|Waterworks (''Wasserkunst'') and fountain from 1602 in [[Wismar]], Germany]]
Christianity places an [[Ablution in Christianity|emphasis on hygiene]].<ref name="Squatriti">{{cite book|last=Warsh|first=Cheryl Krasnick|title=Children's Health Issues in Historical Perspective|publisher=Wilfrid Laurier Univ. Press|others=Veronica Strong-Boag|year=2006|isbn=978-0-88920-912-1|page=315|quote=... Thus bathing also was considered a part of good health practice. For example, Tertullian attended the baths and believed them hygienic. Clement of Alexandria, while condemning excesses, had given guidelines for Christian] who wished to attend the baths ...}}</ref> Despite the denunciation of the [[mixed bathing]] style of Roman pools by [[early Christian]] clergy, as well as the pagan custom of women naked bathing in front of men, this did not stop the Church from urging its followers to go to public baths for bathing,<ref name="Squatriti" /> which contributed to hygiene and good health according to the [[Church Father]]s, [[Clement of Alexandria]] and [[Tertullian]].<ref name="Mary Thurlkill">{{cite book|last=Thurlkill|first=Mary|title=Sacred Scents in Early Christianity and Islam: Studies in Body and Religion|publisher=Rowman & Littlefield|year=2016|isbn=978-0-7391-7453-1|pages=6–11|quote=... Clement of Alexandria (died {{circa|215 CE}}) allowed that bathing contributed to good health and hygiene ... Christian skeptics could not easily dissuade the baths' practical popularity, however; popes continued to build baths situated within church basilicas and monasteries throughout the early medieval period ...}}</ref><ref name="Paolo Squatriti">{{cite book|last=Squatriti|first=Paolo|title=Water and Society in Early Medieval Italy, AD 400–1000, Parti 400–1000|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2002|isbn=978-0-521-52206-9|page=54|quote=... but baths were normally considered therapeutic until the days of Gregory the Great, who understood virtuous bathing to be bathing "on account of the needs of body" ...}}</ref> The Church built [[public bathing]] facilities that were separate for both sexes near [[Christian monasticism|monasteries]] and pilgrimage sites; also, the [[popes]] situated baths within church [[basilica]]s and monasteries since the early Middle Ages.<ref name="Mary Thurlkill" /> Pope [[Gregory the Great]] urged his followers on value of [[bathing]] as a bodily need.<ref name="Paolo Squatriti" />

Contrary to popular belief, [[bathing]] and [[sanitation]] were not lost in Europe with the collapse of the [[Roman Empire]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.vlib.us/medieval/lectures/black_death.html|title=The Great Famine and the Black Death – 1315–1317, 1346–1351 – Lectures in Medieval History – Dr. Lynn H. Nelson, Emeritus Professor, Medieval History, KU|work=vlib.us}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.middle-ages.org.uk/middle-ages-hygiene.htm|title=Middle Ages Hygiene|work=middle-ages.org.uk}}</ref> [[Public bathing|Public bathhouses]] were common in medieval [[Christendom]] larger towns and cities such as [[Constantinople]], Paris, [[Regensburg]], Rome and [[Naples]].<ref>{{cite book|title=The Middle Ages: Facts and Fictions|first=Winston |last= Black|year= 2019| isbn=  9781440862328| page =61 |publisher=ABC-CLIO|quote=Public baths were common in the larger towns and cities of Europe by the twelfth century.}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Perception and Action in Medieval Europe|first=Harald|last=  Kleinschmidt|year= 2005| isbn=  9781843831464| page =61 |publisher=Boydell & Brewer}}</ref> And great bathhouses were built in [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine centers]] such as [[Constantinople]] and [[Antioch]].<ref>{{citation | editor-first = Alexander | editor-last = Kazhdan |editor-link=Alexander Kazhdan | title = Oxford Dictionary of Byzantium | publisher = Oxford University Press | year = 1991 | isbn = 978-0-19-504652-6}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Kourkoutidou-Nikolaidou |first1=E. |last2=Tourta |first2=A. |date=1997 |title=Wandering in Byzantine Thessaloniki |publisher=Kapon Editions |isbn=960-7254-47-3 |page=87}}</ref>

There is little record of other sanitation systems (apart from [[sanitation in ancient Rome]]) in most of Europe until the [[High Middle Ages]]. Unsanitary conditions and overcrowding were widespread throughout Europe and Asia during the [[Middle Ages]]. This resulted in [[pandemic]]s such as the [[Plague of Justinian]] (541–542) and the [[Black Death]] (1347–1351), which killed tens of millions of people.<ref>Carlo M. Cipolla, ''Before the [[Industrial Revolution]]: European Society and Economy 1000—1700'', W.W. Norton and Company, London (1980) {{ISBN|0-393-95115-4}}</ref> Very high infant and child mortality prevailed in Europe throughout [[medieval]] times, due partly to deficiencies in sanitation.<ref>Burnett White, ''Natural History of Infectious Diseases''</ref>

In medieval European cities, small natural waterways used for carrying off [[wastewater]] were eventually covered over and functioned as sewers. London's [[River Fleet]] is such a system. Open drains, or gutters, for waste water run-off ran along the center of some streets. These were known as "kennels" (i.e., canals, channels), and in Paris were sometimes known as "split streets", as the wastewater running along the middle physically split the streets into two halves. The first closed sewer constructed in Paris was designed by Hugues Aubird in 1370 on [[Rue Montmartre]] (Montmartre Street) and was {{convert|300|m}} long. The original purpose of designing and constructing a closed sewer in Paris was less-so for waste management as much as it was to hold back the stench coming from the odorous waste water.<ref name="George Commair 2009">George Commair, "The Waste Water Network: and underground view of Paris," in ''Great Rivers History: Proceedings and Invited Papers for the EWRI Congress and History Symposium'', 17–19 May 2009, Kansas City, Missouri, ed. Jerry R. Roger, (Reston: American Society of Civil Engineers, 2009), 91–96</ref>

In [[Dubrovnik]], then known as Ragusa (Latin name), the Statute of 1272 set out the parameters for the construction of septic tanks and channels for the removal of dirty water. Throughout the 14th and 15th century the sewage system was built, and it is still operational today, with minor changes and repairs done in recent centuries.<ref>Medieval Sewerage of the City of Dubrovnik, Ivica Žile; Ministarstvo kulture Uprava za zaštitu kulturne baštine Konzervatorski odjel u Dubrovniku, 2007.</ref>

[[Pail closet]]s, [[outhouse]]s, and [[cesspit]]s were used to collect human waste. The use of human waste as [[fertilizer]] was especially important in China and Japan, where cattle manure was less available. However, most cities did not have a functioning sewer system before the [[Industrial era]],{{citation needed|date=January 2020}} relying instead on nearby rivers or occasional rain showers to wash away the sewage from the streets.{{citation needed|date=January 2020}} In some places, [[waste water]] simply ran down the streets, which had [[Step-stone bridge|stepping stones]] to keep pedestrians out of the muck, and eventually drained as runoff into the local watershed.{{citation needed|date=April 2016}}
[[File:Sir J. Harington, Diagram of the water-closet Wellcome M0012969.jpg|thumb|right|John Harington's toilet]]
In the 16th century, [[John Harington (writer)|Sir John Harington]] invented a flush toilet as a device for Queen [[Elizabeth I]] (his godmother) that released wastes into [[cesspool]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Sir John Harrington – inventor of the toilet or loo|url=https://www.historic-uk.com/CultureUK/The-Throne-of-Sir-John-Harrington/|access-date=16 August 2020|website=Historic UK|language=en-GB|archive-date=17 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200817041144/https://www.historic-uk.com/CultureUK/The-Throne-of-Sir-John-Harrington/|url-status=live}}</ref>

After the adoption of [[gunpowder]], municipal outhouses became an important source of raw material for the making of [[saltpeter]] in European countries.<ref>Firearms: A Global History to 1700, Kenneth Chase</ref>

In London, the contents of the city's outhouses were collected nightly by commissioned wagons and delivered to the nitrite beds where it was laid into specially designed soil beds to produce earth rich in mineral nitrates. The nitrate rich-earth would be then further processed to produce saltpeter, or [[potassium nitrate]], an important ingredient in [[black powder]] that played a part in the making of gunpowder.<ref>Instructions for the Manufacture of Saltpetre, Joseph LeConte, 1823–1901</ref>

===Classic and early modern Mesoamerica===
The [[Classic Maya]] at [[Palenque]] had underground aqueducts and [[flush toilet]]s; the Classic Maya even used household water filters using locally abundant limestone carved into a porous cylinder, made so as to work in a manner strikingly similar to Modern [[ceramic water filter]]s.<ref>{{cite book|title=Environmental and Water Resources Milestones in Engineering History|date= 15–19 March 2007|publisher=ASCE Publications|location=Tampa, Florida, US|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_tS1Zb_5KKsC&q=palenque+aqueduct+water+engineering&pg=PA73|isbn=9780784471968|access-date=15 May 2016|archive-date=19 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419172047/https://books.google.com/books?id=_tS1Zb_5KKsC&pg=PA73&lpg=PA73&dq=palenque+aqueduct+water+engineering|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Penn State">{{cite web|title=Maya plumbing: First pressurized water feature found in New World|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2010/05/100504155421.htm |date= 5 May 2010 |agency= Penn State |work=Science Daily|access-date=6 March 2014|archive-date=8 January 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190108035201/https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2010/05/100504155421.htm|url-status=live}}</ref>

In Spain and [[Spanish colonization of the Americas|Spanish America]], a community operated watercourse known as an [[acequia]], combined with a simple sand filtration system, provided [[potable]] water.

=== Sewage farms for disposal and irrigation===

“[[Sewage farm]]s" (i.e. wastewater application to the land for disposal and agricultural use) were operated in Bunzlau (Silesia) in 1531, in Edinburgh (Scotland) in 1650, in Paris (France) in 1868, in Berlin (Germany) in 1876 and in different parts of the US since 1871, where wastewater was used for beneficial crop production.<ref>{{cite book|url=http://www-wds.worldbank.org/external/default/WDSContentServer/WDSP/IB/1999/09/17/000178830_98101911161131/Rendered/PDF/multi_page.pdf|title=Wastewater Irrigation in Developing Countries: Health Effects and Technical Solutions|last2=Adin|first2=A|last3=Fattal|first3=B|last1=Shuval|first1=H.I|access-date=29 July 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=http://www.iwapublishing.com/books/9781780404844/evolution-sanitation-and-wastewater-technologies-through-centuries|title=Evolution of sanitation and wastewater technologies through the centuries|date=2014|publisher=IWA (International Water Association)|isbn=9781780404844|location=[S.l.]|access-date=21 March 2017|archive-date=4 May 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170504182308/http://www.iwapublishing.com/books/9781780404844/evolution-sanitation-and-wastewater-technologies-through-centuries|url-status=live}}</ref> In the following centuries (16th and 18th centuries) in many rapidly growing countries/cities of Europe (e.g. Germany, France) and the United States, "sewage farms" were increasingly seen as a solution for the disposal of large volumes of the wastewater, some of which are still in operation today.<ref>{{cite web|last2=Bahri|first2=A|last3=Brissaud|first3=F|last4=Angelakis|first4=A. N.|title=Wastewater Recycling and Reuse Practices in Mediterranean Region: Recommended Guidelines 2003|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228797648|last1=Kamizoulis|first1=G|access-date=29 July 2016|archive-date=19 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419172049/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228797648_Wastewater_recycling_and_reuse_practices_in_Mediterranean_region_Recommended_Guidelines|url-status=live}}</ref> Irrigation with sewage and other wastewater effluents has a long history also in China and India;<ref>{{cite book |last1=Vigneswaran |first1=Saravanamuthu |last2=Sundaravadivel |first2=M. |editor1=Saravanamuthu (Vigi) Vigneswaran |series=Encyclopedia of Life Support Systems|title=Wastewater Recycle, Reuse, and Reclamation |edition=eBook |isbn=978-1-905839-24-7 |pages=47–76 |publisher=UNESCO |url-access=limited |url=https://www.eolss.net/ebooklib/bookinfo/wastewater-recycle-reuse-reclamation.aspx |chapter=Recycle and Reuse of Domestic Wastewater |date=30 November 2009 |volume=1 |archive-date=10 January 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170110170943/http://www.eolss.net/ebooks/sample%20chapters/c07/e2-14-01.pdf |chapter-url=https://www.eolss.net/ebooks/sample%20chapters/c07/e2-14-01.pdf}}</ref> while also a large "sewage farm" was established in Melbourne, Australia, in 1897.<ref>{{cite book |title=Natural Systems for Waste Management and Treatment |last2=Crites |first2=Ronald |last3=Middlebrooks |first3=E. |publisher=McGraw-Hill Professional |isbn=9780071346627 |edition=2nd |language=en |last1=Reed |first1=Sherwood |date=August 1998}}</ref>

==Modern age==
===Water supply===
{{globalize|section|date=October 2025}}
[[London water supply infrastructure]] developed over many centuries from early mediaeval conduits, through major 19th-century treatment works built in response to [[cholera]] threats, to modern, large-scale reservoirs. An ambitious engineering project to bring fresh water from [[Hertfordshire]] to London was undertaken by [[Hugh Myddleton]], who oversaw the construction of the [[New River (London)|New River]] between 1609 and 1613. The [[New River Company]] became one of the largest private water companies of the time, supplying the [[City of London]] and other central areas.<ref name="waterhistory">{{cite web |url=http://www.waterhistory.org/histories/london/ |title=Water-related Infrastructure in Medieval London |publisher=waterhistory.org |access-date=24 March 2007 |archive-date=15 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141015013936/http://www.waterhistory.org/histories/london/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The first civic system of piped water in England was established in [[Derby]] in 1692, using wooden pipes,<ref>{{cite book |title=The Making of Home |author=Judith Flanders |publisher=Thomas Dunne Books |year=2014 |isbn=978-1-250-06735-7 |page=246}}</ref> which was common for several centuries.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.sewerhistory.org/photosgraphics/pipes-wood/ |title=The History of Sanitary Sewers - Pipes - Wood |access-date=15 April 2021 |archive-date=15 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210415071857/http://www.sewerhistory.org/photosgraphics/pipes-wood/ |url-status=usurped }}</ref> The Derby Waterworks included waterwheel-powered pumps for raising water out of the [[River Derwent, Derbyshire|River Derwent]] and storage tanks for distribution.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://engineering-timelines.com/who/Sorocold_G/sorocoldGeorge4.asp |title=George Sorocold – Derby Waterworks |access-date=15 April 2021 |archive-date=15 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210415071857/http://engineering-timelines.com/who/Sorocold_G/sorocoldGeorge4.asp |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Chelsea Waterworks 1752.jpg|thumb|left|[[Chelsea Waterworks Company|Chelsea Waterworks]], 1752. Two Newcomen beam engines pumped Thames water from a canal to reservoirs at [[Green Park]] and [[Hyde Park, London|Hyde Park]].]]
Until the [[Enlightenment era]], little progress was made in water supply and sanitation. It was in the 18th century that a rapidly growing population fueled a boom in the establishment of private water supply networks in [[London water supply infrastructure|London]].<ref name="ph.ucla.edu"/> The [[Chelsea Waterworks Company]] was established in 1723 "for the better supplying the [[City of Westminster|City]] and [[Liberty of Westminster|Liberties]] of [[Westminster]] and parts adjacent with water".<ref name="London Encyclopaedia">''The London Encyclopaedia'', Ben Weinreb & Christopher Hibbert, Macmillan, 1995, {{ISBN|0-333-57688-8}}</ref><ref>[http://www.privy-council.org.uk/output/page44.asp Royal Charters, Privy Council website] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070824225331/http://www.privy-council.org.uk/output/page44.asp |date=24 August 2007 }}</ref> The company created extensive ponds in the area bordering [[Chelsea, London|Chelsea]] and [[Pimlico]] using water from the [[Tideway|tidal Thames]]. Other waterworks were established in London, including at [[West Ham]] in 1743, at [[Lea Bridge]] before 1767, [[Lambeth Waterworks Company]] in 1785, [[West Middlesex Waterworks Company]] in 1806<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ph.ucla.edu/epi/snow/1859map/westmiddlesex_waterworks_a2.html |title=UCLA Department of Epidemiology ''West Middlesex Waterworks history'' |access-date=9 January 2014 |archive-date=14 March 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130314103158/http://www.ph.ucla.edu/epi/snow/1859map/westmiddlesex_waterworks_a2.html |url-status=live }}</ref> and [[Grand Junction Waterworks Company]] in 1811.<ref name="ph.ucla.edu">{{Cite web |url=http://www.ph.ucla.edu/epi/snow/1859map/lambeth_waterworks_a2.html |title=UCLA Department of Epidemiology ''Lambeth Waterwork history'' |access-date=9 January 2014 |archive-date=24 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924072219/http://www.ph.ucla.edu/epi/snow/1859map/lambeth_waterworks_a2.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The [[trap (plumbing)|S-bend]] [[pipe (material)|pipe]] was invented by [[Alexander Cummings]] in 1775 but became known as the U-bend following the introduction of the U-shaped trap by [[Thomas Crapper]] in 1880. The first screw-down [[Tap (valve)|water tap]] was patented, in 1845, by Guest and Chrimes, a brass foundry in [[Rotherham]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://plumber.whangarei.biz/a-little-about-tap-history/ |title=A Little About Tap History |access-date=17 December 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140109195319/http://plumber.whangarei.biz/a-little-about-tap-history/ |archive-date=9 January 2014 }}</ref> Maughan, of London, would develop the first instantaneous, gas powered, domestic water heater, in 1868.<ref>{{Cite web |last=CuriousHistory |date=18 October 2014 |title=How water heaters came into existence? |url=https://www.curioushistory.com/how-water-heaters-came-into-existence/ |access-date=25 April 2026 |language=en-US}}</ref> The Mixer tap being invented, by Thomas Campbell of [[Saint John, New Brunswick]], in 1880, to combine hot and cold water.<ref>Mario Theriault, ''Great Maritime Inventions 1833–1950'', Goose Lane, 2001, p. 33.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Two New Brunswick Inventions that Changed Our Lives |url=https://www.talesofourvillage.ca/bathroombrilliance |access-date=25 April 2026 |website=Tales of Our Village: Exploring Atlantic Canada’s History |language=en-CA}}</ref>

The first documented use of [[sand filter]]s to purify the water supply dates to 1804, when the owner of a bleachery in [[Paisley, Scotland]], John Gibb, installed an experimental filter, selling his unwanted surplus to the public. The first treated public water supply in the world was installed by engineer [[James Simpson (engineer)|James Simpson]] for the [[Chelsea Waterworks Company]] in London in 1829.<ref name="History of the Chelsea Waterworks" /> The practice of water treatment soon became mainstream, and the virtues of the system were made starkly apparent after the investigations of the physician [[John Snow (physician)|John Snow]] during the [[1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak]] demonstrated the role of the water supply in spreading the cholera epidemic.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=t1exE1cfKXIC&dq=%22institut+de+france%22+and+%22john+snow%22&pg=PA87 ''Concepts and practice of humanitarian medicine'' (2008) Par S. William Gunn, M. Masellis] {{ISBN|0-387-72263-7}} [https://books.google.com/books?id=NSHXLkgFBBQC&dq=%22institut+de+france%22+and+snow&pg=PA290]</ref>

=== Sewer systems===
A significant development was the construction of a network of [[Sewerage|sewers]] to collect wastewater. In some cities, including Rome, [[Istanbul]] ([[Constantinople]]) and [[Fustat]], networked ancient sewer systems continue to function today as collection systems for those cities' modernized sewer systems. Instead of flowing to a river or the sea, the pipes have been re-routed to modern sewer treatment facilities.

Before modern sewers were invented, cesspools that collected human waste were the most widely used sanitation system. In ancient [[Mesopotamia]], vertical shafts carried waste away into cesspools. Similar systems existed in the [[Indus Valley]] civilization in modern-day Pakistan and in Ancient [[Crete]] and Greece. In the [[Middle Ages]] waste was collected into cesspools that were periodically emptied by workers known as 'rakers' who would often sell it as [[fertilizer]] to farmers outside the city.

Archaeological discoveries have shown that some of the earliest sewer systems were developed in the third millennium BCE in the ancient cities of [[Harappa]] and [[Mohenjo-daro]] in present-day Pakistan. The primitive sewers were carved in the ground alongside buildings. This discovery reveals the conceptual understanding of waste disposal by early civilizations.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Webster|first=Cedric|date=February 1962|title=The Sewers of Mohenjo-Daro|journal=Journal (Water Pollution Control Federation)|volume=34|issue=2|pages=116–123|jstor=25034575}}</ref>

The tremendous [[Urbanization|growth of cities]] in Europe and North America during the [[Industrial Revolution]] quickly led to crowding, which acted as a constant source for the outbreak of disease.<ref name="Abellan">{{cite conference |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/319623260 |title=Water supply and sanitation services in modern Europe: developments in 19th–20th centuries |last1=Abellán |first1=Javier |date=2017 |location=University of Salamanca |conference=12th International Conference of the Spanish Association of Economic History }}</ref>{{Rp|4–8}} As cities grew in the 19th century concerns were raised about [[public health]].<ref name="Burian">{{cite journal |last1=Burian |first1=Steven J. |last2=Nix |first2=Stephan J. |last3=Pitt |first3=Robert E. |last4=Durrans |first4=S. Rocky |year=2000 |title=Urban Wastewater Management in the United States: Past, Present, and Future |url=http://www.sewerhistory.org/articles/whregion/urban_wwm_mgmt/urban_wwm_mgmt.pdf |journal=Journal of Urban Technology |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=33 |doi=10.1080/713684134 |s2cid=23561154 |archive-date=11 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170811224512/http://www.sewerhistory.org/articles/whregion/urban_wwm_mgmt/urban_wwm_mgmt.pdf |url-status=usurped}}</ref>{{rp|33–62}} As part of a trend of municipal [[sanitation]] programs in the late 19th and 20th centuries, many cities constructed extensive [[gravity sewer]] systems to help control outbreaks of [[disease]] such as [[typhoid]] and [[cholera]].<ref name="Staley1899">{{cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/separatesystems03piergoog |title=The Separate System of Sewerage, Its Theory and Construction |last2=Pierson |first2=George S. |publisher=Van Nostrand |year=1899 |location=New York |last1=Staley |first1=Cady |author-link1=Cady Staley}}</ref>{{Rp|29–34|date=May 2009}} [[storm drain|Storm]] and [[sanitary sewer]]s were necessarily developed along with the growth of cities. By the 1840s the luxury of [[indoor plumbing]], which mixes human waste with water and flushes it away, eliminated the need for [[cesspool]]s.

[[File:London Sewage system being built in 1860.jpg|thumb|The London sewer system being built in 1860 led by the chief engineer [[Joseph Bazalgette]] (top right)]]
Modern sewerage systems were first built in the mid-nineteenth century as a reaction to the exacerbation of sanitary conditions brought on by heavy [[industrialization]] and [[urbanization]]. Baldwin Latham, a British civil engineer contributed to the rationalization of sewerage and house drainage systems and was a pioneer in sanitary engineering. He developed the concept of oval sewage pipe to facilitate sewer drainage and to prevent sludge deposition and flooding.<ref name="Latham1878">{{cite book|author=Baldwin Latham|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LDoDAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA1|title=Sanitary engineering: A guide to the construction of works of sewerage and house drainage, with tables for facilitating the calculations of the engineer|publisher=E. & F.N. Spon|year=1878|page=1}}</ref> Due to the contaminated water supply, [[cholera]] outbreaks occurred in [[Cholera outbreaks and pandemics|1832, 1849 and 1855]] in London, killing tens of thousands of people. This, combined with the [[Great Stink]] of 1858, when the smell of untreated human waste in the [[River Thames]] became overpowering, and the report into sanitation reform of the [[royal commission]]er [[Edwin Chadwick]], led to the [[Metropolitan Commission of Sewers]] appointing engineer [[Joseph Bazalgette]] to construct a vast underground sewage system for the safe removal of waste.<ref>{{cite news |title=Story of cities #14: London's Great Stink heralds a wonder of the industrial world |url=https://www.theguardian.com/cities/2016/apr/04/story-cities-14-london-great-stink-river-thames-joseph-bazalgette-sewage-system |access-date=18 April 2025 |work=The Guardian}}</ref><ref name="Ashton-Ubido">{{cite journal |last=Ashton |first=John |author2=Ubido, Janet |year=1991 |title=The Healthy City and the Ecological Idea |url=http://www.johnrashton.securemachines.co.uk/documentbank/the%20healthy%20city%20and%20the%20ecological%20idea.pdf |url-status=dead |journal=Journal of the Society for the Social History of Medicine |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=173–181 |doi=10.1093/shm/4.1.173 |pmid=11622856 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224102422/http://www.johnrashton.securemachines.co.uk/documentbank/the%20healthy%20city%20and%20the%20ecological%20idea.pdf |archive-date=24 December 2013 |access-date=8 July 2013}}</ref> Contrary to Chadwick's recommendations, Bazalgette's system, and others later built in [[Continental Europe]], did not pump the sewage onto farm land for use as fertilizer; it was simply piped to a natural waterway away from population centres, and pumped back into the environment.

==== Liverpool, London and other places in the UK ====
[[File: The Prince of Wales opening the Metropolitan Main-drainage works at Crossness, ILN, 1865.JPG|thumb|upright|[[Edward VII|Edward, Prince of Wales]] opening Bazalgette's [[Crossness Pumping Station]], 1865]]
As recently as the late 19th-century, sewerage systems in some parts of the rapidly industrializing United Kingdom were so inadequate that [[water-borne disease]]s such as [[cholera]] and [[typhoid]] remained a risk. From as early as 1535, there were efforts to stop polluting the [[River Thames]] in London. Beginning with an Act passed that year that was to prohibit the dumping of excrement into the river. Leading up to the Industrial Revolution the River Thames was identified as being thick and black due to sewage, and it was even said that the river "smells like death".<ref>{{cite book|title="Filthy River" in Thames: Sacred River|date=2007|publisher=Nan A. Talese; Doubleday |location=New York|pages=270–275|last1=Ackroyd|first1=Peter}}</ref>

As Britain was the first country to industrialize, it was also the first to experience the disastrous consequences of major [[urbanisation|urbanization]] and was the first to construct a modern sewerage system to mitigate the resultant unsanitary conditions.<ref name="Abe">Abellán, Javier (2017). [https://www.academia.edu/34533153/Water_supply_and_sanitation_services_in_modern_Europe_developments_in_19th-20th_centuries "Water supply and sanitation services in modern Europe: developments in 19th–20th centuries"]. 12th International Congress of the Spanish Association of Economic History: University of Salamanca, Spain.</ref> During the early 19th century, the River Thames was effectively an open sewer, leading to frequent outbreaks of [[cholera]] epidemics. Proposals to modernize the sewerage system had been made during 1856, but were neglected due to lack of funds. However, after the ''[[Great Stink]]'' of 1858, [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|Parliament]] realized the urgency of the problem and resolved to create a modern sewerage system.{{r|Abellan|p=9}}

===== Liverpool =====
However, ten years earlier and 200 miles to the north, [[James Newlands]], a Scottish Engineer, was one of a celebrated trio of pioneering officers appointed under a private Act, the Liverpool Sanitory Act by the Borough of Liverpool Health of Towns Committee. The other officers appointed under the Act were William Henry Duncan, Medical Officer for Health, and Thomas Fresh, Inspector of Nuisances (an early antecedent of the environmental health officer). One of five applicants for the post, Newlands was appointed Borough Engineer of Liverpool on 26 January 1847.

He made a careful and exact survey of Liverpool and its surroundings, involving approximately 3,000 geodetical observations, and resulting in the construction of a contour map of the town and its neighbourhood, on a scale of one inch to 20 feet (6.1 m). From this elaborate survey Newlands proceeded to lay down a comprehensive system of outlet and contributory sewers, and main and subsidiary drains, to an aggregate extent of nearly 300 miles (480&nbsp;km). The details of this projected system he presented to the Corporation in April 1848.

In July 1848, James Newlands' sewer construction programme began, and over the next 11 years 86 miles (138&nbsp;km) of new sewers were built. Between 1856 and 1862, another 58 miles (93&nbsp;km) were added. This programme was completed in 1869. Before the sewers were built, life expectancy in Liverpool was 19 years, and by the time Newlands retired it had more than doubled.

===== London =====
[[File:Portrait of Sir Joseph William Bazalgette (1819-1891) Wellcome M0016460.jpg|thumb|upright|Bazalgette as the "Sewer Snake", ''[[Punch (magazine)|Punch]]'', 1883]]
[[Joseph Bazalgette]], a [[civil engineer]] and Chief Engineer of the [[Metropolitan Board of Works]], was given responsibility for [[London sewer system#History|similar work in London]]. According to the [[BBC]], "Bazalgette drove himself to the limits in realising his subterranean dream".<ref>{{cite news |title=London Sewers – Seven Wonders |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/england/sevenwonders/london/sewers_mm/index.shtml |access-date=17 April 2025 |publisher=BBC}}</ref> He designed an extensive underground sewerage system that diverted waste to the [[Thames Estuary]], downstream of the main center of population. Six main interceptor sewers, totaling almost 100 miles (160&nbsp;km) in length, were constructed, some incorporating stretches of [[Subterranean rivers of London|London's 'lost' rivers]]. Three of these sewers were north of the river, the southernmost, low-level one being incorporated in the [[Thames Embankment]].
